articles.paper_title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate

glossary.definition: A mechanism that lets a model, at each step, compute a weighted mix of all its inputs, putting more weight on the parts that matter most right now.
Which source words correspond to which target words in a translation, such as 'chat' lining up with 'cat'.
The paper's name for the vector the encoder produces for each source word, describing that word in the context of the whole sentence.
Two recurrent networks reading a sentence in opposite directions, so each word's vector reflects both what came before and what comes after.
The weighted average of all source annotations, recomputed for every target word, that the decoder uses to choose its next word.
A function that turns a list of scores into positive weights that add up to 1.

quiz.q: What problem with basic encoder-decoder translation did attention solve?
options: Every sentence had to be squeezed into one fixed-size vector, which hurt long sentences
The decoder could not generate words
quiz.explain: With attention, the decoder no longer depends on a single summary; it can consult every source word's annotation at every step.

quiz.q: How are the attention weights computed for one target word?
options: They are fixed by the programmer
A small network scores each source annotation against the decoder's current state, and a softmax turns the scores into weights
Words are weighted by their length
Only the first source word gets weight
quiz.explain: The scores depend on what the decoder needs right now, so the weights change for every word it produces.

quiz.q: What did the attention weights reveal when visualized?
options: Sensible word alignments between the two languages, including reordering, learned without any alignment labels
quiz.explain: The model learned which source words matched each output word, even where French and English order differ.

articles.excerpt: In the summer of 2014, a young researcher visiting Yoshua Bengio's lab in Montreal was frustrated. The new neural translation systems squeezed every sentence, however long, into a single vector before translating it. That felt wrong. No human translator memorizes a whole sentence, closes the book,…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Three Tricks That Made Word Vectors Cheap
articles.subtitle: Negative sampling, subsampling and phrases: the follow-up that turned word2vec into everyone's default
articles.paper_title: Distributed Representations of Words and Phrases and their Compositionality

glossary.definition: A word2vec model that learns a vector for each word by predicting the words around it in a sentence.
A function that turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1. Over a large vocabulary it needs one score per word, which is slow.
Training a word's vector to score its real neighbours high and a few randomly drawn words low, instead of computing probabilities over the whole vocabulary.
Randomly skipping very frequent words like 'the' during training, so the model spends its effort on informative words.
A group of words that means something different from its parts, like 'New York' or 'Air Canada', treated as a single token.
A function that squashes any number into the range 0 to 1, used here to turn a score into a yes-or-no probability.

quiz.q: What does negative sampling replace in skip-gram training?
options: A softmax over the entire vocabulary, which needed a score for every word
quiz.explain: Instead of normalising over hundreds of thousands of words, each step only scores the true neighbour and a handful of random 'negative' words.

quiz.q: With threshold t = 0.00001, a word making up 1% of all text is discarded with probability about 1 - sqrt(t/f). Roughly how often is it dropped?
quiz.explain: sqrt(0.00001 / 0.01) = sqrt(0.001) ≈ 0.032, so it is dropped about 97% of the time. Very common words rarely carry useful context.

quiz.q: Why treat 'Air Canada' as one token?
options: Its meaning is not the sum of 'air' and 'Canada', so it deserves its own vector
quiz.explain: An airline is not a kind of air or a part of Canada. Detecting such phrases lets the model learn a vector for what the phrase actually means.

articles.excerpt: In early 2013, a team at Google showed that simple models could learn word vectors with surprising structure: king minus man plus woman landed near queen. But the training still had an expensive step at its heart, and it treated "New York" as two unrelated words. A few months later, the same group…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Read It, Summarise It, Say It in French
articles.subtitle: The paper that paired two recurrent networks into an encoder-decoder and quietly introduced the GRU
articles.paper_title: Learning Phrase Representations using RNN Encoder-Decoder for Statistical Machine Translation

glossary.definition: Two networks working in sequence: the encoder reads an input sequence into a fixed-size vector, and the decoder generates an output sequence from that vector.
The single fixed-size vector the encoder produces after reading the whole input, often written c. It is the only thing the decoder knows about the input.
A number between 0 and 1 per hidden unit that decides how much of the old hidden state to keep and how much to replace with the new proposal.
A number between 0 and 1 per hidden unit that decides how much of the old hidden state to use when drafting the new proposal.
Statistical machine translation that cuts a sentence into short phrases, looks up translations for each in a phrase table, and picks the combination a weighted scoring formula likes best.
A scoring formula that adds up several feature scores, each multiplied by a tuned weight, to rank candidate translations.
An automatic translation metric that measures how many word sequences in the machine output also appear in human reference translations.

quiz.q: In this paper's main experiment, how was the encoder-decoder used?
options: As a complete translator that replaced the whole pipeline
To score existing phrase pairs, added as one more feature in a phrase-based system
Only as a language model over French sentences
To align words between the two languages
quiz.explain: The network scored each English-French phrase pair in the phrase table, and that score became an extra feature in the existing log-linear model.

quiz.q: In the paper's gated unit, what happens when the update gate is close to 1?
options: The old hidden state is wiped
The new proposal replaces the old state
The old hidden state is carried forward almost unchanged
quiz.explain: The new state is z times the old state plus (1 - z) times the proposal, so z near 1 keeps the old state.

quiz.q: Why did later work add attention to this design?
options: The decoder could not handle French
Squeezing a whole long sentence into one fixed-size vector loses detail
Gated units were too slow to train
BLEU could not measure the output
quiz.explain: Every input, short or long, had to fit into the same fixed-size summary vector. Attention lets the decoder look back at all encoder states instead.

articles.excerpt: A phrase like "a cup of tea" becomes "une tasse de thé" in French. The words line up nicely. But "I miss you" becomes "tu me manques", where the subject and object swap places. No word-for-word lookup gets that right. In 2014, translation systems handled this with huge tables of memorised phrase…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Building Word Vectors From the Pieces Inside Words
articles.subtitle: fastText's simple trick: a word is the sum of its character chunks, so even unseen words get a vector
articles.paper_title: Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information

glossary.definition: A run of n consecutive characters taken from a word, such as pla from play.
A word that never appeared in the training text, so a plain word-vector model has no vector for it.
How words are built from smaller meaningful parts, such as roots, prefixes and endings.
The word2vec training task where a word's vector is trained to predict the words that appear around it.
Mapping each n-gram string to one of a fixed number of buckets with a hash function, so memory stays bounded however many distinct n-grams exist.
When two different n-grams land in the same bucket and therefore share one vector.

quiz.q: How does this model give a vector to a word it never saw in training?
options: It returns a vector of zeros
It adds up the vectors of the character n-grams inside the word
It copies the vector of the most frequent word
It retrains the model on that word
quiz.explain: Each n-gram has its own vector, learned from many training words. An unseen word still breaks into known n-grams, so their sum gives it a vector.

quiz.q: Why are the boundary symbols < and > added around each word?
options: To make all words the same length
So that n-grams at the start or end of a word are different from the same letters in the middle
Because the hash function needs them
quiz.explain: With boundaries, ing> means the word ends in ing, while ing alone can appear anywhere. Prefixes and suffixes become their own pieces.

quiz.q: Where did subword vectors help most, according to the paper?
options: Semantic analogies about capitals and countries
Syntactic tasks and rare words, especially in languages with many word forms
quiz.explain: Shared pieces capture endings and roots, so the gains were largest on syntactic analogies, rare words and morphologically rich languages.

articles.excerpt: A word2vec model trained on millions of sentences knows "play" and "played" well. Then it meets "replayed", which happened to appear nowhere in its training text. It has no vector for it at all, even though any child can see the word is "re" plus "played". The problem gets much worse in languages…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Sorting a Million Documents Into Piles by Meaning
articles.subtitle: BERTopic finds the themes in a pile of text by clustering sentence embeddings, then naming each cluster with its most telling words
articles.paper_title: BERTopic: Neural topic modeling with a class-based TF-IDF procedure

glossary.definition: A method that discovers the main themes in a collection of documents and describes each theme with a list of words.
A vector representing the meaning of a whole sentence or document, so similar texts get nearby vectors.
Squeezing high-dimensional vectors into a few dimensions while keeping nearby points nearby, which makes clustering easier.
Grouping points that sit in dense regions, and labelling scattered points as outliers instead of forcing them into a group.
A word score that is high when a word is frequent in one document but rare across the collection.
BERTopic's variant of TF-IDF that treats all documents in one cluster as a single long document, to find the words that characterise that cluster.

quiz.q: What are the four main steps of BERTopic, in order?
options: Embed documents, reduce dimensions, cluster, describe clusters with c-TF-IDF
quiz.explain: Documents are embedded by meaning, squeezed into fewer dimensions, clustered by density, and each cluster is then described by its most distinctive words.

quiz.q: Why does c-TF-IDF treat a whole cluster as one document?
options: So word scores reflect what is typical of the cluster compared with other clusters, giving topic keywords
Because clusters contain only one document
quiz.explain: Joining a cluster's documents lets frequency within the cluster, compared with frequency across all clusters, pick out the words that define it.

quiz.q: What is a known limitation of BERTopic's basic approach?
options: It assigns each document to a single topic, although real documents often mix several
quiz.explain: Clustering puts each document in one group, so a document about both sport and politics must pick one. The paper notes this assumption.

articles.excerpt: A company receives fifty thousand customer complaints a month. Nobody can read them all, but everybody wants to know: what are people actually complaining about? Delivery delays? Refunds? A broken app update? Finding the themes in a pile of text without labels is called topic modelling. For two…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Teaching an Autoencoder to Dream
articles.subtitle: Variational autoencoders: fuzzy codes, a smooth map of possibilities, and one clever trick that made it trainable
articles.paper_title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes

glossary.definition: A model that learns the patterns of a dataset well enough to create new examples that look like they came from it.
The hidden space of codes a model uses to describe its data. Points in it correspond to possible outputs.
The distribution the model assumes codes come from before seeing any data, here a simple bell curve centred on zero.
Writing a random sample as a fixed formula plus independent noise, so gradients can flow through the sampling step.
A measure of how different one probability distribution is from another. Zero means they are identical.
The objective a VAE maximizes: how well it reconstructs the data, minus a penalty for codes that stray from the prior. Often called the ELBO.

quiz.q: How does a VAE's encoder differ from a plain autoencoder's?
options: It outputs a single exact code
It outputs a small cloud of possible codes, described by a mean and a spread
It outputs the label of the image
quiz.explain: Each input maps to a distribution over codes. Sampling from it forces nearby codes to decode into similar outputs.

quiz.q: Why is the reparameterization trick needed?
options: Because you cannot backpropagate through a random sampling step directly; rewriting it as mean plus spread times noise makes it differentiable
quiz.explain: With z = mu + sigma times epsilon, the randomness lives in epsilon, and gradients can flow to mu and sigma.

quiz.q: What does the KL term in the VAE objective encourage?
options: Codes that stay close to a simple standard bell curve, keeping the latent space smooth and free of holes
quiz.explain: By pulling every input's code cloud toward the same simple prior, the KL term makes the space continuous, so random points decode to sensible outputs.

articles.excerpt: A plain autoencoder is a brilliant compressor and a terrible artist. Train one on faces, pick a random point in its code space, decode it, and you usually get a smeared mess, not a new face. The codes it learned are scattered islands in a vast ocean of nonsense. In December 2013, Diederik Kingma…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: The Counterfeiter and the Detective
articles.subtitle: Generative adversarial nets: two networks locked in a game, and an idea sketched in a Montreal bar that learned to fake reality
articles.paper_title: Generative Adversarial Nets

glossary.definition: The network in a GAN that turns random noise into fake samples, trying to make them indistinguishable from real data.
The network in a GAN that looks at a sample and outputs the probability that it is real rather than generated.
Training two models against each other, so that each one's improvement forces the other to improve.
A two-player game where one player tries to maximize a score that the other tries to minimize.
A GAN failure where the generator produces only a few kinds of outputs, ignoring much of the variety in the real data.
A list of random numbers fed into the generator. Different noise vectors produce different generated samples.

quiz.q: What does the discriminator in a GAN do?
options: Estimates whether a sample is real data or a fake from the generator
quiz.explain: It is the detective: it outputs the probability that its input came from the real dataset.

quiz.q: According to the paper's theory, what happens at the ideal end of training?
options: The discriminator wins and always detects fakes
The generator's samples match the real data distribution, and the discriminator can only guess, outputting one half everywhere
The generator copies the training set exactly
quiz.explain: At the theoretical optimum, fakes and real data are indistinguishable, so the best possible detective is a coin flip.

quiz.q: What is mode collapse?
options: The generator producing only a narrow set of outputs instead of the full variety of the data
quiz.explain: A generator can fool the discriminator by perfecting a few outputs, so it stops exploring the full range of real data.

articles.excerpt: One evening in 2014, a PhD student named Ian Goodfellow was at a bar in Montreal, celebrating a friend's graduation. His friends were describing a plan to build a computer program that could generate realistic photos. Goodfellow thought their approach was too complicated. Then, as he has told the…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Creating Images by Removing Noise
articles.subtitle: Denoising diffusion: destroy a picture with static, step by step, then train a network to run the film backwards
articles.paper_title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

glossary.definition: A generative model that learns to reverse a gradual noising process, turning pure random noise into a realistic sample step by step.
The fixed procedure that adds a little Gaussian noise to an image at each of many steps until only noise remains.
The learned procedure that removes noise step by step, starting from pure noise and ending with a clean image.
Random values drawn from a bell curve, like the static on an old television screen.
The plan for how much noise to add at each step of the forward process.
Fréchet Inception Distance: a score comparing the statistics of generated images with real ones. Lower is better.

quiz.q: What does the network in a diffusion model learn to predict during training?
options: The noise that was added to a noisy image
Whether an image is real or fake
The next pixel from left to right
quiz.explain: Given a noisy image and the step number, the network predicts the noise, which can then be subtracted out.

quiz.q: How do you generate a brand-new image with a trained diffusion model?
options: Start from a random training image
Start from pure random noise and repeatedly apply the learned denoising step
Ask a discriminator to approve it
quiz.explain: Sampling runs the reverse process: begin with static and remove a little predicted noise at each of many steps.

quiz.q: What was the main practical drawback of the original DDPM?
options: Slow sampling, since generating one image took about a thousand network evaluations
quiz.explain: Quality was excellent, but each sample required running the network once per step, around 1,000 times.

articles.excerpt: Take a photo of a cat. Add a sprinkle of random static. Then a little more. Keep going for a thousand tiny steps, and eventually the cat is gone: you are left with pure television snow. Now imagine running that film backwards. Start from snow, and at each step remove just a little noise, until a…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Diffusion in a Smaller World
articles.subtitle: Latent diffusion: compress the image first, dream in the compressed space, and suddenly anyone can generate art on a gaming PC
articles.paper_title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models

glossary.definition: A compressed representation of images where each image becomes a much smaller grid of numbers that still captures its content.
Shrinking an image while keeping everything that matters to a human viewer, discarding fine pixel-level detail that the eye barely notices.
A pair of networks: an encoder that compresses an image into a small code, and a decoder that rebuilds the image from it.
Attention where one set of things, like image regions, looks up information in another, like the words of a text prompt.
Giving a generative model extra information, such as a caption or a class label, to steer what it creates.
A sampling trick that compares the model's predictions with and without the prompt and pushes further in the prompt's direction, making images follow text more closely.

quiz.q: What is the key efficiency idea of latent diffusion?
options: Run the diffusion process on a small compressed representation instead of full-resolution pixels
Generate only black and white images
quiz.explain: An autoencoder first compresses images, so the expensive diffusion steps work on a grid many times smaller.

quiz.q: How does a text prompt steer the image in a latent diffusion model?
options: The text is pasted onto the image
Cross-attention layers inside the denoising U-Net let image regions look up information from the encoded prompt
The prompt changes the random seed only
quiz.explain: At each denoising step, the network attends to the text encoding, so the words shape what emerges from the noise.

quiz.q: Why does the autoencoder only need to be trained once?
options: Because the same compressed space can be reused for many diffusion models and tasks
quiz.explain: The compression stage is separate and general, so different diffusion models for different tasks can all share it.

articles.excerpt: In August 2022, something unusual happened in AI. A model that could turn a sentence like "an astronaut riding a horse, oil painting" into a detailed picture was released with its weights free for anyone to download. It ran on an ordinary gaming graphics card. Within weeks, millions of people were…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: From Colouring Book to Street Photo
articles.subtitle: pix2pixHD turned label maps into 2048 × 1024 images by painting coarse to fine and judging at three distances
articles.paper_title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis and Semantic Manipulation with Conditional GANs

glossary.definition: An image where every pixel holds a class id, such as road, car or sky, instead of a colour. It is the input pix2pixHD turns into a photo.
A generative adversarial network whose generator and discriminator both see an input condition, here the label map, so the output must match it.
A generator split into a global network that lays out the scene at low resolution and a local enhancer that adds detail at full resolution.
Several discriminators with the same design, each judging the image at a different downsampled size, so together they check both overall layout and fine texture.
The patch of the input image that one output value of a network can see.
A loss that asks the generator's image to produce the same intermediate discriminator features as the real photo, which steadies GAN training.
A map marking the pixels where one object ends and another begins, even when both have the same class, such as two touching cars.

quiz.q: Why use three discriminators on different image sizes instead of one?
options: One discriminator would need a huge receptive field to judge a 2048 × 1024 image as a whole; the downsampled copies let small critics see the global layout while the full-size one checks texture
quiz.explain: The same network sees four times more of the scene on an image shrunk by four, so the pyramid covers both global layout and fine detail without a giant critic.

quiz.q: How does pix2pixHD stop two touching cars from merging into one strange car?
options: It adds an instance boundary map to the input, marking where one object ends and the next begins
It removes cars from the dataset
quiz.explain: A label map gives both cars the same class, so their pixels form one blob. The boundary channel tells the generator where each instance ends.

quiz.q: In the feature matching loss, what does the discriminator do?
options: It tries to maximise the loss
It only serves as a fixed feature extractor for that term; the generator minimises the difference
quiz.explain: The paper states that the discriminator does not maximise the feature matching loss; only the generator is trained to reduce it.

articles.excerpt: Colour a picture the way a child fills in a colouring book: this region is road, that one is sky, these blobs are cars and those are trees. Press a button, and a realistic street photograph comes back at 2048 × 1024 pixels, with the cars, trees and road surfaces where you drew them. Then click a…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Same Model, Fifty Times Fewer Steps
articles.subtitle: DDIM showed that a trained diffusion model can skip most of its denoising steps without retraining
articles.paper_title: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models

glossary.definition: A generative model trained to remove noise step by step, so it can turn pure noise into a realistic image.
The fixed recipe that gradually adds noise to a training image until it becomes pure noise.
A sequence of steps where each step depends only on the one just before it.
A way of generating where the same starting noise always produces exactly the same image, because no fresh randomness is added along the way.
The starting noise image from which a sample is generated. With a deterministic sampler it acts like a code for the final image.
The trained network that looks at a noisy image and estimates the noise that was added to it.

quiz.q: Why could DDIM reuse models already trained as DDPMs?
options: It uses a different loss that happens to match
Its new family of forward processes has the same single-step noise levels, so the DDPM training objective still applies
It only works on new models
quiz.explain: The training loss only depends on how noisy an image is at each step, which DDIM keeps the same. Only the sampling procedure changes.

quiz.q: What happens when DDIM's randomness parameter is set to zero?
options: The same starting noise always gives the same image
quiz.explain: With no fresh noise added during sampling, the path from noise to image is fixed, so the starting noise acts like a code for the image.

quiz.q: What was DDIM's main practical benefit?
options: Good samples in far fewer steps, for example 50 instead of 1,000
Removing the need for a neural network
quiz.explain: By skipping steps along a deterministic path, DDIM produced good images 10 to 50 times faster than the original sampler.

articles.excerpt: In 2020, diffusion models produced some of the most convincing generated images anyone had seen. There was one embarrassing catch: to make a single picture, the model had to run a neural network about a thousand times in a row, each pass removing a sliver of noise. A GAN could produce an image in…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Teaching a Language Model to Paint in Tiles
articles.subtitle: VQGAN compresses images into a short sequence of visual words so a transformer can write pictures like text
articles.paper_title: Taming Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis

glossary.definition: A learned list of vectors, each standing for a visual pattern. Every patch of an image is replaced by the index of its closest codebook vector.
Replacing a continuous vector with the nearest entry in a fixed codebook, turning it into a whole-number index.
Generating a sequence one element at a time, each predicted from all the elements before it.
A loss that compares images by features from a pre-trained vision network, so it rewards looking similar rather than matching pixel by pixel.
A GAN discriminator that judges many small regions of an image as real or fake, pushing the decoder to produce sharp local detail.
One element of a sequence a transformer reads. Here, one codebook index standing for a patch of the image.

quiz.q: Why not run a transformer directly on pixels of a 256 by 256 image?
options: That is 65,536 pixels per colour channel, and attention cost grows with the square of sequence length
quiz.explain: Attention compares every position with every other. A sequence of tens of thousands of pixels is far too long, which is why VQGAN compresses the image to a 16 by 16 grid of tokens.

quiz.q: What do the adversarial and perceptual losses add to the VQ autoencoder?
options: Sharp, realistic detail even when the image is compressed into very few tokens
quiz.explain: Plain pixel losses give blurry reconstructions at high compression. Perceptual and patch-based adversarial losses reward realistic textures, so a short code can still decode into a crisp image.

quiz.q: How does the model generate images larger than its training size?
options: The transformer predicts tokens with a sliding attention window over the token grid
It trains a new model for each size
quiz.explain: Each new token only attends to a local window of previous tokens, so generation can continue across a grid much larger than seen in training.

articles.excerpt: By 2020, transformers could write paragraphs that read like a person wrote them. So why not pictures? Treat an image as a sequence of pixels and predict the next pixel, the way GPT predicts the next word. The problem is size. A modest 256 by 256 colour image is nearly two hundred thousand numbers,…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Small Fixes That Made Diffusion Grow Up
articles.subtitle: Learned noise levels, a gentler schedule and a hybrid loss: the tune-up that set diffusion up to beat GANs
articles.paper_title: Improved Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models

glossary.definition: The plan for how much noise is added at each step of the forward process, from almost none to pure noise.
How spread out a random value is. Here, how much fresh randomness the model adds at each step of generation.
A score for how probable the model thinks real data is. Higher means the model covers the data distribution better.
A quantity that is always below the true log-likelihood, so maximising it pushes the likelihood up. Often abbreviated VLB.
Fréchet Inception Distance, a common score for generated images that compares their statistics to real images. Lower is better.
For generative models, how much of the variety in the real data the generated samples cover.

quiz.q: What did the paper let the network learn that DDPM had fixed by hand?
options: The variance of each reverse step, interpolated between two sensible bounds
quiz.explain: DDPM fixed the reverse-step variance to a constant. Learning it, as a blend between two known bounds, improved likelihood and allowed sampling with fewer steps.

quiz.q: Why replace the linear noise schedule with a cosine one?
options: The linear schedule destroyed information too quickly, so many late steps were nearly pure noise and wasted
It was required for learned variances
quiz.explain: With the linear schedule, images, especially small ones, became almost pure noise well before the final steps. The cosine schedule adds noise more evenly.

quiz.q: Compared with BigGAN at similar FID, what did the diffusion model show?
options: Higher recall, meaning it covered more of the data's variety
quiz.explain: GANs often miss parts of the distribution. The paper found diffusion models achieved better recall, a sign of fuller coverage.

articles.excerpt: By early 2021, diffusion models made beautiful pictures but had an awkward report card. Their likelihood scores, the standard test of how well a model captures the data, trailed other model families. They needed hundreds or thousands of steps to sample. And nobody was sure they could match GANs on…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Untangling the Knobs of Diffusion Models
articles.subtitle: How NVIDIA separated diffusion into independent design choices, then tuned each one to get better images in far fewer steps
articles.paper_title: Elucidating the Design Space of Diffusion-Based Generative Models

glossary.definition: Written sigma, the standard deviation of the Gaussian noise added to an image. Generation starts at a very high sigma and ends at almost zero.
The trained network D that takes a noisy image and its noise level and predicts the clean image.
A step-by-step method for following a path described by a differential equation, here the path from pure noise to a clean image.
A second-order solver: take a trial step, measure the slope where you land, then redo the step using the average of the two slopes.
Scaling the network's input, output and skip connection by amounts that depend on the noise level, so the network always sees and predicts numbers of a comfortable size.
Frechet Inception Distance, a standard score for how close generated images are to real ones. Lower is better.
One call of the denoiser network during sampling. The number of calls per image is the main cost of generating with a diffusion model.

quiz.q: In the paper's view, what is the main cost of sampling an image?
options: The number of denoiser network evaluations
quiz.explain: Every step calls the big network. The paper's improved sampler reached its CIFAR-10 results with 35 network evaluations per image.

quiz.q: Why does Heun's method usually beat Euler's method for the same accuracy target?
options: It corrects each step using the slope at the trial landing point, so its error shrinks much faster as steps get smaller, letting it use fewer steps overall
It only works on small images
quiz.explain: Heun spends two evaluations per step but is second order, so far fewer steps are needed for the same accuracy.

quiz.q: What does preconditioning do when the noise level is very small?
options: It makes the skip connection pass almost all of the input through, so the network only predicts a small correction
It switches to a different network
quiz.explain: At low noise the input is nearly clean, so c_skip is close to 1 and the network's job is a small fix, which is easier and more stable.

articles.excerpt: By 2022, diffusion models made stunning images, but every paper described them in its own language. One spoke of discrete Markov chains, another of stochastic differential equations, another of score functions. Changing one detail, such as the step sizes, often meant re-deriving the whole method. A…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: One Program, Forty-Nine Atari Games
articles.subtitle: Deep Q-networks: how an agent learned to play from raw pixels and a score, with no rules and no human tips
articles.paper_title: Human-level Control through Deep Reinforcement Learning

glossary.definition: Learning by trial and error: an agent takes actions in an environment and learns from the rewards it receives.
The learner that observes the environment and chooses actions.
A number the environment gives the agent after an action, such as points in a game. The agent tries to collect as much as possible over time.
An estimate of the total future reward you will get if you take a particular action in a particular situation and play well afterwards.
Storing past experiences in a memory and training on random samples from it, instead of only on the latest moment.
A slowly updated copy of the network used to compute training targets, which keeps learning stable.
Trying actions that are not currently believed to be best, in order to discover better strategies.

quiz.q: What did DQN receive as input when playing Atari games?
options: Raw screen pixels and the game score
quiz.explain: The same network and settings were used for every game, learning only from pixels and score changes.

quiz.q: Why does DQN use experience replay?
options: To break the strong correlation between consecutive frames and reuse each experience many times
To make the game run faster
quiz.explain: Training on random past moments, rather than a stream of nearly identical consecutive frames, makes learning far more stable and data-efficient.

quiz.q: What does a Q-value represent?
options: The expected total future reward of taking an action in a state and acting well afterwards
quiz.explain: Q-values look ahead: they include the immediate reward plus discounted future rewards.

They can see the screen and a score. That is all. Within a few hours, they are playing better than most people. In 2015, a London startup that Google…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: The Machine That Mastered Go a Decade Early
articles.subtitle: AlphaGo: neural intuition plus careful search cracked the game experts thought computers could not win
articles.paper_title: Mastering the Game of Go with Deep Neural Networks and Tree Search

glossary.definition: A network that looks at a board position and outputs a probability for each possible move, suggesting which moves are worth considering.
A network that looks at a board position and predicts who is likely to win from there.
A search method that explores possible future move sequences by simulating many games, focusing effort on the most promising lines.
Training a game-playing system by having it play against copies of itself.
All the possible sequences of moves a player could consider. In Go it is astronomically large.
Playing a game out quickly to the end from some position, using a fast simple policy, to estimate who would win.

quiz.q: What did AlphaGo's policy network do?
options: Suggest which moves are promising in a given position
Count the stones on the board
quiz.explain: It narrowed the search by giving each legal move a probability, so the program could focus on the few that strong players would consider.

quiz.q: Why was Go considered much harder for computers than chess?
options: Go has far more possible moves per turn and longer games, and positions are very hard to evaluate
Computers cannot draw a Go board
quiz.explain: With around 250 legal moves per position and games of about 150 moves, brute-force search is hopeless, and judging who is ahead is subtle.

quiz.q: How was the value network trained?
options: On positions from games AlphaGo played against itself, predicting the eventual winner
quiz.explain: Self-play generated millions of positions with known outcomes, and the network learned to predict the winner from a position.

On one side sat Lee Sedol, one of the greatest Go players of his generation. On the other, a person placing stones on behalf of a program called AlphaGo. In the second game, AlphaGo played…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Learn Fast, But Not Too Fast
articles.subtitle: Proximal Policy Optimization: the simple, sturdy algorithm behind game-playing bots, robot hands and ChatGPT's fine-tuning
articles.paper_title: Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms

glossary.definition: The agent's strategy: a function that, given a situation, gives the probability of taking each possible action.
A family of methods that directly adjust the policy, making actions that led to good outcomes more likely.
How much better an action turned out than what the agent expected on average in that situation. Positive means better than expected.
The new policy's probability of an action divided by the old policy's probability. A ratio of 1.2 means the action became 20% more likely.
Limiting a number to a range. PPO clips the probability ratio so a single update cannot change the policy too much.
A zone around the current policy within which updates are considered safe, because the data collected by the old policy still describes them well.

quiz.q: What problem does PPO's clipping solve?
options: Destructively large policy updates that can collapse performance
quiz.explain: If one update changes the policy too much, the agent can suddenly perform terribly. Clipping removes the incentive to move far from the old policy.

quiz.q: If an action had a positive advantage, what does the policy gradient try to do?
quiz.explain: Positive advantage means the action worked better than expected, so the policy should choose it more often.

quiz.q: Why was PPO preferred over TRPO by many practitioners?
options: It gave theoretical guarantees TRPO lacked
It achieved similar stability with a much simpler, first-order method that is easy to implement
It does not need any data
quiz.explain: TRPO enforced its trust region with complex second-order maths. PPO approximates the same behaviour with a clipped objective and ordinary gradient descent.

Next match, the batters read it immediately and the bowler is hammered. A good coach would have said, "That worked. Use…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: The Paper That Taught Machines Where to Look
articles.subtitle: How one simple idea replaced decades of sequence models and gave us ChatGPT
articles.paper_title: Attention Is All You Need

glossary.definition: A way for a model to decide which parts of the input matter most for each output, by giving every part a weight and mixing them together.
Attention where every word in a sentence looks at every other word in the same sentence to understand its context.
A small chunk of text, like a word or part of a word, that the model reads as one unit.
An older kind of network that reads a sequence one step at a time, carrying a memory forward from each step to the next.
Three vectors made from each token. The query says what a token is looking for, the key says what it offers, and the value is the information it passes on.
A function that turns a list of scores into positive weights that add up to 1, so bigger scores get bigger shares.
Extra numbers added to each token's embedding so the model knows where in the sentence the token sits.
A standard score for machine translation that measures how much a system's output overlaps with human translations. Higher is better.

quiz.q: What did the Transformer remove that earlier translation models depended on?
options: Recurrence, reading words one at a time
quiz.explain: Transformers process all tokens at once with self-attention instead of stepping through the sentence word by word.

quiz.q: In self-attention, what decides how much one word listens to another?
options: How well the first word's query matches the second word's key
A fixed table written by the researchers
quiz.explain: Each word's query is compared with every key using a dot product. Higher scores become bigger attention weights after the softmax.

quiz.q: Why does the Transformer need positional encodings?
options: To make training slower but more accurate
Because attention on its own has no sense of word order
To translate between languages with different alphabets
To reduce the number of parameters
quiz.explain: Attention treats the input as a set. Without position information, 'dog bites man' and 'man bites dog' would look identical.

articles.excerpt: In 2017, the best translation systems in the world read sentences the way you read a long receipt: one item at a time, struggling to remember what came at the top. Eight researchers at Google asked a strange question. What if the model could look at every word at once, and simply decide which ones…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Read Seven Thousand Books, Then Take Any Test
articles.subtitle: GPT-1: the quiet 2018 report that introduced generative pre-training, the recipe behind every chatbot since
articles.paper_title: Improving Language Understanding by Generative Pre-Training

glossary.definition: A model that predicts the next token in a piece of text, given the tokens before it.
Training a model on a huge amount of unlabeled data with a general task, like next-word prediction, before adapting it to specific tasks.
Continuing to train a pre-trained model on a smaller labeled dataset for a particular task.
Reusing what a model learned on one task to do better on another, usually with much less data.
A Transformer that keeps only the decoder half, where each token can attend to the tokens before it but not after it.
A chunk of text, often a word or a piece of a word, that the model reads as one unit.
Performing a task without any task-specific training examples.

quiz.q: What task was GPT pre-trained on?
options: Predicting the next token in a large collection of books
quiz.explain: The model learned language by predicting the next token across thousands of unpublished books, with no labels needed.

quiz.q: How did GPT handle different tasks like entailment or multiple-choice questions?
options: A completely different architecture for each task
By converting each task's inputs into a single sequence of text with special separator tokens, then adding a small output layer
By retraining from scratch for each task
quiz.explain: Task-specific input formatting let the same pre-trained Transformer handle many tasks with minimal changes.

quiz.q: Which kind of Transformer did GPT use?
options: Encoder only, reading in both directions
Decoder only, where each token sees only earlier tokens
quiz.explain: GPT kept the decoder, with masked attention, which is natural for predicting the next word.

articles.excerpt: In June 2018, OpenAI posted a blog post and a short technical report. It did not appear at a big conference. It had no flashy demo. Its main claim was modest-sounding: a model pre-trained on a pile of books did better on a collection of language understanding tests. But hidden in that report was…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Fill in the Blanks, Understand Everything
articles.subtitle: BERT: reading in both directions with a fill-in-the-blank game, and the model that changed Google Search
articles.paper_title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding

glossary.definition: Able to use context from both the left and the right of a word at the same time.
A pre-training task where some words in a sentence are hidden and the model must predict them from the surrounding words.
BERT's second pre-training task: given two sentences, predict whether the second really follows the first in the original text.
The half of a Transformer where every token can attend to every other token, producing a contextual vector for each one.
Briefly training a pre-trained model on a specific labeled task, usually updating all of its weights.
A vector for a word that depends on the sentence it appears in, so 'bank' in 'river bank' and 'bank loan' get different vectors.

quiz.q: Why couldn't BERT simply be trained to predict the next word, like GPT?
options: With full bidirectional attention, each word could see itself and the answer, so the task would be trivial
quiz.explain: If every word can attend to every other word, predicting the next word is cheating. Masking hides the targets so bidirectional context can be used fairly.

quiz.q: In BERT's masked language model, what happens to the selected 15% of tokens?
options: All are deleted from the sentence
Most become a [MASK] token, some become a random word, and some stay unchanged
They are moved to the end of the sentence
quiz.explain: 80% become [MASK], 10% a random token and 10% stay the same, so the model cannot rely on always seeing [MASK] during pre-training.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of a contextual embedding over a word2vec vector?
options: The same word gets different vectors depending on its sentence, capturing its meaning in context
quiz.explain: BERT's output for 'bank' changes with the surrounding words, which resolves ambiguity that a single fixed vector cannot.

articles.excerpt: Try this: "I went to the to deposit my salary." You filled the gap with "bank" instantly. But notice how you did it. You used "went to the" on the left and "deposit my salary" on the right. Without the right side, the blank could be "market," "gym" or "beach." In October 2018, a team at Google…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Just Show It a Few Examples
articles.subtitle: GPT-3: 175 billion parameters, no fine-tuning, and the surprise that a model could learn new tasks from its prompt
articles.paper_title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners

glossary.definition: Picking up a task from instructions or examples given in the prompt itself, without any change to the model's weights.
The text you give a language model to continue, which can include instructions and examples.
Giving a model a handful of worked examples of a task in its prompt before asking it to do a new one.
Asking a model to do a task from an instruction alone, with no examples.
One of the learned numbers inside a model. GPT-3 has about 175 billion of them.
When test questions accidentally appear in a model's training data, which can make benchmark scores look better than true ability.

quiz.q: What is in-context learning?
options: Fine-tuning the model's weights on a new dataset
The model picking up a task from examples in its prompt, with no weight updates
Training a model in a classroom
quiz.explain: GPT-3 was given examples as text in the prompt and continued the pattern, without any gradient updates.

quiz.q: What happened to few-shot performance as model size grew from millions to 175 billion parameters?
options: It improved substantially, and the gap between zero-shot and few-shot widened
quiz.explain: Larger models made much better use of examples in context, which is the paper's central finding.

quiz.q: Which of these was a limitation the authors acknowledged?
options: GPT-3 could not write any coherent text
GPT-3 could repeat itself, lose coherence over long passages, and reflect biases in its training data
GPT-3 was too small to be useful
GPT-3 could not answer any questions
quiz.explain: The paper has a long, frank limitations section, including repetition, weak common-sense physics, bias and the cost of training.
