Nobody trained it to translate. Nobody changed a single one of its weights. It looked at two examples, spotted the pattern, and continued it. In…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: The Straight Lines That Launched a Race
articles.subtitle: Scaling laws: how language model quality improves predictably with size, data and compute, and why that changed AI strategy
articles.paper_title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models

glossary.definition: A simple mathematical relationship describing how a model's performance changes as you scale up its size, data or compute.
A relationship of the form y = a times x to the power b. On a log-log plot it appears as a straight line.
A chart where both axes use a logarithmic scale, so each step along an axis means multiplying by ten.
The total amount of calculation used to train a model, usually counted in floating point operations (FLOPs).
The model's average next-token prediction loss on text it was not trained on. Lower means better language modelling.
How much a model learns from each example it sees. A more sample-efficient model reaches a given loss with less data.

quiz.q: What did the paper find about how loss depends on model size?
options: Loss stops improving after 1 billion parameters
Loss falls as a smooth power law, a straight line on a log-log plot, across many orders of magnitude
quiz.explain: Across more than seven orders of magnitude, test loss improved predictably as a power law in model size, data and compute.

quiz.q: According to the paper, which architectural details mattered most for performance?
options: The exact ratio of depth to width
Very little: within a wide range, total parameter count mattered far more than shape
The number of attention heads above all
quiz.explain: Depth, width and head count had only weak effects compared with total scale.

quiz.q: What did the paper recommend for a fixed compute budget?
options: Train a small model for a very long time
Train a very large model and stop well before it fully converges
Spend most of the compute on data cleaning
Never train beyond one epoch of a small dataset
quiz.explain: Larger models are more sample-efficient, so the paper concluded it was best to scale models up and stop early. Chinchilla later revised how the budget should be split.

articles.excerpt: Most of machine learning is unpredictable. You change something, run an experiment for days, and find out whether it helped. Nobody can tell you in advance how good your model will be. In January 2020, a team at OpenAI published a set of charts that looked almost too clean to be real. Plot a…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: The Giant Models Were Underfed
articles.subtitle: Chinchilla: a smaller model trained on four times more data beat models up to seven times its size
articles.paper_title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models

glossary.definition: The choice of model size and amount of training data that gives the lowest loss for a fixed training compute budget.
The total number of tokens of text a model processes during training.
Floating point operations: the basic arithmetic steps a computer performs. Total training FLOPs measure training compute.
A set of models trained with the same total compute but different sizes, used to find which size gives the lowest loss for that budget.
Describes a model that has not seen enough data for its size, so it could have reached a lower loss with more training tokens.
Using a trained model to produce outputs. Smaller models are cheaper and faster at inference.

quiz.q: What was Chinchilla's main finding about compute-optimal training?
options: Model size should grow much faster than data
Model size and training tokens should be scaled up in roughly equal proportion
Models should never be larger than 1 billion parameters
quiz.explain: If you double the compute-optimal model size, you should roughly double the number of training tokens too.

quiz.q: How did Chinchilla (70B parameters) compare with Gopher (280B parameters)?
options: It used the same compute budget, was four times smaller, saw about four times more data, and performed better
It used ten times more compute
quiz.explain: Same compute, different split: a smaller model trained on 1.4 trillion tokens beat the bigger one trained on 300 billion.

quiz.q: Why does a smaller, well-trained model matter after training too?
options: It is cheaper and faster to run for every user query
It needs more GPUs to serve
quiz.explain: Inference costs scale with model size, so a smaller model with the same quality is much cheaper to deploy.

articles.excerpt: By early 2022, the race to build bigger language models was in full swing. GPT-3 had 175 billion parameters. Google, DeepMind and Microsoft with NVIDIA had built models with 280 billion and even 530 billion. The assumption was simple: bigger models, better results. Then a DeepMind team ran an…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: What If an Image Is Just a Sentence of Patches?
articles.subtitle: The Vision Transformer: chop a picture into squares, read them like words, and match the best convolutional networks
articles.paper_title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale

glossary.definition: A small square piece of an image, such as 16 by 16 pixels, treated as one token by the Vision Transformer.
The vector made by flattening a patch's pixels and passing them through a learned linear layer.
Assumptions built into a model's design, like a convolutional network's assumption that nearby pixels matter most.
An extra learnable token added to the sequence whose final vector is used to classify the whole image.
A learned vector added to each patch embedding so the model knows where in the image the patch came from.
The large collection of images a model learns from first, before being fine-tuned on a specific task.

quiz.q: How does the Vision Transformer turn an image into a sequence?
options: It reads pixels one by one
It splits the image into fixed-size patches, flattens each, and projects it into a vector, like a word embedding
It converts the image to a caption first
It uses a convolutional network to describe each object
quiz.explain: A 224 by 224 image with 16 by 16 patches becomes a sequence of 196 patch tokens.

quiz.q: Why did ViT underperform ResNets when trained only on ImageNet's 1.3 million images?
options: It lacks the built-in assumptions of convolutions, so it needs more data to learn them
quiz.explain: Convolutions bake in locality and translation equivariance. ViT has to learn such patterns from data, which takes more examples.

quiz.q: What happened when ViT was pre-trained on very large datasets?
options: It still lost badly to ResNets
It matched or beat state-of-the-art convolutional networks while using less compute to pre-train
It only worked on black and white images
quiz.explain: With 14 million or 300 million images, the lack of built-in bias stopped mattering, and scale won.

articles.excerpt: For thirty years, computer vision and convolutional networks were nearly inseparable. From LeNet reading cheques to ResNet winning ImageNet, the idea that images need sliding filters seemed as natural as gravity. In October 2020, a team at Google Research in Zurich posted a paper with a playful…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Teaching Vision With the Internet's Captions
articles.subtitle: CLIP: 400 million image-text pairs, one shared space for pictures and words, and classifiers you create by typing
articles.paper_title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision

glossary.definition: Training a model to pull matching pairs together and push non-matching pairs apart in an embedding space.
A single vector space where both images and texts are placed, so a picture and a sentence describing it end up close together.
Classifying images into categories the model was never explicitly trained on, by comparing images with text descriptions of each category.
Learning from the free-form text that naturally accompanies images online, instead of from a fixed list of labels.
A score from -1 to 1 measuring how closely two vectors point in the same direction.
When the data a model is used on looks different from the data it was trained on, such as sketches instead of photos.

quiz.q: What is CLIP trained to do?
options: Match each image in a batch with its correct caption, among many wrong ones
Label images with one of 1,000 ImageNet classes
quiz.explain: CLIP learns by contrast: correct image-caption pairs should score high, mismatched pairs low.

quiz.q: How does CLIP classify images zero-shot?
options: By retraining on each new dataset
By turning each class name into a sentence like 'a photo of a dog', embedding it, and picking the class whose text is closest to the image
By counting pixels of each colour
quiz.explain: The text encoder creates a classifier on the fly from class names, with no task-specific training.

quiz.q: What was one notable weakness of CLIP?
options: It could not recognise any common objects
It struggled with tasks like counting objects and with some specialised or abstract tasks, such as handwritten digits
It needed labeled ImageNet data to work
It only worked on black-and-white images
quiz.explain: The paper notes poor performance on systematic tasks like counting and on datasets unlike its web training data, such as MNIST.

articles.excerpt: To teach a computer to recognise dogs, cats and 998 other things, ImageNet's creators organised thousands of crowd workers to label over a million photos. Every new kind of object a model needed to know meant more labeling. Meanwhile, the internet was already full of labels nobody had to pay for.…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Vision Transformers Without a Private Photo Archive
articles.subtitle: DeiT trained a competitive image transformer on ImageNet alone, helped by one extra token that listens to a teacher
articles.paper_title: Training data-efficient image transformers & distillation through attention

glossary.definition: Assumptions built into a model's design, such as a convolution's focus on nearby pixels, that help it learn from less data.
Training a student model to imitate the predictions of a trained teacher model, in addition to (or instead of) the true labels.
An extra learnable vector added to the patch tokens in a vision transformer, whose final state is used to predict the image's label.
DeiT's second extra vector, which travels through the transformer like the class token but is trained to match the teacher's prediction.
Distillation where the student learns from the teacher's single top class, used as a label, rather than from its full set of probabilities.
Creating varied training examples by randomly cropping, mixing, recolouring or otherwise transforming images, so the model sees more variety.

quiz.q: What problem with the original Vision Transformer did DeiT set out to fix?
options: It needed pre-training on hundreds of millions of images and expensive infrastructure
It could not process colour images
quiz.explain: ViT reached strong results only after pre-training on a huge private dataset. DeiT trained a competitive transformer on ImageNet alone, on one computer in under three days.

quiz.q: How is the distillation token trained differently from the class token?
options: Its output is trained to match the teacher's top prediction, while the class token matches the true label
It only sees the class token
quiz.explain: Both tokens pass through the same transformer layers, but they are supervised by different targets. That keeps the distillation token from becoming a copy of the class token.

quiz.q: Which kind of teacher worked especially well for DeiT?
quiz.explain: The paper highlights convnet teachers. A convnet's built-in focus on local patterns seems to pass useful habits to the transformer student.

articles.excerpt: In 2020, Google showed that a pure transformer could classify images as well as the best convolutional networks. There was a catch you could not get around: the strongest results came after pre-training on a private collection of hundreds of millions of images, on infrastructure few labs could…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Shift the Window, See the Whole Picture
articles.subtitle: How local windows that slide by half a step let Transformers handle big, detailed images
articles.paper_title: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows

glossary.definition: Self-attention computed only among the patches inside one small square window, instead of across the whole image.
A second way of cutting the image into windows, moved by half a window, so patches that were split apart in one layer share a window in the next.
Rolling the image grid so edge pieces wrap around to the other side, letting shifted windows be computed as the same number of full-size windows.
Joining each 2 by 2 group of neighbouring patches into one token, which halves the grid's height and width and doubles the channels.
A learned number added to each attention score that depends only on how far apart, and in which direction, two patches are.
The general-purpose network that turns an image into feature maps, on top of which task-specific heads for detection or segmentation are built.

quiz.q: Why does Swin's attention cost grow only linearly with image area?
options: Each patch attends only to the fixed number of patches in its own window
It uses a smaller embedding size for big images
quiz.explain: With a fixed window of 7 by 7 patches, each patch compares itself with 49 others no matter how big the image is, so total work grows with the number of patches, not its square.

quiz.q: What problem do shifted windows solve?
options: They make windows smaller to save memory
They let information cross the borders between windows from the previous layer
They remove the need for position information
quiz.explain: Plain windows never talk to each other. Moving the grid by half a window in the next layer puts former neighbours from different windows into the same window.

quiz.q: What does patch merging give Swin that the original Vision Transformer lacked?
options: A pyramid of feature maps at several resolutions, like a CNN
Larger image patches at the input
quiz.explain: Merging 2 by 2 patches between stages shrinks the grid from 56 to 28 to 14 to 7 for a 224 pixel image, giving the multi-scale maps that detection and segmentation heads expect.

articles.excerpt: In 2020, the Vision Transformer showed that you could cut a photo into patches, treat them like words, and classify images very well. Then people tried to use it for the jobs vision systems actually do all day: finding every car in a street scene, or labelling every pixel of a road. Those jobs need…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: The Model That Rewrote the Internet's Captions
articles.subtitle: How BLIP learned to search, check and write about images, then used those skills to clean its own training data
articles.paper_title: BLIP: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training for Unified Vision-Language Understanding and Generation

glossary.definition: The short text attached to an image on a web page. It is free to collect at scale, but often describes the page, a product or a file name rather than the picture.
Training one model on huge numbers of image and text pairs so it can later be adapted to tasks such as search, captioning and question answering.
Multimodal mixture of Encoder-Decoder: BLIP's single model that can act as a text encoder, an image-grounded text encoder, or an image-grounded text decoder.
A training objective that pulls the vectors of a matching image and caption together and pushes non-matching pairs apart, so search can be a fast vector comparison.
A yes-or-no classifier that reads an image and a caption together, through cross-attention, and predicts whether the caption truly describes the image.
Captioning and Filtering: BLIP's data-cleaning step, where a captioner writes new captions for web images and a filter removes captions that do not match.

A way of generating text that picks each next word at random from the smallest set of likely words whose probabilities add up to a threshold, giving more varied sentences than always taking the top word.

quiz.q: Why does BLIP keep separate self-attention layers for its text encoder and text decoder while sharing the rest?
options: Self-attention is the largest layer, so splitting it saves memory
Reading a caption lets every word see every other word, while writing one must only look at earlier words, so the two jobs need different self-attention
Cross-attention cannot be shared between tasks
The decoder does not look at the image
quiz.explain: The encoder reads bidirectionally and the decoder writes left to right. The paper found that sharing everything except self-attention works best, because that is where the two jobs genuinely differ.

quiz.q: In CapFilt, what does the filter do?
options: It blurs images with private information
It removes web and synthetic captions that its image-text matching head judges not to match the image
It picks the best image for each caption
quiz.explain: The filter is an image-grounded text encoder fine-tuned for matching. Any caption, web or synthetic, that it predicts does not match is dropped.

quiz.q: Why did nucleus sampling make better training captions than beam search, even though more of its captions were filtered out?
options: Its captions were more varied and surprising, so the surviving ones carried more new information
Beam search cannot produce full sentences
quiz.explain: Beam search tends to give safe, generic captions that teach little. Sampling gives diverse captions; some are wrong and get filtered, but the rest add more learning signal.

articles.excerpt: Open any large web scrape of photos and read the text attached to them. A picture of a dog on a beach is labelled "summer sale 20% off". A plate of noodles is labelled "IMG4471". A mountain lake is labelled with the name of the travel blog. Researchers trained their best vision-language models on…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: The GPT-3-Sized Model Anyone Could Study
articles.subtitle: How Meta rebuilt a 175-billion-parameter model, shared the weights and published the messy diary of training it
articles.paper_title: OPT: Open Pre-trained Transformer Language Models

glossary.definition: Releasing the trained parameters of a model so other people can run, inspect and fine-tune it themselves, instead of only calling it through an API.
A training method that splits the model's weights, gradients and optimizer state across all GPUs, so no single GPU holds a full copy.
Splitting the big matrix multiplications inside each layer across several GPUs, which work on their slices at the same time.
Training with 16-bit numbers for most of the work to save memory and time, while keeping sensitive values in 32-bit.
Multiplying the loss by a large factor before backpropagation so tiny gradients do not round to zero in 16-bit numbers, then dividing it back out before the update.
A training failure where the loss suddenly shoots up and does not recover, often caused by numerical instability.
A model trained only to predict the next token of web-scale text, with no extra training to follow instructions or behave safely.

quiz.q: What did OPT give researchers that GPT-3 did not?
options: Access to the trained weights, plus code and a training logbook
quiz.explain: OPT was designed to be roughly GPT-3-sized and comparable in quality. The new part was openness: weights for researchers, code and a record of the training run.

quiz.q: Why does loss scaling help in 16-bit training?
options: It stops tiny gradients from rounding to zero by moving them into the range 16-bit numbers can represent
It removes the need for an optimizer
quiz.explain: Multiplying the loss by S multiplies every gradient by S. Values too small for 16-bit become representable, and dividing by S afterwards restores their true size.

quiz.q: OPT-175B was trained on about 180 billion tokens. What does the Chinchilla rule of thumb of about 20 tokens per parameter suggest?
options: It was trained on far too many tokens
It was trained on far fewer tokens than compute-optimal, about 3.5 trillion
quiz.explain: 20 tokens per parameter times 175 billion parameters is about 3.5 trillion tokens, nearly 20 times what OPT-175B saw.

articles.excerpt: Suppose you are a researcher in 2021 and you want to know why GPT-3 says biased things. You can type prompts into a paid API and read the answers. You cannot look at a single weight or activation, and you cannot retrain it to test a fix. Studying the most talked-about model in AI meant poking a…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: A Field Guide to Large Language Models
articles.subtitle: The survey that sorted the LLM explosion into four stages: pre-training, adaptation, use and evaluation
articles.paper_title: A Survey of Large Language Models

glossary.definition: The first and most expensive training phase, where a model learns to predict the next token on a huge collection of general text.
An observed rule describing how a model's loss falls as you increase its size, its training data or its compute.
Abilities that are hard to see in smaller models but appear clearly in large ones, such as following new instructions or reasoning step by step.
Fine-tuning a pre-trained model on many tasks written as natural-language instructions with answers, so it learns to follow requests.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: people compare model answers, a reward model learns their preferences, and the language model is tuned to score well on it.
Doing a new task from instructions and a few examples placed in the prompt, without changing the model's weights.

quiz.q: Which four aspects does the survey organise LLM research around?
options: Pre-training, adaptation tuning, utilization and capacity evaluation
quiz.explain: The abstract names exactly these four: how models are pre-trained, adapted, used and evaluated.

quiz.q: GPT-3 has about 175 billion parameters and was trained on about 300 billion tokens. Roughly how many training tokens per parameter is that?
quiz.explain: 300 billion divided by 175 billion is about 1.7. Chinchilla, with 70 billion parameters and 1.4 trillion tokens, used about 20 per parameter.

quiz.q: What does the survey's abstract say happens once language models pass a certain scale?
options: They show special abilities not present in small models
quiz.explain: Beyond a certain parameter scale, models not only improve but show abilities small models lack. That observation is why the field coined the term large language model.

articles.excerpt: In the months after ChatGPT launched in late 2022, it felt as if a new language model paper appeared every hour. Training tricks lived in scattered preprints, blog posts and model cards. A student trying to understand how these systems were built had no map. A group at Renmin University of China…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Teaching a Blind Scholar to See, Without Retraining Them
articles.subtitle: BLIP-2 kept an image model and a language model frozen and trained only a small Q-Former that writes 32 visual notes for the LLM
articles.paper_title: BLIP-2: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training with Frozen Image Encoders and Large Language Models

glossary.definition: A pretrained model whose weights are not updated during further training. It is used as-is, like a fixed tool.
BLIP-2's small trainable transformer that uses a fixed set of learned query vectors to pull language-relevant information out of a frozen image encoder.
A fixed number of trainable vectors (32 in BLIP-2) that ask the image features questions through cross-attention and carry the answers out.
Attention where one set of vectors (here the queries) looks at another set (here the image patch features) to gather information from it.
Continuous vectors placed in front of a language model's input in place of word tokens, steering what the model generates.
When further training on a new task damages abilities a model had already learned.

quiz.q: Which parts of BLIP-2 are trained?
options: The image encoder and the LLM
Only the Q-Former and a small projection layer; the image encoder and LLM stay frozen
quiz.explain: Keeping both large models frozen is what makes BLIP-2 cheap to train and protects the LLM's language skills.

quiz.q: Why does BLIP-2 first train the Q-Former against the image encoder alone (stage 1), before connecting the LLM?
options: So the queries already extract language-relevant visual information; without it, the paper found training with the LLM worked much worse
Because the LLM cannot be loaded at first
quiz.explain: The paper's ablation shows that skipping representation learning hurts zero-shot results, and with OPT, performance even degraded as training continued.

quiz.q: The image encoder gives 257 vectors of size 1,024; the Q-Former outputs 32 vectors of size 768. Roughly how much smaller is the Q-Former's output?
quiz.explain: 257 × 1,024 = 263,168 numbers versus 32 × 768 = 24,576, about 10.7 times fewer.

articles.excerpt: You have two experts. One is a superb photographer who notices everything in a picture but can only describe it in long lists of numbers. The other is a brilliant scholar who has read nearly everything and reasons well in words, but has never seen an image. You want them to answer questions about…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: One Small Layer That Taught a Chatbot to See
articles.subtitle: MiniGPT-4 showed that a frozen eye, a frozen chatbot and one trained projection can reproduce GPT-4's flashiest image tricks
articles.paper_title: MiniGPT-4: Enhancing Vision-Language Understanding with Advanced Large Language Models

glossary.definition: A pre-trained network whose weights are kept fixed during training, so it is used but never changed.
A small transformer from BLIP-2 that uses 32 learnable queries to squeeze an image's features into 32 compact vectors.
An open chatbot made by fine-tuning LLaMA on shared conversations. MiniGPT-4 uses it, frozen, as its language model.
A single linear layer that multiplies a vector by a learned matrix and adds a bias, moving it from one vector space into another.
Vectors fed into a language model at the input, in the same places word embeddings would go, but which do not correspond to any real word.
When a model confidently describes things that are not actually there, such as objects missing from the image.

quiz.q: Which part of MiniGPT-4 is trained?
options: Only one projection layer between the vision side and Vicuna
quiz.explain: The vision encoder, the Q-Former and Vicuna all stay frozen. Only the single projection layer that connects them is learned.

quiz.q: Why did the authors add a second training stage?
options: The vision encoder forgot how to see
Training only on short captions made the model's answers repetitive and fragmented
The projection layer was too large for one GPU
quiz.explain: After the first stage on short image-caption pairs, outputs often repeated phrases or broke off. A small, carefully curated set of detailed descriptions fixed this.

quiz.q: What is the paper's main hypothesis about GPT-4's image abilities?
options: They come from a huge new vision encoder
They come mostly from having a strong language model, once visual features are properly aligned with it
They require training on billions of video clips
They are impossible to reproduce without secret data
quiz.explain: The authors bet that the skill lives in the language model. Their result supports it: aligning features with an advanced LLM was enough to reproduce many of GPT-4's demos.

articles.excerpt: In March 2023, OpenAI showed GPT-4 looking at a hand-drawn sketch of a website and writing the code for it. It could also look at a meme and explain the joke. Nobody outside OpenAI knew how it worked, and the guess was that it needed a giant, secret training run. A month later, a small team…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: How a Text Predictor Learned to Be Helpful
articles.subtitle: InstructGPT: human demonstrations, human rankings and reinforcement learning, the recipe that became ChatGPT
articles.paper_title: Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback

glossary.definition: Making an AI system's behaviour match what its users and designers actually intend, such as being helpful, honest and harmless.
Training a pre-trained model further on examples of the desired behaviour, here prompts paired with ideal responses written by people.
A model trained to predict which of several responses humans would prefer, giving a score that stands in for human judgement.
Reinforcement learning from human feedback: optimising a model to maximise a reward model trained on human preferences.
A term that discourages the fine-tuned model from drifting too far from its starting point, which helps prevent it from gaming the reward model.
A drop in performance on some standard tasks that can come with alignment training.
When a language model states made-up information as if it were true.

quiz.q: What are the three steps of the InstructGPT training recipe?
options: Supervised fine-tuning on human demonstrations, training a reward model on human rankings, then optimising with reinforcement learning
Collect images, label them, train a classifier
quiz.explain: Demonstrations teach the format, rankings teach preferences, and PPO optimises the model against the learned reward.

quiz.q: What surprising comparison did the paper report?
options: Labelers preferred GPT-3's raw outputs over InstructGPT's
Labelers preferred outputs from a 1.3 billion parameter InstructGPT over those of the 175 billion parameter GPT-3
InstructGPT could not follow any instructions
quiz.explain: Despite being over 100 times smaller, the aligned model was preferred, showing how much the training method matters.

quiz.q: Why is a KL penalty used during the reinforcement learning step?
options: To make the model forget everything
To keep the model close to its supervised starting point, so it does not exploit quirks of the reward model
quiz.explain: Without it, the model could find strange outputs that score highly with the reward model but that humans would dislike.

articles.excerpt: Ask the raw GPT-3 to "Explain the moon landing to a six-year-old," and it might reply with a list of similar requests: "Explain the theory of gravity to a six-year-old. Explain the theory of relativity to a six-year-old." Perfectly reasonable, if your only goal is to continue text that looks like…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Show Your Working: The Prompt That Unlocked Reasoning
articles.subtitle: Chain-of-thought prompting: a few worked examples with steps made giant language models dramatically better at maths and logic
articles.paper_title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

glossary.definition: A series of intermediate reasoning steps written out in natural language before giving a final answer.
Putting a handful of worked examples in the prompt so the model can imitate their format on a new question.
One worked example included in a prompt to show the model what to do.
An ability that is absent in smaller models and appears only once models pass a certain scale.
A standard set of test questions used to compare models fairly.
A follow-up technique that samples many different reasoning chains and takes the most common final answer.

quiz.q: What changes in a chain-of-thought prompt compared with a standard few-shot prompt?
options: Each example answer includes the intermediate reasoning steps, not just the final answer
The prompt is written in code
quiz.explain: The exemplars demonstrate reasoning, so the model writes its own steps before answering new questions.

quiz.q: How did chain-of-thought prompting interact with model size?
options: It helped equally at every size
It only gave large gains for very large models, around 100 billion parameters and up
quiz.explain: Smaller models produced fluent but illogical chains; the benefit emerged at large scale.

quiz.q: Which ablation showed that the reasoning content mattered, not just extra text?
options: Replacing the reasoning with a string of dots of the same length, which did not help
quiz.explain: Simply giving the model more tokens to 'think' with did not help; the actual natural-language steps did.

articles.excerpt: Here is a puzzle for a language model: "The cafeteria had 23 apples. If they used 20 to make lunch and bought 6 more, how many apples do they have?" In early 2022, Google's 540-billion-parameter language model PaLM, one of the largest in the world, could get questions like this wrong when asked for…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Let the Model Look Things Up
articles.subtitle: Retrieval-augmented generation: pairing a language model with a searchable library so it can cite facts instead of guessing
articles.paper_title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

glossary.definition: Knowledge stored implicitly in a model's weights, learned during training.
Knowledge stored outside the model, such as a collection of documents, that the model can search and read.
The component that finds the documents most relevant to a query, here by comparing embedding vectors.
Searching by comparing learned embedding vectors of queries and documents, instead of matching exact keywords.
The sequence-to-sequence model that writes the final answer, conditioned on the question and the retrieved documents.
A task that a person could not reasonably do without looking up facts, such as answering open trivia questions.
A precomputed, searchable store of document embeddings that makes fast nearest-neighbour lookup possible.

quiz.q: What are the two kinds of memory combined in RAG?
options: Parametric memory in the generator's weights and non-parametric memory in a searchable document index
Two copies of the same model
quiz.explain: The generator knows things from training, and the retriever adds fresh, inspectable knowledge from Wikipedia.

quiz.q: How could RAG's knowledge be updated without retraining?
options: By swapping in a newer document index
quiz.explain: The paper showed that replacing an older Wikipedia index with a newer one changed answers about who held various positions, with no retraining.

quiz.q: What kind of retrieval did RAG use?
options: Dense retrieval: comparing embedding vectors of the question and the passages
quiz.explain: A BERT-based encoder turned questions and passages into vectors, and the closest passages were retrieved.

articles.excerpt: Ask a friend who reads a lot, "Who won the 2018 Booker Prize?" They might be sure, they might half remember, or they might confidently get it wrong. Now give that same friend a phone with Wikipedia open. Their answer becomes reliable, up to date, and you can check where it came from. Large language…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Fine-Tune a Giant by Training a Tiny Add-On
articles.subtitle: LoRA: freeze the huge model, learn two skinny matrices, and cut trainable parameters by up to ten thousand times
articles.paper_title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

glossary.definition: Further training a pre-trained model on a specific task or dataset.
A grid of learned numbers inside a layer that transforms its input vector into an output vector.
Roughly, the number of independent directions a matrix can represent. A low-rank matrix can be written as the product of two thin matrices.
A small set of extra trainable parameters added to a frozen pre-trained model so it can learn a new task.
Parameters that are kept fixed during training and receive no updates.
How long a model takes to produce an output once it is deployed.

quiz.q: What does LoRA train during fine-tuning?
options: Only two small low-rank matrices per adapted weight matrix, while the original weights stay frozen
quiz.explain: The weight update is represented as B times A, two thin matrices, and only they are trained.

quiz.q: Why does LoRA add no extra delay when the model is deployed?
options: Because the learned update B times A can be added into the original weight matrix before deployment
Because it uses a faster GPU
It does add a large delay
quiz.explain: W plus BA is just another matrix of the same size, so the deployed model has exactly the original architecture.

quiz.q: Why is B initialised to zero?
options: So that at the start of training the update BA is zero and the model behaves exactly like the pre-trained model
Because random values are not allowed
quiz.explain: Starting from zero means fine-tuning begins from the original model and moves away only as the data demands.

articles.excerpt: Suppose you want GPT-3 to write in your company's style, or to answer questions about Indian tax law. The standard approach in 2020 was full fine-tuning: keep training all 175 billion parameters on your data. Then you have a new 175-billion-parameter model, about 350 gigabytes, just for one task.…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Your Language Model Was the Reward Model All Along
articles.subtitle: Direct Preference Optimization: aligning models with human preferences using one simple loss, no reinforcement learning required
articles.paper_title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model

glossary.definition: Pairs of responses to the same prompt where a person marked one as better (chosen) and the other as worse (rejected).
A frozen copy of the starting model, used as an anchor so the trained model does not drift too far.
A classic way to turn scores into preference probabilities: the chance that A beats B depends on the difference of their scores, passed through a sigmoid.
The logarithm of the probability a model assigns to a piece of text. Language models naturally compute it.
A setting in DPO that controls how strongly the model is held close to the reference model.
An exact formula for the answer to a problem, rather than an answer found by iterative search.

quiz.q: What does DPO remove from the RLHF pipeline?
options: The separately trained reward model and the reinforcement learning loop
quiz.explain: DPO trains the language model directly on preference pairs with a classification-style loss.

quiz.q: In DPO's loss, what makes the loss small?
options: The model assigning the same probability to both responses
The model raising the chosen response's probability, relative to the reference model, more than the rejected one's
The model forgetting the reference model
quiz.explain: The loss depends on the difference between how much the model favours the chosen and the rejected response compared with the reference.

quiz.q: What is the role of the reference model in DPO?
options: It anchors the trained model so it does not drift too far from sensible language
quiz.explain: All probabilities are measured relative to the frozen reference, which plays the role of RLHF's KL penalty.

articles.excerpt: The recipe that turned GPT-3 into ChatGPT is famously fiddly. Train a reward model on human preferences. Then run reinforcement learning with PPO, juggling four large models at once: the policy, a reference copy, the reward model and a value model. Tune a dozen settings, sample text constantly, and…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Small Enough to Share, Strong Enough to Matter
articles.subtitle: LLaMA: open models trained on public data that rivalled giants, and set off an explosion of open-source AI
articles.paper_title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models

glossary.definition: A large model pre-trained on broad data that can be adapted to many downstream tasks.
Releasing a trained model's parameters so others can download, run and modify it.
The total computing cost of running a model for users after training, which grows with model size and usage.
A simpler, cheaper variant of layer normalization that rescales vectors by their root mean square.
An activation function with a learned gate, used in the feed-forward layers, that often trains better than ReLU.
A way of encoding token positions by rotating query and key vectors, so attention naturally depends on relative distance.

quiz.q: What was LLaMA's key strategy compared with models like GPT-3?
options: Make models as large as possible
Train smaller models on many more tokens, so they are cheap to run and still strong
quiz.explain: Optimising for inference cost, not just training cost, favours smaller models trained longer.

quiz.q: What kind of data was LLaMA trained on?
options: Only publicly available datasets, such as filtered web crawls, Wikipedia, books, code, arXiv and Stack Exchange
quiz.explain: The authors deliberately used only publicly available data so their work could be reproduced and shared.

quiz.q: Roughly how did LLaMA-13B compare with GPT-3 (175B)?
options: It was much worse on every benchmark
It outperformed GPT-3 on most benchmarks despite being over ten times smaller
It could not run on a GPU
quiz.explain: A well-trained 13B model beating a 175B model highlighted how much data and training choices matter.

Then Meta released LLaMA: a family of models…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Five Words That Made Models Show Their Working
articles.subtitle: Zero-shot chain of thought: no examples, just a nudge to reason before answering
articles.paper_title: Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners

glossary.definition: Asking a model to do a task with only an instruction or question, and no worked examples in the prompt.
Prompting with a handful of hand-written examples that show step-by-step reasoning before their answers, so the model imitates the style.
The paper's method: add a trigger such as Let's think step by step, let the model write its reasoning, then ask a second time for the final answer.
A short fixed piece of text added to the prompt to steer what kind of continuation the model writes.
The second prompt in Zero-shot-CoT, which feeds the reasoning back and asks for the answer in a fixed format, followed by a simple parser that pulls it out.

quiz.q: What makes Zero-shot-CoT different from the original chain-of-thought prompting?
options: It fine-tunes the model on reasoning data
It needs no hand-written reasoning examples, only a generic trigger phrase
It samples many answers and votes
quiz.explain: Original chain-of-thought prompting needs a few hand-written worked examples per task. Zero-shot-CoT uses the same short trigger for every task.

quiz.q: Why does the method use a second prompt after the reasoning?
options: To check the reasoning for mistakes
To get the final answer in a fixed, easy-to-parse format
quiz.explain: Free-form reasoning can end in many ways. The second prompt, such as Therefore, the answer (arabic numerals) is, makes the model state the answer cleanly so a simple parser can read it.

quiz.q: According to the paper, how did the benefit of Zero-shot-CoT change with model size?
options: It helped little in small models and a lot in large ones
quiz.explain: The gains grew with scale: small models barely improved, while large models such as text-davinci-002 and PaLM 540B improved sharply.

A different set of worked examples for maths, another for logic puzzles, another for dates. Then a team from the University of Tokyo and Google tried…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Passing the Medical Exam Is Not Being a Doctor
articles.subtitle: How Med-PaLM aced exam questions, failed the bedside test, and learned clinical manners from a handful of examples
articles.paper_title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge

glossary.definition: The paper's benchmark: six existing medical question-answering datasets plus one new one, covering licensing exams, research questions and everyday health questions.
A new dataset from the paper made of medical questions that people commonly search for online, answered in free text rather than by picking an option.
Asking a model to reason through the same question several times with some randomness, then taking a majority vote over the final answers.
A short sequence of learned vectors placed in front of a model's input. Unlike written words, the vectors are tuned by gradient descent while the model itself stays frozen.
The paper's method: learn a soft prompt that sits in front of a written instruction and a few clinician-written example answers, adapting a frozen model to medicine cheaply.
Having people, here clinicians and lay users, rate model answers on qualities such as agreement with medical consensus, possible harm, bias and helpfulness.

quiz.q: Why was a high score on multiple-choice medical exams not enough for the authors?
options: Exams are too easy for any model
Choosing an option says little about whether a free-text answer to a real person is accurate, complete and safe
Exam questions were leaked into training data
Doctors do not take multiple-choice exams
quiz.explain: Flan-PaLM reached state-of-the-art exam scores, but clinicians reading its long answers found key gaps. That is why the paper built a human evaluation framework.

quiz.q: What does instruction prompt tuning train?
options: Only a small soft prompt placed in front of written instructions and examples, with the model frozen
A new tokenizer for medical words
quiz.explain: The large model stays frozen. Only a few learned prompt vectors change, guided by a small set of clinician-written examples.

quiz.q: How did Med-PaLM compare with clinicians in the paper's human evaluation?
options: It clearly beat them on every axis
It performed encouragingly but remained inferior to clinicians
It was rated worse than the untuned Flan-PaLM
quiz.explain: The abstract is direct: Med-PaLM performs encouragingly, but remains inferior to clinicians.

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Ask the Model Many Times, Then Take a Vote
articles.subtitle: Self-consistency samples several lines of reasoning and keeps the answer most of them reach
articles.paper_title: Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models

glossary.definition: Showing a language model examples that work through a problem step by step, so it writes out its own steps before giving an answer.
Generating text by always picking the single most likely next token, which gives one fixed output for a prompt.
Generating text by drawing each next token at random according to the model's probabilities, so repeated runs can differ.
A setting that flattens (higher) or sharpens (lower) the model's next-token probabilities before sampling, controlling how varied the outputs are.
Adding up over the details you do not care about, here the different reasoning paths, to score only the thing you do care about, the final answer.

quiz.q: What does self-consistency replace in chain-of-thought prompting?
options: Greedy decoding of a single reasoning path
quiz.explain: Instead of taking the one most likely reasoning path, it samples many and picks the answer most of them agree on.

quiz.q: Why does voting over sampled paths help on reasoning problems?
options: Correct paths tend to reach the same answer, while mistakes tend to scatter across different wrong answers
quiz.explain: A problem with one right answer can be reached in many valid ways, while errors usually lead to different wrong numbers. So the right answer collects the most votes.

quiz.q: When would majority voting make things worse?
options: When the model makes the same mistake more often than it gets the answer right
When more than five paths are sampled
quiz.explain: Voting amplifies whatever answer is most common. If one particular wrong answer is more likely than the right one, more samples make the vote settle on that wrong answer.

articles.excerpt: Ask a language model a tricky word problem once and it may slip on step three and confidently give the wrong number. Ask it again, letting it phrase things a little differently, and it may get it right. Ask ten times and you will often see one answer turning up again and again. A Google team turned…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Letting a Language Model Back Up and Try Again
articles.subtitle: Tree of Thoughts turns one-shot reasoning into a search: propose ideas, judge them, and abandon dead ends
articles.paper_title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models

glossary.definition: Prompting a language model to write out intermediate reasoning steps before its answer, in a single left-to-right pass.
In Tree of Thoughts, one coherent chunk of text that is a meaningful intermediate step, such as one equation, a writing plan, or one word placed in a crossword.
The part of Tree of Thoughts where the language model itself judges how promising a partial solution is, either by valuing it alone or by voting among several.
A search that expands every kept option one level at a time; Tree of Thoughts keeps only the best few at each level.
A search that follows one option as deep as it can and backs up to try another when it reaches a dead end.
Abandoning a partial solution that has turned out to be hopeless and returning to an earlier point to try a different option.
A puzzle: combine four given numbers with addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, using each number once, to make exactly 24.

quiz.q: What can Tree of Thoughts do that plain chain-of-thought prompting cannot?
options: Explore several candidate steps, judge them, and back up from dead ends
Train the model's weights on the task
quiz.explain: Chain of thought commits to one left-to-right path. Tree of Thoughts keeps several partial solutions, evaluates them, and abandons the hopeless ones.

quiz.q: Who judges whether a partial solution looks promising in Tree of Thoughts?
options: The same language model, prompted to evaluate states
quiz.explain: The state evaluator is the language model itself, prompted to value a state or vote between states. No extra training is needed.

quiz.q: What is the main price of Tree of Thoughts?
options: It makes many more model calls per problem, so it costs more time and money
It cannot solve the Game of 24
quiz.explain: Proposing and evaluating many branches means many calls. That is worthwhile for hard search problems and wasteful for easy ones.

articles.excerpt: Give a strong language model the numbers 4, 9, 10 and 13, and ask it to make 24 with plus, minus, times and divide. A child with a pencil will try something, see it go nowhere, cross it out and try again. The model cannot cross anything out. It writes its first step, then keeps building on it, even…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: The Engineering Playbook of Llama 3
articles.subtitle: How Meta built an open 405-billion-parameter model with a plain Transformer, very careful data, 16,000 GPUs and six rounds of tasting
articles.paper_title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models

glossary.definition: A Transformer where every parameter is used for every token, as opposed to a mixture-of-experts model that routes each token through only some parts.
An attention variant where several query heads share one key and value head, shrinking the memory needed to cache keys and values.
The stored keys and values of earlier tokens, kept during generation so they are not recomputed for every new token.
Splitting training across GPUs in four ways at once: within weight matrices (tensor), across sequence chunks (context), across layers (pipeline) and across batches (data).
Generating several answers to a prompt, scoring them with a reward model, and keeping the best as new fine-tuning data.
Training a model directly on pairs of preferred and rejected answers, without a separate reinforcement learning loop.
Training a model on more tokens than the compute-optimal amount for its size, so a small model becomes stronger and cheaper to serve.

quiz.q: Llama 3's flagship has about 405 billion parameters and was trained on about 15.6 trillion tokens. Using the rule compute ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens, roughly how much training compute is that?
quiz.explain: 6 × 4.05 × 10^11 × 1.56 × 10^13 ≈ 3.8 × 10^25, which matches the figure the paper reports.

quiz.q: Why did the authors choose a plain dense Transformer instead of a mixture of experts?
options: Mixture of experts cannot be trained
To maximise training stability and simplicity at scale, putting the effort into data and infrastructure
quiz.explain: The paper deliberately chose a standard architecture to reduce risk, and spent its innovation on data quality, scale and post-training.

quiz.q: What does grouped-query attention save during generation?
options: Memory for the key-value cache, because many query heads share each key and value head
quiz.explain: With 8 key-value heads instead of 128, the cache per token is 16 times smaller, which matters a lot at long context lengths.

The menu is deliberately ordinary, but the ingredients, the stations and the…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: When One GPU Is Not Enough
articles.subtitle: Megatron-LM: slicing each Transformer layer across GPUs, the trick that let language models grow past a single chip
articles.paper_title: Megatron-LM: Training Multi-Billion Parameter Language Models Using Model Parallelism

glossary.definition: Training with many GPUs that each hold a full copy of the model and process different examples, then average their gradients.
Splitting a single model across several GPUs because it is too large to fit on one.
A form of model parallelism that splits the matrices inside each layer across GPUs, so every GPU computes part of every layer.
A form of model parallelism that puts different layers on different GPUs, passing activations along like an assembly line.
A communication step where every GPU contributes a set of numbers and every GPU receives their sum.
How close a multi-GPU system comes to the ideal speedup. 100% means doubling the GPUs doubles the throughput.

quiz.q: What problem does model parallelism solve that data parallelism cannot?
options: A model whose parameters and training state do not fit in one GPU's memory
quiz.explain: Data parallelism copies the whole model to every GPU, which fails once the model is larger than a single GPU's memory.

quiz.q: How does Megatron-LM split a Transformer's feed-forward layer?
options: The first weight matrix by columns and the second by rows, so each GPU can apply the activation independently and only one sum is needed at the end
By giving each GPU a different training example
By putting each layer on a different continent
quiz.explain: Column-then-row splitting keeps the non-linear activation local to each GPU and needs just one all-reduce in the forward pass.

quiz.q: What made Megatron's approach easy to adopt?
options: It needed a new programming language
It required only a few communication operations added to ordinary PyTorch code, with no new compiler
It removed the need for GPUs
quiz.explain: The authors emphasised a simple implementation using existing tools, which helped it spread widely.

articles.excerpt: In 2019, one of the best GPUs for AI had 32 gigabytes of memory. That sounds like a lot until you do the arithmetic for a language model with 8 billion parameters. Just storing the weights, the gradients and the optimizer's bookkeeping during training takes well over 100 gigabytes. The model simply…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Faster Attention by Doing More Maths
articles.subtitle: FlashAttention: the GPU's real bottleneck was memory traffic, and fixing it made exact attention several times faster
articles.paper_title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness

glossary.definition: High Bandwidth Memory: the GPU's large main memory, tens of gigabytes, which is big but comparatively slow to read and write.
The GPU's small on-chip memory, close to the compute units: extremely fast but only a few hundred kilobytes per unit.
Designed around the cost of moving data between levels of memory, not just around the number of arithmetic operations.
Breaking a large computation into small blocks that fit in fast memory, and processing them one at a time.
Computing a softmax incrementally, block by block, by keeping a running maximum and running sum and rescaling as new blocks arrive.
A single program that runs on the GPU to perform one operation, such as a matrix multiply or a whole attention computation.
Recalculating intermediate values during the backward pass instead of storing them, trading extra arithmetic for less memory.

quiz.q: What was the main bottleneck in standard attention on GPUs, according to the paper?
options: Reading and writing the large attention matrix to and from slow GPU main memory
quiz.explain: Attention spends most of its time moving data to and from HBM, not computing. FlashAttention reduces that traffic.

quiz.q: Does FlashAttention approximate attention?
options: Yes, it drops most of the attention weights
No, it computes exactly the same result as standard attention, just in a different order
Yes, it only attends to nearby tokens
quiz.explain: It is exact. The speedup comes from reorganising the computation, not from skipping any of it.

quiz.q: How can FlashAttention compute a softmax without seeing all the scores at once?
options: It keeps a running maximum and running sum, and rescales earlier partial results when a new block changes the maximum
It sorts all the scores first
quiz.explain: The online softmax trick lets each block be processed and combined correctly as it streams through fast memory.

articles.excerpt: For five years after the Transformer arrived, a small army of researchers tried to make attention faster. Most of their ideas approximated it: only attend to nearby words, or to a random sample, or to a compressed summary. Many of these methods cut the number of calculations dramatically.…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Borrowing an Old OS Trick to Serve Chatbots
articles.subtitle: PagedAttention and vLLM: managing a model's memory like virtual memory pages, and serving several times more users per GPU
articles.paper_title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention

glossary.definition: Stored keys and values for every token generated so far, kept so the model does not recompute them at each new token.
How many requests or tokens a serving system completes per second.
Processing many users' requests together on the GPU so its parallel hardware is used efficiently.
Wasted memory caused by reserving space that is not used, or by gaps between allocations that are too small to reuse.
An operating system technique that maps a program's contiguous-looking addresses onto scattered physical pages of memory.
In PagedAttention, the map from each sequence's logical blocks of tokens to the physical memory blocks where their keys and values are stored.
Letting several users share the same memory until one of them needs to change it, and only then making a private copy.

quiz.q: What is the KV cache?
options: Stored attention keys and values for all previous tokens, reused when generating each new token
quiz.explain: Without it, generating each token would require recomputing keys and values for the whole sequence.

quiz.q: What problem did existing serving systems have with the KV cache?
options: They stored it on the CPU
They reserved large contiguous chunks for the maximum possible length, wasting most of the memory through fragmentation
They deleted it after every token
quiz.explain: The paper found that existing systems used only a small fraction of KV cache memory for actual token data.

quiz.q: How does PagedAttention store each sequence's KV cache?
options: In one big contiguous block sized for the maximum length
In small fixed-size blocks that can sit anywhere in memory, tracked by a block table, like pages in virtual memory
quiz.explain: Non-contiguous blocks are allocated on demand, so almost no memory is wasted and blocks can be shared between sequences.

In 2023, researchers at UC Berkeley looked at how existing systems used GPU memory while generating text, and found…

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Teaching Neural Networks to Count in Whole Numbers
articles.subtitle: How 8-bit integers, a little algebra and practice during training made fast on-phone vision practical
articles.paper_title: Quantization and Training of Neural Networks for Efficient Integer-Arithmetic-Only Inference

glossary.definition: Storing and computing numbers with a small set of allowed values, such as the 256 values of an 8-bit integer, instead of full floating point.
The real-number step between two neighbouring integer levels. With scale S, moving the integer up by one adds S to the real value.
The integer that stands for the real value 0.0, chosen so that zero is represented exactly.
A wider register, here 32 bits, that collects the running sum of many 8-bit products without overflowing.
Rounding values to the integer grid during training while still computing in floating point, so the network learns to tolerate the rounding it will meet at inference.
Merging a batch normalization layer's scale and shift into the weights and bias of the convolution before it, so inference needs one layer instead of two.

quiz.q: In the scheme r = S(q - Z), why must the zero-point Z be an integer?
options: So that the real value 0.0 is represented exactly, which matters for zero-padding
So the scale can be negative
quiz.explain: Zero-padding and ReLU produce many exact zeros. If 0.0 fell between two integer levels, every padded value would carry a small systematic error.

quiz.q: How does integer-only inference apply the real-valued rescale factor M = S1 S2 / S3?
options: As a fixed-point integer multiply followed by a bit shift
With a lookup table of logarithms
quiz.explain: M is written as M0 times 2 to the power -n, with M0 between 0.5 and 1 stored as a 32-bit fixed-point integer. Multiplying by M0 and shifting right by n needs only integer hardware.

quiz.q: Why train with fake quantization instead of rounding a finished float model?
options: The network learns weights that still work after rounding, which matters most for compact models
It removes the need for biases
quiz.explain: Rounding after training adds errors the network never saw. Simulating the rounding during training lets it adapt, keeping accuracy high even for efficient models like MobileNets.

articles.subject: ml
articles.title: Why Chatbots Cling to Their First Few Words
articles.subtitle: Attention sinks: the odd habit that broke long conversations, and the four-token fix that keeps them stable
articles.paper_title: Efficient Streaming Language Models with Attention Sinks

glossary.definition: The stored keys and values of earlier tokens, kept so a language model does not recompute them for every new token.
The maximum number of tokens a model was trained to attend to at once.
Keeping only the most recent tokens in the KV cache and dropping older ones as new tokens arrive.
An early token, usually the very first, that receives a large share of attention regardless of its meaning.
A measure of how surprised a language model is by text. Lower is better; a sudden jump means the model has broken down.
The function that turns attention scores into weights that are positive and add up to exactly 1.

quiz.q: What goes wrong when a model with plain sliding window attention evicts its very first tokens?
options: Perplexity jumps sharply and text quality collapses
quiz.explain: The first tokens act as attention sinks. Removing them disturbs the attention pattern the model learned, and quality collapses.

quiz.q: Why do models dump attention on the first token?
options: It always holds the most important word
Softmax weights must add up to 1, so heads with nothing to attend to need somewhere harmless to put the leftover weight, and the first token is visible to every later token
It is a bug in training code
quiz.explain: When a head finds nothing relevant, it still has to distribute its weight. The first token, seen by every position during training, becomes the default dumping ground.

quiz.q: What does StreamingLLM NOT do?
options: Keep generation stable over very long streams
Let the model recall facts from text that has left the window
quiz.explain: Tokens outside the sinks and the recent window are gone. StreamingLLM keeps the model fluent, not omniscient; it does not extend what the model can remember.

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Reading Constraints Like a Pro
articles.subtitle: Big-O without fear: how to know if your idea is fast enough before you write a line

glossary.definition: How the number of steps an algorithm takes grows as the input gets bigger.
A notation that describes the growth rate of an algorithm's cost, ignoring constant factors and smaller terms.
The limits given in a problem, such as n up to 100,000, which tell you how fast your solution must be.
How the extra memory an algorithm uses grows as the input gets bigger.
The average cost per operation over a long sequence, even if a few individual operations are expensive.

quiz.q: A problem says n can be up to 200,000. Which complexity is the safest target?
quiz.explain: n^2 would be about 4 x 10^10 steps, far too many. n log n is roughly 3.6 million steps, comfortably fast.

quiz.q: What is the Big-O of a loop over i from 0 to n, with an inner loop over j from 0 to i?
quiz.explain: The inner loop runs 0 + 1 + ... + (n-1), about n^2 / 2 times. Dropping the constant 1/2 gives O(n^2).

quiz.q: Why do we drop constants in Big-O?
options: Big-O describes how cost grows, and for large inputs the growth rate dominates the constant
quiz.explain: Big-O is about shape of growth. An O(n) loop with 3 steps per item still grows linearly, and will eventually beat any O(n^2) loop.

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: The Toolbox Every Fast Solution Is Built From
articles.subtitle: The C++ STL you will use every day, what each tool costs, and when to reach for it

glossary.definition: A standard library object that stores a collection of values, such as a vector, set or map.
A small object that points at a position inside a container, like a bookmark you can move forward and read through.
A function that tells sort or an ordered container which of two values should come first.
A structure that turns each key into a number and uses it to jump straight to a bucket, giving average constant-time lookups.
A tree that keeps its keys in sorted order and its height around log n, so searches, inserts and deletes stay fast.
The average cost per operation over a long sequence, even when a few individual operations are expensive.

quiz.q: You need to know, for each new number, the smallest stored number that is at least as big. Which container fits?
quiz.explain: A set keeps values sorted, and lower_bound finds the first value that is not less than x in O(log n). An unordered_set has no order to search.

quiz.q: What does a default std::priority_queue<int> give you from top()?
quiz.explain: The default priority_queue is a max-heap. For a min-heap, use priority_queue<int, vector<int>, greater<int>>.

quiz.q: Why can unordered_map be risky in competitive programming?
options: Its average O(1) can degrade badly when many keys collide
It uses more memory than a vector of the same size in every case
quiz.explain: Lookups are O(1) on average, but carefully chosen inputs can make many keys land in the same bucket, making each lookup slow.

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: What to Do When You Have Never Seen the Problem
articles.subtitle: A repeatable way to go from a blank page to a working, explained solution

glossary.definition: The most direct solution that tries every possibility. Usually too slow, but always a correct starting point.
The part of a solution that dominates its running time, such as an inner loop that repeats work.
A fact that stays true at every step of an algorithm, which you can rely on when reasoning about it.
A reusable problem-solving technique, like two pointers or binary search on the answer, that fits a family of problems.
An unusual input at the boundaries, such as an empty array, one element, or all values equal, that often breaks code.

quiz.q: What should you do right after restating the problem and trying a small example?
options: Describe a brute force and its complexity
Pick a data structure at random
quiz.explain: A brute force proves you understand the problem, gives a fallback, and shows exactly where the time goes, which tells you what to optimise.

quiz.q: A problem says 'subarray' and all numbers are positive. Which pattern is a strong first guess?
quiz.explain: Contiguous ranges plus positive numbers mean the window sum only grows when you extend it and only shrinks when you move the left end, which is exactly what a sliding window needs.

quiz.q: Your brute force recomputes the sum of the same ranges again and again. What is the usual fix?
options: Precompute something once, such as prefix sums, and reuse it
quiz.explain: Repeated work is the bottleneck. Storing it once, as prefix sums, a hash map or a DP table, removes the repetition.

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Trusting the Function You Are Still Writing
articles.subtitle: Recursion explained: base cases, the leap of faith, the call stack, and how to count what it costs

glossary.definition: A function solving a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem.
The smallest version of the problem, answered directly without another recursive call. It stops the recursion.
The step that reduces the problem to one or more smaller versions and combines their answers.
The memory where the computer keeps each unfinished function call, with its own variables, until it returns.
A drawing of every call a recursive function makes, used to count total work.
A crash that happens when recursion goes so deep that the call stack runs out of memory.

quiz.q: What happens if a recursive function has no reachable base case?
options: It keeps calling itself until the call stack runs out of memory and the program crashes
quiz.explain: Without a base case the calls never stop, each one using stack memory, until a stack overflow.

quiz.q: How many calls does the naive recursive Fibonacci make for fib(5)?
quiz.explain: fib(5) calls fib(4) and fib(3), which call further down; drawing the tree gives 15 calls in total, because the same values are recomputed many times.

quiz.q: What is the 'leap of faith' in recursion?
options: Assuming the recursive call correctly solves the smaller problem, and only checking that you use its answer correctly
quiz.explain: You reason about one level at a time: if the smaller call is right, is this level right? Together with a correct base case, that proves the whole function.
