Ask someone comfortable with recursion, and the solution is often three or four lines that look almost too simple to be right. The difference is not…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: A Row of Light Switches Inside Every Number
articles.subtitle: Binary, AND, OR, XOR and shifts: the small toolkit behind bitmasks, fast tricks and half of competitive programming

glossary.definition: A single binary digit, 0 or 1. An int in C++ is typically 32 bits; a long long is 64.
An operator that works on each bit position separately: AND (&), OR (|), XOR (^), NOT (~).
Moving all bits left or right. Shifting left by k multiplies by 2 to the power k; shifting right divides, rounding down for non-negative numbers.
A number whose 1 bits mark the positions you care about, used to test, set or clear those bits.
The standard way computers store negative integers, where -x is ~x + 1.
The rightmost bit, worth 1. It decides whether a number is odd or even.

quiz.q: What is 13 & 6? (13 is 1101, 6 is 0110 in binary)
quiz.explain: AND keeps a 1 only where both numbers have a 1. 1101 & 0110 = 0100, which is 4.

quiz.q: How do you check whether bit k of x is set?
quiz.explain: Shift x right by k so bit k lands in the last position, then AND with 1 to read just that bit.

quiz.q: Why write 1LL << 40 instead of 1 << 40?
options: 1 is an int, usually 32 bits, so shifting it by 40 is undefined; 1LL is a 64-bit long long
quiz.explain: Shifting a 32-bit int by 32 or more is undefined behaviour. Making the 1 a long long gives 64 bits of room.

articles.excerpt: Here is a puzzle interviewers love: every number in an array appears twice, except one. Find it, in one pass, with no extra memory. A hash map works but uses memory. Sorting works but is slow. The real answer is a single line: XOR all the numbers together. Pairs cancel to zero, and the lonely…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Answering a Million Range Questions Instantly
articles.subtitle: Prefix sums: one pass of preparation that turns every range sum into a single subtraction

glossary.definition: The total of all elements from the start of an array up to a given position.
A question about a contiguous slice of an array, such as the sum of elements from index l to index r.
Doing work once, up front, so that many later questions become cheap to answer.
An array that stores how much each element changes compared with the one before it. Its prefix sums rebuild the original array.
An extra value placed at the edge of a data structure, like a leading zero, so edge cases disappear from the code.

quiz.q: With P[i] defined as the sum of the first i elements (so P[0] = 0), what is the sum of a[l..r] (0-indexed, inclusive)?
quiz.explain: P[r + 1] covers a[0..r] and P[l] covers a[0..l-1]. Subtracting removes everything before l.

quiz.q: Why does the leading zero in the prefix array help?
options: It removes the special case for ranges that start at index 0
quiz.explain: Without it, a range starting at 0 would need P[-1]. The extra 0 at the front acts as a sentinel, so one formula works for every range.

quiz.q: You must add 5 to every element in 100,000 different ranges, then print the final array once. What is the best tool?
options: Update each range element by element
Rebuild the prefix sum after every update
A difference array, then one prefix-sum pass at the end
quiz.explain: A difference array records each range update in O(1) with two edits. One prefix-sum pass at the end turns it back into the final array.

articles.excerpt: Your interviewer hands you an array of 100,000 numbers and then asks 100,000 questions: "What is the sum from index 3,120 to index 88,004?" If you add up each range from scratch, you could be doing ten billion additions. Your program times out before the third coffee. There is a trick that answers…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Two Fingers on a Sorted List
articles.subtitle: The two pointers pattern: squeeze from both ends, and prove you never skip the answer

practice_problems.name: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted

glossary.definition: Here, simply an index into the array that marks a position you are looking at.
Two indices that start at the two ends of an array and move toward each other.
Two indices that both move left to right, one leading and one following, also called fast and slow pointers.
A fact that stays true at every step of a loop, which is what lets you prove the algorithm is correct.
Always moving in one direction, never backwards. Both pointers only ever move forward, which bounds the total work.

quiz.q: In a sorted array, the current pair sums to more than the target. Which pointer moves?
quiz.explain: The right value is the largest in play. Pairing it with anything at or after left is still too big, so it can be discarded by moving right leftwards.

quiz.q: Why is the two-pointer scan O(n) and not O(n squared)?
options: Each step moves one pointer inward and neither ever moves back, so there are at most n steps
It stops at the first pair
It only works on small arrays
quiz.explain: The gap between the pointers shrinks by one every step, so the loop runs at most n times.

quiz.q: In 3Sum, why do we sort first?
options: So that for each fixed first number, the remaining pair can be found with two pointers and duplicates can be skipped easily
Because the output must be sorted
quiz.explain: Sorting enables the inward squeeze for the remaining two numbers and puts equal values next to each other, so duplicates are easy to skip.

articles.excerpt: Two friends are looking for a pair of books on a long, sorted shelf whose prices add up to exactly 500 rupees. One starts at the cheap end, the other at the expensive end. Each time they compare, one of them takes a step inward. Within one walk along the shelf, they either find the pair or prove it…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: The Caterpillar That Reads Arrays in One Pass
articles.subtitle: Sliding windows: grow the right edge, shrink the left, and never look back

glossary.definition: A contiguous stretch of an array or string, described by a left and a right index.
A window that always contains exactly k elements and slides one step at a time.
A window whose right edge grows and whose left edge shrinks according to a validity rule.
The summary you keep about the current window, such as its sum or a count of each character, updated as elements enter and leave.
Averaged over the whole run. Each element enters and leaves the window once, so the total work is linear even if one step does a lot.

quiz.q: In a variable-size window, why must the shrinking step be a while loop and not an if?
options: Adding one element can make the window invalid by more than one step, so you may need to remove several elements
quiz.explain: One new element can break the rule badly, for example a long run of repeats. You keep removing from the left until the window is valid again.

quiz.q: Why can a plain sliding window fail for 'shortest subarray with sum at least k' when negative numbers exist?
options: Shrinking the window may increase its sum, so 'shrink while too big' no longer moves toward the answer
Hash maps do not support negatives
quiz.explain: The window logic assumes growing makes the sum bigger and shrinking makes it smaller. Negatives break that, so prefix sums with a monotonic deque are used instead.

quiz.q: What is the total time of a sliding window over n elements?
options: O(n squared) because of the nested while loop
O(n), because each element enters once and leaves at most once
quiz.explain: The inner while loop looks nested, but the left pointer only moves forward, so across the whole run it moves at most n times.

articles.excerpt: "Find the longest substring without repeating characters." A brute force checks every substring: about n²/2 of them, each checked for repeats. On a string of 100,000 characters, that is billions of steps. There is a way to read the string once, left to right, keeping only a small summary of what is…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: The Notebook That Turns O(n²) Into O(n)
articles.subtitle: Hash map patterns: remember what you have seen, count, and group by a key

glossary.definition: A structure that stores key-value pairs and finds a key in constant time on average by turning it into a bucket number.
The value you still need to reach a target, such as target minus the current number.
A hash map from each item to how many times it has appeared.
A standard form of an item, such as its sorted letters, chosen so that items that belong together get the same key.
When two different keys land in the same bucket of a hash table, which slows lookups if it happens a lot.

quiz.q: In Two Sum, when should you insert the current number into the map?
options: It does not matter for any input
quiz.explain: Checking first prevents pairing a number with itself, for example target 8 with a single 4. Inserting afterwards keeps the answer correct.

quiz.q: Which canonical key groups 'eat', 'tea' and 'ate' together?
quiz.explain: All anagrams have the same letters, so sorting gives the same string. Length or first letter would also group words that are not anagrams.

quiz.q: What is the worst-case time of a single unordered_map lookup?
quiz.explain: It is O(1) on average, but if many keys land in the same bucket, a lookup may scan all of them.

articles.excerpt: Two Sum is probably the most famous interview question in the world. Given a list of numbers, find two that add up to a target. Most people's first answer checks every pair, and with 100,000 numbers that is about five billion checks. The fix is so small it feels like cheating: keep a notebook of…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: The Gambler Who Knows When to Walk Away
articles.subtitle: Kadane's algorithm finds the best subarray in one pass by asking one question at every step

glossary.definition: A contiguous, non-empty slice of an array, like elements 3 to 7. Order is kept and nothing is skipped.
The largest sum of any subarray that ends exactly at the current index. Kadane's algorithm keeps only this one number.
The best answer seen so far over all positions, updated after each step.
Solving a problem by building answers to small subproblems and reusing them, instead of recomputing.

quiz.q: At index i, what does Kadane's algorithm decide?
options: Whether to extend the best subarray ending at i-1 or start fresh at i
quiz.explain: The best subarray ending at i either continues the best one ending at i-1, or starts at i alone. Take whichever sum is larger.

quiz.q: What does a correct Kadane's implementation return for [-3, -1, -2]?
quiz.explain: Subarrays must be non-empty, so the best is the single element -1. Initialising the answer to 0 is a classic bug.

quiz.q: Why does Maximum Product Subarray need two running values?
options: A very negative product can become the largest after multiplying by a negative number
It does not; one value is enough
quiz.explain: Multiplying by a negative flips signs, so the smallest product so far can turn into the biggest. Track both the maximum and minimum ending here.

articles.excerpt: A trader looks back at a year of daily profits and losses: up 3, down 7, up 4, up 2, down 1, up 5. What stretch of consecutive days would have made the most money? Checking every start and end day is easy to write and slow to run: about n² stretches. Jon Bentley tells the story of this problem in…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Mirrors, Anagrams and Letter Counts
articles.subtitle: String patterns for interviews: count arrays of 26, expand around the centre, and build strings without hidden quadratic costs

complexity.time: O(n) for counting and two-pointer checks; O(n^2) for expand-around-centre

glossary.definition: An array of 26 counters, one per lowercase letter, used instead of a hash map when the alphabet is small and fixed.
A word formed by rearranging all the letters of another, like 'listen' and 'silent'.
A string that reads the same forwards and backwards, like 'racecar' or 'abba'.
Finding palindromes by starting from each possible middle and growing outwards while both ends match.
A string that cannot be changed in place, so every 'change' creates a new copy. In C++ std::string is mutable, but s = s + c still builds a new string.

quiz.q: How do you check if two lowercase strings are anagrams in O(n)?
options: Sort both and compare in O(n)
Count letters with one array of 26: add for the first string, subtract for the second, and check all zero
quiz.explain: Anagrams have identical letter counts. One frequency array, incremented for one string and decremented for the other, ends at all zeros exactly when they match.

quiz.q: How many centres does expand-around-centre try for a string of length n?
options: 2n − 1, because even-length palindromes have a centre between two characters
quiz.explain: Each character is an odd-length centre, and each gap between neighbours is an even-length centre: n + (n − 1) centres.

quiz.q: Why is s = s + c inside a loop over n characters slow?
options: Each step copies the whole string built so far, so the total work is O(n squared)
quiz.explain: s + c creates a new string of the current length each time. Use s += c or push_back, which append in amortised O(1).

articles.excerpt: String questions look endless: anagrams, palindromes, "longest substring with at most k changes", "group words that are rearrangements of each other". Then you notice something. Almost all of them reduce to two tools you already know: counting letters, and two pointers moving in from the ends or…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Peeling a Grid Like an Onion
articles.subtitle: Spiral order, in-place rotation, set-zeroes with O(1) space and the staircase search, all from careful row and column bounds

complexity.time: O(m · n) for traversals, O(m + n) for the staircase search

glossary.definition: Storing or visiting a grid row by row, left to right, so cell (r, c) of an m by n grid sits at position r · n + c.
One ring of a matrix: the outermost rows and columns that remain after the outer rings have been removed.
Flipping a square matrix over its main diagonal, so the value at (i, j) moves to (j, i).
Two small arrays of row and column offsets, such as up, right, down, left, used to step to neighbours with one loop instead of four copies of code.
Reusing part of the input itself, such as the first row and column, to store flags, so no extra array is needed.
Searching a matrix whose rows and columns are both sorted by starting at the top-right corner and stepping left or down, removing one column or row per step.

quiz.q: In spiral order, why must you check top ≤ bottom before walking the bottom row?
options: To avoid an out-of-bounds access in every case
After the top row is consumed, the bottom row may be the same row, and walking it again repeats values
Because the bottom row is walked left to right
quiz.explain: On a matrix with an odd number of rows, the last layer is a single row. Once it is consumed as the top row, top passes bottom, and without the check it would be printed a second time backwards.

quiz.q: Which pair of in-place steps rotates a square matrix 90 degrees clockwise?
options: Reverse every row, then reverse every column
Reverse every column, then transpose twice
quiz.explain: Transposing sends row i to column i; reversing each row then puts the first column on the right. For [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]] you get [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]].

quiz.q: In the staircase search starting at the top-right, the current value is larger than the target. What can you discard?
quiz.explain: Every value below the current one in its column is at least as large, so none can equal the smaller target. Move one column left.

articles.excerpt: "Print this matrix in spiral order" sounds like a warm-up. Then you write it and the output for a 3 by 4 grid repeats a 6, or a single-row matrix comes out doubled, or the code walks off the edge. Grid problems are rarely about a clever algorithm. They are about keeping four boundaries straight…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: A Receptionist Watching the Door
articles.subtitle: Interval problems: sort by start to merge, and sweep +1 and -1 events to count overlaps

glossary.definition: A range with a start and an end, such as a meeting from 9:00 to 10:30 or an array range from index 3 to 7.
Two intervals overlap when one starts before the other ends.
Replacing overlapping intervals with one interval that covers all of them.
A technique that processes events in sorted order, as if a line moved across the timeline, keeping a running state.
A point where something changes, such as an interval starting (+1) or ending (-1).

quiz.q: After sorting intervals by start, when does the current interval overlap the last merged one?
options: When its start is at most the last merged end
quiz.explain: Sorted by start, a new interval overlaps the previous merged block exactly when it starts before (or at) that block's end.

quiz.q: To find the maximum number of guests present at once, what do you sort?
options: All arrival and departure events by time
quiz.explain: Turn each guest into a +1 at arrival and a -1 at departure, sort all events, and track the running count.

quiz.q: Two events happen at the same time: one departure and one arrival. Which should be processed first if a guest leaving at 5 and one arriving at 5 do not overlap?
quiz.explain: If touching endpoints do not count as overlapping, process the departure first so the count does not briefly include both guests.

articles.excerpt: A calendar app must show your busy blocks, merging back-to-back and overlapping meetings into single stretches. A restaurant wants to know the most customers it ever had at once. A booking system must check whether a new reservation clashes with existing ones. These sound like different problems.…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Every Number Has a Seat With Its Name on It
articles.subtitle: Cyclic sort: when values lie in 1 to n, swap each one to its own index and read missing and duplicate numbers straight off the array

practice_problems.name: Find All Numbers Disappeared in an Array
Find All Duplicates in an Array

glossary.definition: An in-place method for arrays whose values lie in 1 to n: repeatedly swap the current value into index value − 1 until the current slot holds its own value or a value with no free home.
The index a value belongs at, v − 1 for value v when values run from 1 to n.
After cyclic sort, a value sitting at an index that is not its home, because its home is already taken by an equal value or because it has no home in range.
A group of positions whose values point to each other's indices in a loop. Swapping each value home resolves one cycle completely.
A related trick that records 'value v was seen' by changing the sign of the element at index v − 1, instead of moving values.

quiz.q: Cyclic sort runs a while loop that sometimes does not advance i. Why is it still O(n)?
options: The loop runs at most twice per index
Every swap puts one value permanently into its home, so there are at most n swaps in total, plus n advances of i
It is actually O(n log n)
quiz.explain: A value placed at its home is never moved again. So the total number of swaps over the whole run is at most n, and i advances n times.

quiz.q: Why does the swap condition check a[v − 1] != v rather than i != v − 1?
options: If an equal copy already sits at the home index, swapping would exchange two equal values forever
quiz.explain: With duplicates, the home may already hold v. Checking i != v − 1 would keep swapping v with v and never advance. Checking the home's content stops the loop.

quiz.q: After cyclic sort of [3, 4, −1, 1], the array is [1, −1, 3, 4]. What is the first missing positive?
quiz.explain: Scan for the first index i where a[i] != i + 1. Index 1 holds −1 instead of 2, so 2 is missing.

articles.excerpt: You are given n numbers, each between 1 and n, and asked which ones are missing. A hash set solves it in O(n) time, but the interviewer adds: "Now do it with O(1) extra space." Sorting takes O(n log n) time. Is there a way to get both? There is, and it rests on one fact that most problems never…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Everyone's Product but Your Own, Without Dividing
articles.subtitle: A classic interview walkthrough: prefix and suffix products, two passes, and the O(1) extra space trick

glossary.definition: The product of all elements before a given position, like a running total but multiplying.
The product of all elements after a given position.
Scanning an array once from the left and once from the right, combining what each pass learned.
The array you must return. Problems often say it does not count as extra space, which allows reusing it as a workspace.

quiz.q: For index i, the answer equals...
options: The total product divided by nums[i]
The product of everything left of i times the product of everything right of i
quiz.explain: Everything except nums[i] is exactly the left part and the right part, so multiply their products.

quiz.q: Why is dividing the total product by nums[i] a bad idea?
options: It fails when nums[i] is 0, and the problem forbids division anyway
quiz.explain: A zero in the array makes the total 0 and division by zero undefined. The prefix-suffix method needs no division at all.

quiz.q: How does the O(1) extra space version avoid a separate suffix array?
options: It recomputes suffixes for each i
It stores prefix products in the output array, then sweeps from the right with a single running suffix variable
It cannot; O(n) space is required
quiz.explain: The output array holds left products after the first pass; one variable carries the right product during the second pass.

articles.excerpt: "For each position, return the product of every other number in the array. No division. O(n) time." It is one of the most asked medium questions at large tech companies, and it is a perfect test of one idea: splitting "everything except me" into "everything before me" and "everything after me".…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Filling the Potholes Between Buildings
articles.subtitle: Trapping Rain Water three ways: prefix maxima, two pointers and a monotonic stack, all from one idea about water levels

complexity.space: O(1) with two pointers, O(n) with prefix arrays or a stack

glossary.definition: An array of non-negative bar heights, each bar one unit wide, standing side by side.
The height water reaches above a given bar: the smaller of the tallest bar to its left and the tallest bar to its right.
For each index, the largest value from the start of the array up to and including that index.
For each index, the largest value from that index to the end of the array.
Of the two tallest walls around a bar, the shorter one, which decides how high water can rise before spilling over.

quiz.q: Heights [0, 2, 0, 4, 1, 0, 3, 1]. How much water sits above index 5 (height 0)?
quiz.explain: Tallest to the left is 4, tallest to the right is 3, so the level is min(4, 3) = 3, and 3 − 0 = 3 units sit above it.

quiz.q: In the two-pointer method, why is it safe to settle the left bar when h[left] < h[right]?
options: Because the left side is always shorter
Because some bar on the right is at least h[right] > h[left], so the left side's maximum is the bottleneck for this bar
quiz.explain: The right side already contains a wall taller than the current left bar, so the water level at left is decided by left_max alone.

quiz.q: How does Container With Most Water differ from Trapping Rain Water?
options: It picks just two walls to hold one rectangle of water and ignores the bars between them; trapping water sums water above every bar
quiz.explain: Container treats the lines as thin walls with nothing between them and maximises one area. Trapping water fills every dip in the solid bars.

articles.excerpt: A row of buildings of different heights stands side by side, each one unit wide. It rains hard. How many units of water stay trapped in the gaps between them after the rain stops? Trapping Rain Water is one of the most famous hard interview problems, and for good reason. The brute force is easy,…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: The Election Where Rivals Cancel Out
articles.subtitle: Boyer-Moore majority vote: find the element that appears more than half the time in one pass and O(1) space, then extend it to n/3

practice_problems.name: Minimum Index of a Valid Split

glossary.definition: A value that appears strictly more than n / 2 times in an array of length n. There can be at most one.
The value the voting pass ends with. If a majority exists it is the candidate, but the candidate is not guaranteed to be a majority.
Removing two different values from the array together. It never stops a true majority from being a majority of what is left.
A second scan that counts the candidate to confirm it really appears more than n / 2 (or n / k) times.
In a stream, a value that appears more than n / k times for some chosen k. Majority is the case k = 2.

quiz.q: After the voting pass on [1, 2, 3, 1, 2], the candidate is 2. Is 2 a majority?
options: Yes, the algorithm always returns the majority
No, 2 appears twice in five elements, and this array has no majority
Yes, because its count ended at 1
The algorithm cannot run on this input
quiz.explain: A candidate always exists, but a majority may not. Only the verification pass can tell. Here 2 appears 2 times, not more than 2.5.

quiz.q: Why can there be at most two elements appearing more than n / 3 times?
options: Three such elements would need more than n positions in total
Because the algorithm keeps two counters
quiz.explain: Each would need more than n / 3 positions, so three of them would need more than n positions, which is impossible.

quiz.q: What does the count variable mean during the pass?
options: How many times the candidate has appeared so far
How many supporters of the candidate are still standing after cancellations
quiz.explain: Each different value cancels one supporter. The count is the candidate's surplus over the values that cancelled it, not its total frequency.

articles.excerpt: A village holds an election and the ballots arrive one at a time on a long paper roll. You may read the roll once, and you have room to remember only one name and one number. Can you still say which name won more than half the votes? It sounds impossible: surely you need a tally for every name. Yet…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: The Odometer for Permutations
articles.subtitle: Next permutation in O(n) and O(1) space: find the pivot, swap with its successor, reverse the tail, plus the k-th permutation by counting

glossary.definition: Dictionary order: compare two sequences at the first position where they differ, and the smaller value there decides.
The part of the array from some index to the end.
The rightmost index i with a[i] < a[i + 1]. It is the position that must increase to get the next permutation.
The smallest value in the suffix that is larger than the pivot value. Because the suffix is descending, it is the rightmost such value.
Writing a number as a sum of digits times factorials, which tells you directly which item comes first, second and so on in the k-th permutation.

quiz.q: What is the next permutation of [1, 3, 5, 4, 2]?
quiz.explain: The pivot is 3 at index 1. Its successor in the suffix [5, 4, 2] is 4. Swap to get [1, 4, 5, 3, 2], then reverse the suffix to [2, 3, 5], giving [1, 4, 2, 3, 5].

quiz.q: Why can the suffix be reversed instead of sorted after the swap?
options: Reversing is always the same as sorting
The suffix is non-increasing before the swap and stays non-increasing after it, so reversing it makes it non-decreasing
It must be sorted; reversing is a bug
quiz.explain: The swap puts the old pivot value into the spot where the successor was, and that keeps the suffix in descending order. Reversing a descending run sorts it in O(n).

quiz.q: What should next permutation return for [3, 2, 1]?
quiz.explain: There is no pivot, because the whole array is descending. The standard convention, used by LeetCode and std::next_permutation, wraps to the smallest arrangement.

Now someone hands you 1 3 5 4 2 and asks for the one that comes right after it, without listing the hundred-odd arrangements before it. And they want it in place, using no extra memory. You could generate all…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Counting Subarrays That Add Up to K
articles.subtitle: Prefix sums meet a hash map: the walkthrough that handles negatives where sliding windows fail

glossary.definition: A contiguous, non-empty slice of an array.
The total of all elements from the start of the array up to a position.
A hash map from a value to how many times it has been seen so far.
Here, the earlier prefix sum you need, P minus k, so that the subarray between them sums to k.

quiz.q: If P[j] is the prefix sum through j and P[i] is the prefix sum before i, what is the sum of elements i through j?
quiz.explain: The difference of two running totals is the total of the stretch between them.

quiz.q: Why must the map start with {0: 1}?
options: It represents the empty prefix before the array, so subarrays starting at index 0 are counted
quiz.explain: A subarray from index 0 to j sums to k when P[j] − 0 = k. The empty prefix with sum 0 must already be in the map for that to be found.

quiz.q: Why does a sliding window fail here when negatives are allowed?
options: With negatives, growing a window can lower its sum and shrinking can raise it, so there is no rule for which end to move
quiz.explain: Sliding windows rely on sums changing in one direction as the window grows. Negative numbers break that monotonicity.

articles.excerpt: "Count the subarrays whose sum equals k." With only positive numbers, a sliding window solves it in one pass. Add a single negative number, and the window falls apart: growing it might shrink the sum, so you no longer know which end to move. The fix combines two tools you already have, prefix sums…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Sorting Three Colours in a Single Sweep
articles.subtitle: The Dutch national flag problem: three pointers, three regions, and an invariant that makes it obviously correct

practice_problems.name: Partition Array According to Given Pivot

glossary.definition: Rearranging an array so elements of one kind come before elements of another, without fully sorting.
A statement about the array that is true before and after every step of the loop.
A contiguous stretch of the array known to contain only one kind of element, such as all 0s.
The part of the array not yet examined, between the mid and high pointers.

quiz.q: When a[mid] is 2 and you swap it with a[high], why does mid NOT move forward?
options: The value swapped in from high has not been examined yet and could be 0, 1 or 2
quiz.explain: The element arriving from the high end is unknown, so mid must look at it on the next step.

quiz.q: When a[mid] is 0 and you swap it with a[low], why can mid move forward safely?
options: Because a[low] is always 1 (or low equals mid), which is already in the right place
quiz.explain: Everything between low and mid is already known to be 1, so the value swapped into mid is a 1 (or the same element), and needs no further check.

quiz.q: What is the time complexity?
options: O(n), because each step either advances mid or shrinks high, so there are at most n steps
quiz.explain: Every iteration shrinks the unclassified zone by one, so the loop runs at most n times.

glossary.definition: A yes-or-no question about an index, like 'is a[i] at least x?'. Binary search needs it to be no for a while, then yes for the rest.
Changing in only one direction. A monotonic predicate switches from no to yes once and never back.
The range of indices that could still contain the answer, shrinking by half each step.
The first position whose value is at least x, which is also where x would be inserted to keep the array sorted.
A range written [lo, hi) that includes lo but not hi. It makes the length simply hi minus lo.

quiz.q: In the template lo = 0, hi = n, while lo < hi, what is the meaning of hi?
options: The last index that might be the answer
One past the last candidate, so the answer lies in [lo, hi)
quiz.explain: With a half-open range, hi itself is never checked. When lo meets hi, that position is the first yes, or n if there is none.

quiz.q: Why is mid computed as lo + (hi - lo) / 2 instead of (lo + hi) / 2?
options: It avoids integer overflow when lo and hi are large
It is required by the compiler
quiz.explain: lo + hi can exceed the largest int for big ranges. lo + (hi - lo) / 2 never does.

quiz.q: On [1, 3, 3, 3, 7], what are lower_bound(3) and upper_bound(3)?
quiz.explain: lower_bound is the first index with value at least 3, which is 1. upper_bound is the first index with value greater than 3, which is 4. Their difference, 3, counts the 3s.

complexity.time: O(n log R), where R is the range of possible answers

practice_problems.name: Capacity To Ship Packages Within D Days

glossary.definition: The range of values the answer could possibly take, such as capacities from the heaviest package to the total weight.
A function that answers 'is this candidate value good enough?' for one guess, usually with a simple greedy pass.
Changing in one direction only. If capacity c works, every capacity above c also works.
A single left-to-right scan that makes the obvious local choice at each step, used here to test one guess.
A family of problems that asks for the smallest possible value of the worst case, such as the lightest possible heaviest day.

quiz.q: What property must the feasibility check have for binary search on the answer to work?
options: If a value works, every larger value also works (or every smaller one, consistently)
quiz.explain: Binary search needs a no-then-yes pattern over the answer space. Monotonic feasibility provides exactly that.

quiz.q: For 'ship packages within D days', what are good search bounds for the capacity?
options: The heaviest package to the total weight
The average weight to the median
quiz.explain: Capacity below the heaviest package can never ship it; capacity equal to the total ships everything in one day. The answer lies between.

quiz.q: Why is the overall time O(n log R) and not O(n squared)?
options: Each of the log R guesses runs one O(n) check
quiz.explain: Binary search makes about log2 of the range guesses, and each guess costs one linear greedy pass over the input.

glossary.definition: A function that decides whether one element should come before another during sorting.
The rules a comparator must follow: never say an element comes before itself, and stay consistent, so equal elements compare false both ways.
A sort that keeps equal elements in their original relative order.
The value that decides an element's position, such as the end time of an interval or the length of a word.
Sorting a list of positions by the values at those positions, so you keep track of where each element originally was.

quiz.q: After sorting an array, where must the closest pair of values be?
quiz.explain: In sorted order, any value between two others is closer to both. So the minimum difference is always between neighbours, and one pass finds it.

quiz.q: Which comparator breaks std::sort?
quiz.explain: a <= b returns true for equal elements, which violates strict weak ordering and can cause wrong results or crashes.

quiz.q: You must sort values but return answers by original position. What do you sort?
options: Indices (or pairs of value and index) by value
A copy, then search each value
quiz.explain: Sorting indices by value gives sorted order while remembering where each value came from.

articles.title: Binary Search on a Clock Whose 12 Moved
articles.subtitle: Searching a rotated sorted array in O(log n): one half is always sorted, so you always know which way to go

complexity.time: O(log n), O(n) worst case with duplicates

practice_problems.name: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array II

glossary.definition: A sorted array that has been cut at some point and the two pieces swapped, such as [15, 18, 22, 3, 6, 9, 12].
The position of the smallest element, where the rotation happened and the order 'wraps around'.
Of the two halves around the middle index, the one that contains no pivot and is therefore in normal increasing order.
The range of indices [lo, hi] that might still contain the answer.

quiz.q: In a rotated sorted array with distinct values, why is at least one of [lo..mid] or [mid..hi] always sorted?
options: The rotation creates only one break point, and it can lie in at most one of the two halves
Because mid is always the pivot
quiz.explain: There is exactly one place where the order wraps around. Whichever half avoids it is sorted.

quiz.q: For [15, 18, 22, 3, 6, 9, 12], lo = 0, hi = 6, mid = 3 (value 3). Which half is sorted?
quiz.explain: a[lo] = 15 > a[mid] = 3, so the left half contains the wrap. The right half from 3 to 12 is sorted.

quiz.q: Why do duplicates break the O(log n) guarantee?
options: When a[lo], a[mid] and a[hi] are all equal you cannot tell which half is sorted, so you can only shrink by one
Binary search cannot compare equal values
quiz.explain: For example [2, 2, 2, 3, 2] and [2, 3, 2, 2, 2] look the same at lo, mid and hi. Shrinking lo and hi by one is safe but can take O(n) steps.

articles.title: Pointer Surgery Without Losing the Patient
articles.subtitle: Linked lists: dummy heads, three-pointer reversal, merging, and drawing before you code

practice_problems.name: Remove Nth Node From End of List

glossary.definition: One element of a linked list, holding a value and a pointer to the next node.
The first node of a linked list. Losing the head means losing the whole list.
An extra node placed before the head so that edits at the front work exactly like edits in the middle.
A pointer that points nowhere, marking the end of a list. Following it crashes the program.
Rearranging the existing nodes by changing their pointers, without creating new nodes or copying values.

quiz.q: When reversing a list, why must you save next before changing curr->next?
options: Because changing curr->next loses the only link to the rest of the list
quiz.explain: Once curr->next points backwards, nothing points to the remaining nodes. Saving next first keeps the rest of the list reachable.

quiz.q: What does a dummy node simplify?
options: Edits at the head, such as deleting the first node or building a new list, which then need no special case
quiz.explain: With a dummy before the head, every real node has a predecessor, so inserting or deleting at the front uses the same code as anywhere else.

quiz.q: How do you remove the 2nd node from the end in one pass?
options: Move a fast pointer 2 steps ahead, then move fast and slow together until fast reaches the end; slow is just before the target
quiz.explain: Keeping a gap of n between two pointers means that when the leader reaches the end, the follower is exactly n nodes from it.

articles.title: The Tortoise and the Hare on a Circular Track
articles.subtitle: Fast and slow pointers: detect cycles, find where they start, and find the middle, all in O(1) extra space

glossary.definition: A loop in a linked structure where following next pointers eventually returns to a node already visited.
A pointer that moves one step at a time.
A pointer that moves two steps at a time.
The first node of the cycle, where the straight part of the list joins the loop.
The tortoise-and-hare method for detecting a cycle and finding its entry with two pointers and O(1) memory.

quiz.q: Why must the fast pointer eventually meet the slow pointer if there is a cycle?
options: Once both are in the cycle, the fast one gains exactly one step per move, so the gap shrinks by one each time until it reaches zero
quiz.explain: Inside the loop, the distance from slow to fast changes by one each step, so it must hit zero; the fast pointer cannot jump over the slow one.

quiz.q: After the pointers meet, how do you find the cycle entry?
options: Move one pointer back to the head, then move both one step at a time; they meet at the entry
quiz.explain: The distance from the head to the entry equals the distance from the meeting point to the entry, modulo the cycle length, so stepping together lands both at the entry.

quiz.q: When the fast pointer reaches the end of a list with no cycle, where is the slow pointer?
quiz.explain: Slow has taken half as many steps as fast, so it is at the middle.

articles.title: The Last Plate In Is the First Plate Out
articles.subtitle: Stack patterns: matching brackets, evaluating expressions, undo, and a min-stack in O(1)

complexity.time: O(n) for a scan; O(1) per push or pop

glossary.definition: A collection where the last item added is the first one removed (last in, first out).
Adding an item to the top of a stack, and removing the item on top.
Last in, first out: the ordering rule of a stack.
A way of writing expressions with operators after their operands, like '3 4 +', which needs no brackets and is evaluated with a stack.
Structures inside structures, like brackets inside brackets or folders inside folders, which close in the reverse order they opened.

quiz.q: Why is a stack the right tool for checking brackets like ({[]})?
options: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed, which is last-in-first-out
It is not; use a queue
quiz.explain: Nesting closes in reverse order of opening, which is exactly what a stack gives you.

quiz.q: How does a Min Stack return the minimum in O(1)?
options: Each entry also stores the minimum of the stack up to that point
quiz.explain: Storing the running minimum with each element means the top always knows the minimum of everything below it, even after pops.

quiz.q: Evaluate the RPN expression 2 3 + 4 *.
quiz.explain: Push 2, push 3, + pops both and pushes 5, push 4, * pops 5 and 4 and pushes 20.

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Who Can See Over the Crowd
articles.subtitle: The monotonic stack: next greater element, previous smaller element and the largest rectangle, each in one linear pass

glossary.definition: A stack whose elements are always kept in sorted order, increasing or decreasing from bottom to top, by popping anything that would break the order before pushing.
For position i, the first position to its right holding a strictly larger value.
For position i, the nearest position to its left holding a smaller value.
Bounding the total cost of many operations together, here by noting each element is pushed once and popped at most once.
How far an element's influence reaches before something blocks it, such as the width over which a bar is the shortest.

quiz.q: In the next-greater-element pass, when is an element's answer decided?
options: When it is popped by a larger element arriving from the right
At the end of the array only
quiz.explain: An element waits on the stack until the first larger value arrives; that arrival pops it and is its answer. Elements never popped have no greater element.

quiz.q: Why is the monotonic stack O(n) even though there is a while loop inside the for loop?
options: The while loop runs at most once
Every index is pushed once and popped at most once, so total pops are at most n
It is actually O(n log n)
quiz.explain: Counting pops across the whole run, not per iteration, gives at most n. This is amortised analysis.

quiz.q: For the largest rectangle in a histogram, what does popping a bar tell you?
options: Both the first smaller bar on its right (the current bar) and on its left (the new stack top), so its maximal width is known
quiz.explain: The popped bar is the shortest across the gap between those two smaller bars, so its rectangle's width is fixed at that moment.

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: The Desk That Keeps Your Latest Books on Top
articles.subtitle: Designing an LRU cache with O(1) get and put by pairing a hash map with a doubly linked list

glossary.definition: An eviction policy that, when the cache is full, removes the entry that was accessed longest ago.
Removing an entry from a full cache to make room for a new one.
A list where each node points to both its next and previous node, so a node can be unlinked in O(1) once you hold a pointer to it.
A dummy head or tail node that is always present, so insertions and removals never need special cases for an empty list.
The order of entries from most recently used to least recently used.

quiz.q: Why does an LRU cache need a doubly linked list and not a singly linked list?
options: To remove a node from the middle in O(1), which needs a pointer to its previous node
Singly linked lists cannot store values
quiz.explain: On every access the node moves to the front, which means unlinking it from wherever it is. With only next pointers, finding its predecessor takes O(n).

quiz.q: Capacity 2. Operations: put(1), put(2), get(1), put(3). Which key is evicted?
quiz.explain: get(1) made key 1 the most recent, so key 2 is the least recently used when key 3 arrives.

quiz.q: What is the most common bug when evicting?
options: Evicting the head instead of the tail
Removing the node from the list but forgetting to erase its key from the hash map
quiz.explain: The map would then point to a deleted node, so a later get returns garbage or crashes. Store the key in each node so you can erase it from the map on eviction.

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Take It or Leave It: Generating Every Subset
articles.subtitle: Subsets, permutations and their duplicate-free versions, built from one recursive idea: make one choice, recurse, undo it

complexity.time: O(n · 2^n) for subsets, O(n · n!) for permutations

glossary.definition: Any selection of the elements, in any number from none to all, where order does not matter. A set of n elements has 2^n subsets.
An arrangement of all the elements in some order. n distinct elements have n! permutations.
The tree of all calls a recursive function makes. Each edge is one choice, and each root-to-leaf path is one complete set of choices.
Building a solution one choice at a time, recursing, and then undoing the choice so the next option starts from the same state.
The shared list of choices made so far on the way down the recursion tree. It grows on the way down and shrinks on the way back.
The rule that, after sorting, a value equal to the one just tried at the same level is skipped, so duplicate inputs do not create duplicate outputs.

quiz.q: How many subsets does a set of 5 distinct elements have?
quiz.explain: Each element is either taken or left, independently, so there are 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32 subsets, including the empty set and the full set.

quiz.q: In the sorted start-index loop for Subsets II, why is the check i > start rather than i > 0?
options: To avoid going out of bounds
Equal values may be used together in one subset; only equal values at the same level are skipped
quiz.explain: i > start means a[i] is not the first choice at this level. Skipping it only then still allows [2, 2], where the second 2 is chosen at a deeper level.

quiz.q: You add path to the result list but later every stored subset is empty. What went wrong?
options: You stored a reference to the shared path, which is emptied as the recursion unwinds
quiz.explain: There is only one path, reused for every branch. Store a copy of it at the moment you record it.

articles.title: Four Ways to Tour a Family Tree
articles.subtitle: Preorder, inorder, postorder and level order: what each visit order means, and how to run them recursively, with a stack, or with a queue

complexity.space: O(h) for depth-first, O(w) for level order

practice_problems.name: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal

glossary.definition: A tree where every node has at most two children, called left and right.
Exploring a tree by going as deep as possible down one branch before backing up. Preorder, inorder and postorder are all depth-first.
Exploring a tree level by level, nearest nodes first, using a queue. Level order traversal is BFS on a tree.
The number of levels on the longest path from the root to a leaf. It bounds the recursion depth of DFS.
The largest number of nodes on any single level. It bounds the queue size of BFS.
A binary tree where every node's left subtree holds smaller keys and its right subtree holds larger keys.

quiz.q: Which traversal of a binary search tree outputs the keys in sorted order?
quiz.explain: Inorder visits the left subtree (all smaller keys), then the node, then the right subtree (all larger keys).

quiz.q: To delete a whole tree safely, freeing children before their parent, which order fits?
quiz.explain: Postorder processes both children before the node itself, so nothing is freed while still needed.

quiz.q: In level order traversal, how do you know where one level ends?
options: Record the queue size at the start of the level and pop exactly that many nodes
Check if a node is a leaf
quiz.explain: At the start of a level the queue holds exactly that level's nodes, so its size tells you how many to process before the next level begins.

articles.title: The Triage Nurse Who Always Knows Who Is Next
articles.subtitle: Binary heaps: the array layout, sift up and sift down, linear-time heapify, priority_queue with greater, and the top-k pattern

complexity.time: O(log n) push and pop, O(1) top, O(n) heapify

practice_problems.name: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
Kth Largest Element in an Array

glossary.definition: A complete binary tree where every parent is no larger than its children (a min-heap) or no smaller (a max-heap), so the best item is always at the root.
A binary tree filled level by level, left to right, with no gaps; this is what lets a heap live in a plain array.
Repairing a heap after adding an item at the end by swapping it with its parent while it beats the parent.
Repairing a heap after replacing the root by swapping the item with its better child while that child beats it.
Turning an unordered array into a heap in place in O(n) time, by sifting down every non-leaf from the last one back to the root.
An abstract container that hands out the highest-priority item first; a binary heap is the usual way to build one.
Keeping the k best items seen so far in a heap of size k whose root is the worst of them, so each new item is compared with that root.

quiz.q: In a heap stored in an array from index 0, where are the children of index i?
quiz.explain: With 0-based indexing the children of i sit at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and the parent of i is (i − 1) / 2 rounded down.

quiz.q: You need the 10 largest numbers from a stream of a million. Which heap do you keep?
options: A max-heap of all million numbers
A min-heap of size 10, evicting its root when it grows past 10
A sorted array of size 10 rebuilt each time
quiz.explain: The min-heap's root is the smallest of your current top 10, the one to throw out when something bigger arrives. Each step costs O(log 10).

quiz.q: Why does bottom-up heapify run in O(n) and not O(n log n)?
options: It skips half the elements entirely
Most nodes are near the bottom and can only sift down a short distance
It only works on sorted input
quiz.explain: Half the nodes are leaves and never move, a quarter move at most one level, and so on. The total work adds up to less than n swaps.

articles.title: Every Problem Is a Map of Roads
articles.subtitle: Nodes, edges, adjacency lists and matrices, and how to spot the graph hiding in grids and puzzles

practice_problems.name: Find if Path Exists in Graph

glossary.definition: A single thing in a graph, such as a city, a person or a grid cell. Also called a node.
A connection between two vertices. It can be one-way (directed) or two-way (undirected), and it can carry a weight such as a distance or cost.
The number of edges touching a vertex. In a directed graph you count in-degree (arrows in) and out-degree (arrows out) separately.
For every vertex, a list of its neighbours. Uses memory proportional to vertices plus edges.
An n by n table where cell (u, v) says whether, or with what weight, an edge goes from u to v.
A graph with far fewer edges than the n² possible, which describes most graphs in interview and contest problems.
A graph that is never stored. Its neighbours are generated on the fly from a rule, such as the moves allowed from a puzzle state.

quiz.q: n = 100,000 cities and m = 200,000 two-way roads. Which representation fits in memory comfortably?
quiz.explain: A matrix needs n² = 10¹⁰ cells. An adjacency list stores n lists with 2m = 400,000 entries in total.

quiz.q: You read the undirected edge 2 – 5. What must you add to the adjacency list?
options: Nothing until all edges are read
quiz.explain: A two-way road must appear in both signposts. Forgetting the reverse direction makes the graph accidentally directed.

quiz.q: In a grid with R rows and C columns, which is usually the best way to find a cell's neighbours?
options: Build an adjacency matrix of size (R × C)²
Loop over four direction offsets and check bounds
Store every edge in an edge list first
quiz.explain: A grid already encodes its edges: each cell's neighbours are one step up, down, left or right. Generating them with offsets needs no extra memory.

articles.title: Ripples on a Pond: Breadth-First Search
articles.subtitle: Exploring a graph in rings to get shortest paths in unweighted graphs, plus multi-source BFS, grid BFS, 0-1 BFS and path reconstruction

glossary.definition: A graph traversal that visits every vertex at distance 1 from the start, then every vertex at distance 2, and so on, using a queue.
A first-in, first-out container: items are added at the back and removed from the front, so they leave in the order they arrived.
The set of discovered vertices waiting in the queue to be expanded; in BFS it holds at most two consecutive distance layers.
For each vertex, the vertex it was discovered from; following it backwards from the target rebuilds a shortest path.
BFS started from several vertices at once, all at distance 0, giving each vertex its distance to the nearest source.
A shortest-path method for graphs whose edge weights are only 0 or 1, using a double-ended queue instead of a heap.

quiz.q: Why does BFS find shortest paths in an unweighted graph?
options: It finishes all vertices at distance d before touching any at distance d + 1, so the first discovery of a vertex uses the fewest edges
It always picks the smallest vertex id
quiz.explain: The queue keeps vertices in order of distance. The first time a vertex is reached, no shorter route can still be waiting.

quiz.q: When should a vertex be marked visited?
options: When it is popped from the queue
When it is pushed onto the queue
Only when it is the target
quiz.explain: Marking on push stops the same vertex from being queued many times by different neighbours. Marking on pop allows duplicates and can blow up time and memory.

quiz.q: In Rotting Oranges, several oranges are rotten at the start. How should BFS begin?
options: Run a separate BFS from each rotten orange and take the minimum
Push every rotten orange into the queue at distance 0, then run one BFS
quiz.explain: Multi-source BFS treats all sources as one combined start. One pass gives every cell its distance to the nearest rotten orange.
