articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Going Deep With a Ball of String
articles.subtitle: Depth-first search: recursive and iterative versions, connected components, flood fill and entry and exit times

complexity.space: O(V) for visited marks and the stack

glossary.definition: A graph traversal that follows one path as far as it can, then backs up to the most recent vertex with an unexplored edge and continues from there.
The marks that record which vertices have already been reached, so no vertex is processed twice and cycles cannot trap the search.
Returning from a vertex once all its edges are explored, back to the vertex the search came from.
A maximal group of vertices in an undirected graph where every vertex can reach every other.
DFS (or BFS) on a grid that spreads from one cell to all connected cells of the same kind, such as all land in one island.
The timer values when DFS first reaches a vertex and when it finishes it. A vertex's descendants are exactly those whose interval lies inside its own.

quiz.q: Graph 0–2, 0–5, 2–3, 2–4, 3–4 with neighbours in increasing order. In what order does recursive DFS from 0 visit the vertices?
quiz.explain: From 0 it goes to 2, from 2 to 3, from 3 to 4. Then everything around 4, 3 and 2 is visited, so it backs up to 0 and finally visits 5.

quiz.q: Why can recursive flood fill crash on a 1000 × 1000 grid that is all land?
options: The recursion can go about a million calls deep and overflow the call stack
quiz.explain: A snake-like path can make every cell one level deeper than the last. An explicit stack on the heap avoids the limit.

quiz.q: With entry and exit times, how do you test whether u is an ancestor of v in the DFS tree?
quiz.explain: DFS enters u, then finishes all of u's descendants, then exits u. So a descendant's interval sits inside u's interval.

articles.excerpt: Give someone a satellite picture of an archipelago and ask how many islands there are. They will put a finger on some land, trace around everything connected to it, mark it as counted, and move on to the next unmarked patch. Nobody teaches them that. It is just how you explore. That instinct is…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: When the Rumour Comes Back to You
articles.subtitle: Finding cycles with DFS: the parent check for undirected graphs, three colours for directed ones, and why they differ

glossary.definition: A path that starts and ends at the same vertex without reusing an edge. In a directed graph it must follow the arrows.
In an undirected DFS, ignoring the edge back to the vertex you just came from, because that is the same road, not a loop.
An edge from a vertex to one of its ancestors on the current DFS path. A graph has a cycle exactly when DFS finds a back edge.
White for not visited, grey for on the current DFS path, black for fully finished. Used to find back edges in directed graphs.
The chain of DFS calls that are still active, which is the path from the start vertex to the current one. The grey vertices are exactly this chain.

quiz.q: Directed graph 0→1, 0→2, 1→2. DFS from 0 visits 1, then 2, then returns to 0 and sees the edge 0→2 to an already visited vertex. Is there a cycle?
options: No, 2 is black: finished, not on the current path
quiz.explain: Two paths meeting at 2 is not a loop. Only an edge into a grey vertex, one still on the current path, closes a directed cycle.

quiz.q: Why does the undirected DFS skip the parent?
options: Because every undirected edge appears in both adjacency lists, so the road you arrived on always leads straight back
Parents are never part of cycles
quiz.explain: Edge u–v is stored as v in adj[u] and u in adj[v]. Without the parent check, every edge would look like a two-vertex cycle.

quiz.q: Course Schedule asks whether all courses can be finished. What does a cycle in the prerequisite graph mean?
options: No valid order exists, so the answer is false
quiz.explain: A cycle means each course in it waits on another in the same loop, so none of them can be taken first.

articles.excerpt: A course catalogue says Algorithms needs Data Structures, Data Structures needs Discrete Maths, and Discrete Maths needs Algorithms. Nobody can ever start. A build tool finds that module A imports B, B imports C and C imports A, and refuses to compile. A spreadsheet shows a "circular reference"…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Friend Groups That Merge at a Party
articles.subtitle: Union-find with path compression and union by size: connectivity, component counts and redundant edges in near-constant time

glossary.definition: A structure that keeps elements in disjoint groups and supports two operations: find which group an element is in, and merge two groups. Also called disjoint set union (DSU).
The root of a group's tree. Two elements are in the same group exactly when they have the same representative.
During find, pointing every element on the walked path directly at the root, so later finds on them take one step.
When merging, hanging the root of the smaller group under the root of the larger one, which keeps trees shallow.
The same idea as union by size, but comparing a rank, an upper bound on tree height, instead of the element count.
A function, written α(n), that grows so slowly it is at most 4 for any input size that could ever be stored. It bounds the amortised cost of union-find with both optimisations.
The average cost per operation over a whole sequence of operations, even if a single operation is occasionally more expensive.

quiz.q: Groups {0, 1, 2, 3} with root 0 and {4, 5} with root 4. You call union(1, 5). What should happen?
options: Find both roots, 0 and 4, then hang 4 under 0 because group 0 is larger
quiz.explain: Union always links roots. Linking 1 or 5 directly would pull a single element out of its group instead of merging the groups.

quiz.q: Why does union by size alone keep every tree's height at most log₂ n?
options: Trees are always balanced binary trees
An element only gets deeper when its group merges into one at least as large, so its group size at least doubles each time
quiz.explain: Group size can double at most log₂ n times before reaching n, so no element can be more than log₂ n links from its root.

quiz.q: Redundant Connection: you process edges in order. How do you spot the edge that creates a cycle?
options: When find(u) equals find(v) before the union
When the group size reaches n
When an element is its own parent
quiz.explain: If u and v already share a representative, they are connected, so one more edge between them closes a loop.

articles.excerpt: A social app processes a stream of "A is now friends with B" events, and after each one it must answer "are X and Y in the same circle?" You could rebuild the graph and run a search for every question, but with a hundred thousand events and questions, that is billions of steps. What you need is a…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Dynamic Programming Is Just Careful Recursion
articles.subtitle: Overlapping subproblems, memoisation and bottom-up tables, built from Fibonacci and Climbing Stairs

glossary.definition: Solving a problem by combining answers to smaller versions of it, computing each smaller answer only once.
When a recursive solution asks the same smaller question many times, such as fib(3) inside both fib(5) and fib(4).
Top-down DP: keep the recursion, but store each result the first time it is computed and return the stored value afterwards.
Bottom-up DP: fill a table from the smallest subproblems upward with a loop, so every value needed is already there.
The parameters that identify one subproblem, such as 'the number of ways to reach step i'.
The formula that computes a state from smaller states, such as ways(i) = ways(i − 1) + ways(i − 2).
The smallest states whose answers are known directly, which stop the recursion or start the table.

quiz.q: How many calls does the plain recursive fib(n) make for n = 5, counting the first call?
quiz.explain: The call tree for fib(5) has 15 nodes because fib(3), fib(2) and smaller values are recomputed many times. With memoisation it drops to 9 calls, and only 6 distinct values are computed.

quiz.q: What are the three things you must define before writing any DP?
quiz.explain: The state says what one subproblem means, the transition builds it from smaller ones, and the base cases start everything off.

quiz.q: When is a problem a good candidate for DP?
options: When the recursive solution solves the same subproblems repeatedly and the answer is built from optimal or counted sub-answers
quiz.explain: DP pays off when there are overlapping subproblems to reuse and the full answer can be assembled from sub-answers.

articles.excerpt: Dynamic programming has a fearsome reputation. Students talk about it as if it were a separate kind of magic, where you either "see the formula" or you do not. Interviewers know this, which is why DP questions appear in so many placement rounds. Here is the secret that takes the fear away: dynamic…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Stairs, Robbers and Secret Codes
articles.subtitle: One-dimensional DP: define dp[i], look back a fixed number of steps, and shrink the table to a few variables

complexity.time: O(n × k) for k choices per step

glossary.definition: A dynamic programming solution whose state is a single index, such as dp[i] for the first i items or for amount i.
How many earlier states a transition reads, such as 2 for House Robber or the number of coin types for Coin Change.
Replacing the dp array with a few variables that hold only the states the transition still needs.
A DP that takes the minimum or maximum over choices, such as the most money or the fewest coins.
A DP that adds up the number of ways over choices, such as the number of decodings or dice sequences.

quiz.q: House values [5, 1, 2, 9, 4, 3], no two adjacent houses. What is the most you can rob?
quiz.explain: dp goes 5, 5, 7, 14, 14, 17. The best plan robs houses with 5, 9 and 3.

quiz.q: Coins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6. Why does picking the largest coin first fail?
options: Greedy takes 4 + 1 + 1 = 3 coins, but 3 + 3 uses only 2
quiz.explain: Greedy is only safe for special coin systems. DP tries every last coin and finds 2.

quiz.q: In Decode Ways for the string '1206', why is the answer 1?
options: '0' cannot stand alone, so it must pair with the '2' before it as '20', which forces the split 1, 20, 6
Strings with zeros have no decoding
quiz.explain: A zero is only valid as part of 10 or 20. That removes the option of reading '12' and leaves exactly one decoding.

articles.excerpt: A robber walks down a street of houses, each holding some money. Robbing two neighbours in a row trips the alarm. Which houses should they hit? A message of digits must be decoded where 1 means A and 26 means Z: how many readings does "2261" have? A vending machine has coins of 1, 3 and 4: what is…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Packing a Backpack With a Weight Limit
articles.subtitle: 0/1 knapsack: a DP over items and capacity, the backwards loop that makes it 1D, and subset sum as a special case

glossary.definition: Choose a subset of items, each with a weight and a value, to maximise total value without exceeding a capacity. Each item is taken whole or not at all, at most once.
The maximum total weight allowed, usually called W.
The special case that asks whether some subset of numbers adds up to exactly a target, a knapsack where only reachability matters.
Running time polynomial in the numeric value W rather than in the number of bits needed to write W, so it is fast only when W is small.
The variant where each item may be taken any number of times.

quiz.q: In the 1D knapsack table, why must the capacity loop run from W down to the item's weight?
options: So that dp[c − w] still holds the value from before this item, which prevents using the same item twice
quiz.explain: Going upward, dp[c − w] may already include the current item, so the item gets added again. Going downward reads only old values.

quiz.q: Items (weight, value): (1, 1), (3, 4), (4, 5), (5, 7). Capacity 7. What is the best value?
quiz.explain: Taking weights 3 and 4 gives value 4 + 5 = 9. Weights 5 and 1 give only 8, and 1 + 3 gives 5.

quiz.q: Partition Equal Subset Sum reduces to which question?
options: Is there a subset summing to exactly half of the total?
quiz.explain: If one part sums to half, the rest sums to the other half. That is subset sum with target total / 2, which needs an even total.

articles.excerpt: You are packing for a trek and your backpack holds 7 kg. On the floor: a stove, a camera, a tent, a sleeping bag, each with a weight and a usefulness score. Every item goes in whole or stays behind. Which combination is most useful without breaking the weight limit? That is the 0/1 knapsack…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: A Vending Machine With Endless Stock
articles.subtitle: Unbounded knapsack: reuse items by looping capacity forwards, and choose the loop order to count combinations or permutations

glossary.definition: The knapsack variant where every item type can be taken any number of times, as long as the total weight stays within capacity.
The total budget the chosen items must fit into: a weight limit, a target sum or an amount of money.
A selection where order does not matter, so 1 + 3 and 3 + 1 count as the same way.
A selection where order matters, so 1 + 3 and 3 + 1 count as two different ways.
An extra array recording which item gave the best value at each capacity, used to rebuild the actual selection.

quiz.q: In the 1D table, why does unbounded knapsack loop capacity forwards while 0/1 knapsack loops backwards?
options: Going forwards lets dp[c − w] already include the same item, which allows reuse; going backwards forbids it
quiz.explain: When c is processed after c − w in the same item pass, dp[c − w] may already contain that item, so the item gets used again.

quiz.q: Coins {1, 2, 3}, target 4. Outer loop over coins, inner loop over sums. What does the table count?
options: 4 combinations where order does not matter
quiz.explain: Coins outside means each multiset is built in a fixed coin order, so 1+3 and 3+1 are the same way: {1111, 112, 22, 13}.

quiz.q: Which change turns the combination count into a count of ordered sequences?
options: Swap the loops: sums on the outside, coins on the inside
quiz.explain: With sums outside, every coin can be the last one added at every sum, so different orders are counted separately: 7 for this example.

articles.excerpt: In Packing a Backpack With a Weight Limit, every item was unique: one laptop, one tent, one camera. Many interview problems remove that limit. Coins come in unlimited supply. A rod can be cut into as many 2-metre pieces as you like. A number can be written as a sum of the same square several times.…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Dealing Cards Into Piles
articles.subtitle: Longest increasing subsequence: the O(n²) DP, the O(n log n) patience-sorting method with binary search, and how to rebuild the sequence itself

complexity.time: O(n log n) with binary search, O(n²) for the basic DP

glossary.definition: Elements picked from an array in their original order, not necessarily next to each other. [1, 5, 9] is a subsequence of [3, 1, 8, 5, 9].
The longest subsequence whose values strictly increase from left to right.
tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1 seen so far. It stays sorted.
Dealing cards into piles left to right, placing each card on the leftmost pile whose top is not smaller; the number of piles equals the LIS length.
For each index, the index of the previous element in the best subsequence ending there, used to rebuild the actual sequence.

quiz.q: In the O(n²) DP, what does dp[i] mean?
options: The LIS of the whole array
The length of the longest increasing subsequence that ends exactly at index i
The number of elements smaller than a[i]
quiz.explain: Fixing the last element makes the subproblem clean: dp[i] = 1 + the best dp[j] over earlier j with a[j] < a[i].

quiz.q: For [3, 4, 5, 1], the final tails array is [1, 4, 5]. Is that an increasing subsequence of the input?
options: No: 1 comes after 4 and 5 in the array, so tails is not a real subsequence, only its length is correct
It is the reverse of one
quiz.explain: tails stores the best possible ending value for each length, from different subsequences. Its length is the LIS length; rebuilding needs parent pointers.

quiz.q: For non-decreasing subsequences (equal values allowed), what changes in the binary search version?
options: Use upper_bound (first element greater than x) instead of lower_bound
quiz.explain: An equal value may extend a subsequence, so it should go after equal tails, which is the first strictly greater position.

articles.excerpt: A stock's price over eight days is [3, 1, 8, 2, 5, 9, 4, 7]. What is the longest run of days, not necessarily consecutive, where each chosen price is higher than the previous one? You may skip days but not reorder them. Checking all 2⁸ subsets works for eight days and is hopeless for 10⁵. The…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Lining Up Two DNA Strands
articles.subtitle: Longest common subsequence and edit distance: one 2D table over prefixes, a match-or-skip decision per cell, and the family of string DPs built on it

complexity.space: O(n × m), or O(min(n, m)) for the length only

glossary.definition: The first i characters of a string. The DP table has one row per prefix of the first string and one column per prefix of the second.
The longest sequence of characters that appears in both strings in the same order, not necessarily contiguously.
The minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and replacements that turn one string into another. Also called Levenshtein distance.
A way of lining two strings up, column by column, where each column is a match, a mismatch, or a character paired with a gap.
Keeping only the previous and current rows of a 2D DP table, since each cell depends only on its row and the one above.

quiz.q: In the LCS table, what does dp[i][j] mean?
options: The LCS length of the first i characters of a and the first j characters of b
The number of matches in row i
quiz.explain: Rows and columns index prefixes, with row 0 and column 0 for the empty prefixes. The answer is dp[n][m].

quiz.q: When a[i−1] ≠ b[j−1] in edit distance, which three cells are compared?
options: dp[i−1][j] (delete), dp[i][j−1] (insert) and dp[i−1][j−1] (replace), each plus 1
quiz.explain: The last operation is a delete, an insert or a replace; take the cheapest and add one.

quiz.q: What is the edit distance from LOVE to MOVIE?
quiz.explain: Replace L with M, then insert I between V and E. The DP table's bottom-right cell is 2.

articles.excerpt: Your phone suggests "receive" when you type "recieve". git diff shows exactly which lines changed between two versions of a file. A biologist compares a gene from a mouse with the same gene from a human and asks how similar they are. All three are the same question: how do two sequences line up?…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: The Robot That Only Moves Right or Down
articles.subtitle: Grid DP: count paths, find the cheapest path, handle obstacles and find the largest square, each cell built from its top and left neighbours

glossary.definition: Dynamic programming where the state is a cell (r, c) of a grid, and each cell's answer is built from neighbouring cells already computed.
A path that only moves right or down, so it never revisits a cell and the grid has a natural processing order.
A blocked cell that no path may enter. Its DP value is 0 paths, or infinite cost.
A single 1D array reused for every row, valid because each cell needs only the row above and the cell to its left.
The first row and first column, which have only one possible neighbour and need their own base cases.

quiz.q: How many right-or-down paths cross a 3 × 4 grid with no obstacles?
quiz.explain: Every path makes 2 down moves and 3 right moves in some order: C(5, 2) = 10. The DP table gives the same number.

quiz.q: In Unique Paths II, a cell in the first row is blocked. What about the cells to its right in that row?
options: They have 0 paths, because the only way in was along the first row
quiz.explain: First-row cells can only be reached from the left. Initialising the whole first row to 1 is a classic bug when obstacles exist.

quiz.q: For Maximal Square, why does dp[r][c] use the minimum of three neighbours?
options: A square ending at (r, c) can only be as big as the smallest square ending at its top, left and top-left neighbours allows, plus one
quiz.explain: If any of the three neighbouring squares is small, the corner square is limited by it. The minimum captures the tightest limit.

articles.excerpt: A warehouse robot starts in the top-left corner of a floor laid out as a grid and must reach the bottom-right corner. It can only move right or down. How many different routes are there? Which route picks up the least dust? What if some cells are blocked by shelves? Grid problems like these are…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Making Change at the Counter
articles.subtitle: Coin Change: why greedy fails, the minimum-coins DP with an infinity start, and the counting version where loop order decides the answer

complexity.time: O(n × A) for n coins and amount A

glossary.definition: A coin value available to use, such as 1, 3 or 4. Each denomination can be used any number of times.
Always taking the largest coin that still fits. Fast, but only correct for some coin systems.
A set of denominations for which the greedy algorithm always gives the minimum number of coins, such as 1, 2, 5, 10.
A value larger than any real answer, used to mark amounts that cannot be made yet, so min() ignores them.
An amount that can be formed exactly from the given coins. Unreachable amounts keep the infinity sentinel.

quiz.q: Coins {1, 3, 4}, amount 6. What does greedy give, and what is optimal?
quiz.explain: Greedy grabs the 4 and is then forced into two 1s. The DP finds 3 + 3.

quiz.q: Why is dp initialised to infinity except dp[0] = 0 in the minimum-coins version?
options: So amounts that cannot be formed never look cheaper than real ones, and stay detectable at the end
quiz.explain: With 0 as the start, an unreachable amount would look like it needs zero coins. Infinity marks it as impossible until a real way is found.

quiz.q: For Coin Change II (number of combinations), which loop goes outside?
quiz.explain: Coins outside builds each multiset in a fixed coin order, so it is counted once. Amounts outside would count different orders separately.

articles.excerpt: A shopkeeper has to give ₹6 in change using coins worth ₹1, ₹3 and ₹4, and wants to hand over as few coins as possible. The instinct is to grab the biggest coin first: a ₹4, then ₹1 and ₹1, three coins. But two ₹3 coins would have done it. That tiny counterexample is why Coin Change is one of the…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Cutting a Ribbon Into Labelled Pieces
articles.subtitle: Word Break: a 1D DP over prefixes, the hidden cost of substrings, a trie speed-up, and listing every sentence for Word Break II

complexity.time: O(n × L) with a trie, where L is the longest word length

glossary.definition: A way of cutting a string into consecutive pieces, here pieces that are all dictionary words.
A position i in the string such that the prefix s[0..i) can be fully segmented into words.
The given set of allowed words, usually stored in a hash set or a trie for fast lookup.
A tree of characters where each path from the root spells a prefix, letting you find every word that starts at a position in one walk.
Recursion that lists all solutions from a position and caches the result per position, used to output every sentence.

quiz.q: What does dp[i] mean in Word Break?
options: The first i characters of s can be cut entirely into dictionary words
The longest word ends at i
quiz.explain: dp[0] is true for the empty prefix, and dp[i] is true if some earlier cut point j has dp[j] true and s[j..i) in the dictionary.

quiz.q: Why can the simple 'try every j' version be slower than O(n²)?
options: Each check builds a substring s[j..i), which costs time proportional to its length, giving O(n³) overall
quiz.explain: Creating and hashing a substring is not free. Limiting j to the last L positions, or walking a trie, removes the extra factor.

quiz.q: Why can Word Break II not be solved in polynomial time in the worst case?
options: The number of valid sentences itself can grow exponentially, and you must output all of them
quiz.explain: A string like 'aaaa...a' with words 'a' and 'aa' has a Fibonacci-like number of segmentations. Memoisation avoids repeated work but cannot shrink the output.

Under both sits a simple question: can this string be cut into pieces that are all real words, and if so, how? Word…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: The Thief Who Never Robs Two Neighbours
articles.subtitle: House Robber on a line, on a circle and on a tree, plus Delete and Earn, all from one take-or-skip choice

complexity.space: O(1) for line and circle, O(h) for the tree

glossary.definition: The two choices at every item in this family: include it, which forbids its neighbours, or leave it, which leaves the neighbours free.
A rule that two chosen items may not be next to each other, on a line, a circle or a tree edge.
The version where the first and last items are neighbours, so choosing both is forbidden.
A tree traversal that finishes both children before handling the parent, so the parent can combine the children's answers.
The total points available for one distinct value, value times its count, used to turn Delete and Earn into House Robber.

quiz.q: Houses on a circle hold [5, 3, 1, 6, 2, 7]. What is the most the thief can take?
quiz.explain: 18 (5 + 6 + 7) uses the first and last house, which are neighbours on a circle. Dropping the first house gives 3 + 6 + 7 = 16; dropping the last gives 11. The answer is 16.

quiz.q: In House Robber III, what does each tree node return to its parent?
options: Only the best total of its subtree
Two numbers: the best total if it is robbed and the best if it is skipped
quiz.explain: The parent's choice depends on whether the child was robbed, so the child must report both cases. One number would lose that information.

quiz.q: Delete and Earn turns into House Robber over what?
options: The sorted distinct values, with value buckets as house amounts and consecutive values as neighbours
quiz.explain: Taking value v deletes v − 1 and v + 1, exactly like robbing a house locks its two neighbours. Each bucket holds v times the count of v.

articles.excerpt: A thief walks down a street at night. Every house holds some cash, and the houses share alarm wiring: rob two neighbours on the same night and the alarm goes off. Grab every big pile you see and you soon find that the big piles sit next to each other. Interviewers love this problem because it comes…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: How Many Ways to Split the Bill?
articles.subtitle: Counting subsets with a given sum, and how Target Sum and partitions with a difference reduce to it

complexity.time: O(n × P), P the target subset sum

glossary.definition: A dynamic programming solution that adds up the number of ways over choices instead of taking a maximum, minimum or yes/no.
The question of whether, or in how many ways, some subset of numbers adds up to exactly a target.
In Target Sum, the numbers that receive a plus sign. Fixing its sum turns sign assignment into subset counting.
Testing whether a number is even or odd. Here, total plus target must be even, or no split exists.
A split of the items into two groups where swapping the two groups gives the same split, so each split corresponds to two subsets.

quiz.q: nums = [1, 0, 1], and you want the number of subsets summing to 1. What is the answer?
quiz.explain: Without the zero there are 2 subsets ({first 1}, {second 1}). The zero can join or not join each of them, so the count doubles to 4.

quiz.q: Target Sum with total 8 and target 3. How many sign assignments reach 3?
quiz.explain: The plus group would need sum (8 + 3) / 2 = 5.5, which is impossible for integers. The parity check returns 0 immediately.

quiz.q: Counting subsets of 1..n that sum to half the total gives 8. How many ways are there to split 1..n into two equal-sum groups?
quiz.explain: Each split is counted twice, once from each group's point of view, because the complement of a valid subset is also valid. Divide by 2.

articles.excerpt: Five friends' dishes arrive on one bill, and two of them are paying. Each dish goes on one person's tab or the other's. One of them says, "I'll pay exactly ₹5 of this." How many different ways can the dishes be assigned so that works out? Then someone points at the free glass of water on the bill,…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: Autocomplete in Your Pocket
articles.subtitle: Tries: a tree of letters that answers 'is this a word?' and 'what starts with this?' in time proportional to the word, not the dictionary

complexity.time: O(L) per insert or lookup, for a word of length L
complexity.space: O(total characters × alphabet size) in the worst case

practice_problems.name: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
Maximum XOR of Two Numbers in an Array

glossary.definition: A tree where each edge is labelled with a character, so every path from the root spells a prefix. Also called a prefix tree.
The first few characters of a string. 'ca' is a prefix of 'card' and of 'cat'.
A flag on a trie node saying that the path to this node spells a complete word, not just a prefix of one.
A counter stored on each node recording how many inserted words pass through it, so 'how many words start with this?' is one lookup.
The number of distinct characters a node may branch on, such as 26 for lowercase English letters or 2 for bits.

quiz.q: You insert car, card, care, cat and dog into an empty trie. How many nodes does it have, counting the root?
quiz.explain: Shared prefixes share nodes. Root, then c-a-r-d-e-t for the 'ca' family (6 nodes), then d-o-g (3 nodes): 1 + 6 + 3 = 10.

quiz.q: After inserting 'card' only, does search('car') return true?
options: Yes, because the path c-a-r exists
No, because the node for 'r' has no end-of-word marker
quiz.explain: The path exists, so startsWith('car') is true, but search needs the end-of-word marker on the last node.

quiz.q: Why is a trie better than a hash set for Word Search II?
options: While walking the grid you can stop as soon as the current path is not a prefix of any word
quiz.explain: A hash set can only answer 'is this whole string a word?'. The trie also answers 'can this path still become a word?', which prunes the search early.

articles.excerpt: You type "ca" into a search box and suggestions appear instantly: car, card, care, cat. The dictionary behind it might hold a million words. Checking each one for the prefix "ca" on every keystroke would be far too slow, and a hash set cannot help, because it only answers "is this exact string…

articles.subject: dsa
articles.title: The Night-Before Revision Sheet
articles.subtitle: One checklist for interview day: which pattern a problem is asking for, what each tool costs, and the edge cases that break code

glossary.definition: A phrase or constraint in a problem statement that points towards a specific technique, such as 'sorted array' pointing to binary search or two pointers.
The stated limits on the input, such as n ≤ 10⁵, which tell you how fast the solution must be.
An unusual input at the boundary, such as an empty array, one element or all values equal, that often breaks otherwise correct code.
Tracing your code by hand on a small input, line by line, to catch bugs before running it.
The average cost per operation over a whole sequence of operations, even if a single operation is occasionally expensive.

quiz.q: The input size is n ≤ 20 and the problem asks for the best subset. What should you consider first?
options: Trying all 2^n subsets, with bitmasks or backtracking
quiz.explain: 2^20 is about a million, which is easily affordable. The small constraint is an invitation to enumerate subsets.

quiz.q: A problem asks for the minimum number of moves in an unweighted grid. Which tool fits?
quiz.explain: In an unweighted graph BFS explores by distance, so the first time it reaches the target is the shortest path. Dijkstra works but is unnecessary.

quiz.q: What is the most useful thing to do the night before an interview?
options: Learn a brand new advanced topic
Revise the patterns you already know, rehearse your explanation routine, and sleep
quiz.explain: New topics learned in a rush rarely stick and add anxiety. Recognising known patterns quickly and explaining clearly is what wins the round.

articles.excerpt: It is the night before your interview. You have solved hundreds of problems over months, and right now they blur together. Was it the sliding window that needed positive numbers, or the prefix sums? Does the heap pop in log n or in n? What was that edge case that broke your code last week? This…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Two Hours, Six Problems, One Rating
articles.subtitle: How programming contests work, what the ratings mean, and why they make you interview-proof

glossary.definition: A website that runs your code on hidden tests and reports whether it is correct and fast enough.
The judge's result for a submission, such as Accepted, Wrong Answer or Time Limit Exceeded.
A number that estimates your contest strength. It goes up or down after each rated contest depending on how you placed against others.
A contest tier on Codeforces, aimed at a range of ratings. Div. 1 is the hardest; Div. 2, 3 and 4 are progressively easier.
On Codeforces, submitting a test case that breaks another contestant's accepted solution during the contest.
Solving, after the contest ends, the problems you could not solve during it.

quiz.q: Your code passes the samples but the judge says Time Limit Exceeded. What is the most likely cause?
options: A typo in the output format
The algorithm's complexity is too high for the largest inputs
You forgot to include a header
quiz.explain: Samples are tiny. The hidden tests include the largest allowed inputs, where an O(n squared) idea on n = 200,000 is far too slow.

quiz.q: Which Codeforces division is easiest?
quiz.explain: Div. 4 is aimed at beginners. Div. 1 is for the strongest contestants.

quiz.q: Why is upsolving considered so important?
options: The problems you just failed are exactly at the edge of your skill, which is where learning happens
It is required to keep your account
quiz.explain: Upsolving does not change your rating, but practising right at the edge of your ability is what makes the next contest go better.

articles.excerpt: At 8:05 pm, twenty thousand people around the world open the same six problems at the same moment. A clock starts counting down from two hours. Somewhere, a student solves problem A in four minutes, problem B in twelve, and then stares at problem C for an hour. By 10:05 pm, every one of them has a…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: The Thirty Lines You Paste Before Every Contest
articles.subtitle: A clean contest template, fast input and output, and the habits that prevent silly verdicts

glossary.definition: A starter file you paste at the beginning of every contest solution, with includes, settings and a few helpers.
Settings that make cin and cout much faster, which matters when reading or writing hundreds of thousands of numbers.
An input format where the first number t says how many independent test cases follow.
When a number grows past the largest value its type can hold and wraps around to a wrong value.
Forcing buffered output to actually be sent. endl does this every time, which is slow in loops.

quiz.q: What do 'ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);' do?
options: Stop syncing C++ streams with C stdio and stop flushing cout before each cin, making I/O much faster
quiz.explain: Unsyncing lets C++ streams buffer independently, and untying cin stops a flush before every read. Together they speed up large inputs a lot.

quiz.q: A loop prints 200,000 lines with endl and gets Time Limit Exceeded. What is the simplest fix?
quiz.explain: endl flushes the output every line. '\n' just adds a newline and lets the buffer flush in big chunks.

quiz.q: Why use long long by default for sums in contests?
options: Sums of up to 200,000 values of up to 10^9 exceed the range of a 32-bit int
quiz.explain: A 32-bit int holds about 2.1 billion. Even two values near 10^9 can overflow it, and sums of many values certainly will.

articles.excerpt: You found the right idea in five minutes. The algorithm is O(n log n). You submit, and the judge says Time Limit Exceeded. You change nothing in the algorithm, swap endl for '\n', and resubmit. Accepted. Some verdicts have nothing to do with how smart your idea is. A good contest template removes…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: The Two-Minute Read That Saves Twenty
articles.subtitle: How to read a contest problem: constraints first, small cases by hand, and spotting the hidden pattern

glossary.definition: The limits printed under the input format, such as 1 ≤ n ≤ 2·10⁵, which reveal the required complexity.
A promise that the total size of all test cases together is bounded, so per-test work can be linear even with many tests.
The small example inputs and outputs in the statement. They show the format but rarely the hard cases.
The narrative wrapper around a problem, like a tale about cows or shops, which usually hides a standard task.
Solving tiny inputs by hand, sometimes all of them, to discover the pattern behind the answer.

quiz.q: A problem has t up to 10^4 test cases and each n up to 2·10^5, with the sum of n over all tests at most 2·10^5. What per-test complexity is safe?
quiz.explain: Because the total n across tests is bounded by 2·10^5, an O(n log n) solution per test sums to roughly the same as one big test, which is fast.

quiz.q: What should you read first in a new problem?
quiz.explain: Constraints tell you which complexities are allowed and the output format tells you exactly what to produce. The story can be skimmed afterwards.

quiz.q: Your formula passes all samples. What should you still do before submitting?
options: Try a few tiny or extreme cases by hand, like n = 1 or all values equal
quiz.explain: Samples are chosen to explain the format, not to catch bugs. Edge cases you check yourself catch the Wrong Answers that samples miss.

articles.excerpt: Contest problems love stories. Farmer John's cows walk along a fence. A shopkeeper rearranges her shelves. A wizard casts spells on a row of potions. Read every word carefully and five minutes have gone before you know what is being asked. Strong contestants read differently. In two minutes they…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: A Map From Newbie to Expert
articles.subtitle: The rating ladder: what to practise at each level, and how to know you are ready to climb

glossary.definition: A difficulty number on Codeforces problems. A problem rated 1400 is one that contestants around 1400 solve about half the time.
Problems you can already solve reliably. Practising only these feels productive but builds little new skill.
Problems a little above your level, roughly 100 to 300 rating points higher, where most improvement happens.
A technique you have never learned, which no amount of speed practice will fix.
The official written solution published after a contest, explaining the intended idea.

quiz.q: You are rated 1300. Which problems give the most improvement per hour?
quiz.explain: The stretch zone, about 100 to 300 points above your rating, is hard enough to teach you something and close enough that you can finish with effort.

quiz.q: How long should you usually try a problem before reading the editorial?
options: Long enough to have a real attempt, often 30 to 60 minutes, then read and re-implement
quiz.explain: A genuine attempt makes the editorial's idea stick. After that, re-implementing it yourself without looking turns understanding into skill.

quiz.q: Which topics typically start appearing around the 1600 to 1900 range?
options: Graphs, DP, number theory and binary search on the answer
quiz.explain: Around expert level, problems combine standard techniques like graph traversal, DP and number theory with an observation.

articles.excerpt: Most people quit competitive programming in the first two months. Not because they lack talent, but because they practise blindly: random problems, some far too easy, some impossibly hard, no sense of progress. The rating graph goes flat, and so does the motivation. Climbers do not walk up a…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Let a Robot Find Your Wrong Answer
articles.subtitle: Stress testing: a brute force, a random generator and a loop that finds the failing test for you

complexity.time: Thousands of tiny tests in seconds

glossary.definition: Running your fast solution and a simple brute force on many random small inputs and comparing their outputs.
A slow but obviously correct solution, used here only as a referee on tiny inputs.
A small program that prints a random valid input, usually tiny, for a given random seed.
An input on which the fast and brute-force solutions disagree, which pinpoints the bug.
The number that starts a random generator. The same seed always produces the same test, so failures can be reproduced.

quiz.q: Why should generated tests be tiny, like n between 1 and 6?
options: The brute force must be fast enough, and a tiny counterexample is easy to debug by hand
quiz.explain: Most bugs show up on small inputs. Tiny tests keep the brute force fast and give you a failing case you can trace on paper.

quiz.q: Why pass a seed to the generator?
options: So the exact failing test can be regenerated and debugged
quiz.explain: With the seed, you can reproduce the same random input any time, which turns a flaky failure into a fixed test case.

quiz.q: Your stress test runs 10,000 cases without a difference, but the judge still says Wrong Answer. What is a likely cause?
options: Your generator never produces the failing pattern, such as large values that overflow or a specific edge case
Stress tests always find every bug
You need more seeds of the same tiny size only
quiz.explain: A stress test only covers what the generator produces. Overflow, maximum sizes or special structures like all-equal arrays may need their own generators.

articles.excerpt: Wrong answer on test 7. You reread your code three times. It looks right. The samples pass. You cannot see test 7. Twenty minutes slip by while you stare at the screen, trying to imagine what the judge could possibly be feeding it. Experienced contestants do something different. In about five…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Wrong Answer on Test 4, Twelve Minutes Left
articles.subtitle: A calm, fast checklist for finding bugs when the clock is running and the test is hidden

glossary.definition: The judge's result for a submission, such as Wrong Answer, Time Limit Exceeded or Runtime Error.
C++ code whose result the language does not define, like reading past the end of an array, which may work locally and fail on the judge.
A compiler option that adds checks at run time and stops the program at the exact line of memory or overflow errors.
Explaining your code line by line, out loud or in writing, which often reveals the bug as you say it.
A specific guess about the bug that you can test quickly, such as 'it overflows when all values are 10 to the 9'.

quiz.q: Your code gets Runtime Error on the judge but runs fine on your laptop. What is a likely cause?
options: Undefined behaviour such as an out-of-bounds index or a stack overflow from deep recursion
quiz.explain: Undefined behaviour can appear to work locally and crash elsewhere. Sanitizers and checking array sizes catch it.

quiz.q: You get Time Limit Exceeded on test 15 of 40. Which check comes first?
options: Estimate your complexity on the maximum input and check for endl, missing fast I/O or resetting large arrays per test
quiz.explain: TLE usually means the complexity is too high for the largest tests, or I/O and per-test overhead are wasting time.

quiz.q: Why change one thing at a time when debugging?
options: So each test tells you whether that specific hypothesis was right
quiz.explain: Changing several things at once means a pass or fail tells you nothing about which change mattered.

articles.excerpt: The red text appears: Wrong Answer on test 4. Your heart rate jumps. You start changing things: < to <=, int to long long, a +1 here, a -1 there, resubmitting each time. Each attempt costs penalty, and none of them is aimed at anything. Debugging under pressure feels like panic, but it can be a…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: The Contest Ends, the Learning Starts
articles.subtitle: Upsolving: how to turn every problem you failed into a technique you own

glossary.definition: Solving, after a contest ends, the problems you could not solve during it.
The official explanation of each problem's intended solution, published after the contest.
Rebuilding a solution from memory instead of rereading it, which makes the idea stick far better.
Revisiting an idea after growing gaps, such as a day, a week and a month, so it moves into long-term memory.
A running list of what went wrong in each failed submission and the real cause, reviewed before contests.

quiz.q: Which problems are most worth upsolving after a contest?
options: Every problem in the round, including the hardest
The next one or two problems just beyond what you solved
Only the ones you already solved
None; just do the next contest
quiz.explain: Problems just beyond your current level teach the most per hour. The very hardest ones are usually too far away to learn from yet.

quiz.q: After reading an editorial, what should you do next?
options: Close it and implement the solution yourself from memory
quiz.explain: Implementing from memory is active recall. It exposes gaps that passive reading hides and makes the technique yours.

quiz.q: What belongs in a mistakes log entry?
options: The real cause of the failure, such as overflow or a misread constraint, in one line
quiz.explain: A short cause is easy to review and reveals patterns, like 'I keep forgetting to reset arrays between tests'.

articles.excerpt: Two students do the same number of contests in a semester. One improves steadily; the other stays flat. When you look at their weeks, the difference is not in the contests at all. It is in the hour after each one. The first student goes back to the problem that beat them, learns why, and codes it.…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: When the Answer Is Something You Build
articles.subtitle: Constructive problems: use small cases to find a structure, then write it down in one clean pass

glossary.definition: A problem that asks you to output an object, such as a permutation or a string, with given properties, or to say that none exists.
A list of answers for n = 1, 2, 3 and so on, worked out by hand or by brute force, used to spot a pattern.
An arrangement of the numbers 1 to n where each appears exactly once.
The judge program that verifies your output has the required property, since many different answers can be correct.
Turning a case for n into a smaller case, such as building the answer for n from the answer for n minus 2.

quiz.q: In CSES Permutations, adjacent numbers must not differ by exactly 1. For which n from 1 to 4 is there no answer?
quiz.explain: For n = 2 and n = 3 every arrangement has a neighbouring pair differing by 1. n = 1 is trivially fine and n = 4 works, for example 2 4 1 3.

quiz.q: Why is a brute force so helpful for constructive problems?
options: It prints valid answers for small n, which reveals the structure your construction should follow
quiz.explain: Seeing all valid answers for n up to 8 often makes the general pattern obvious, and it also tells you which n have no answer.

quiz.q: The statement says 'print any valid answer'. What does that tell you?
options: The judge uses a checker, so you may choose the simplest structure that works
You must print the lexicographically smallest
Output order does not matter at all
quiz.explain: A checker accepts every valid output. That freedom is a hint to look for a simple, regular construction.

articles.excerpt: "Print a permutation of 1 to n where no two neighbours differ by exactly 1, or say NO SOLUTION." There are n! permutations; for n = 10⁶ you cannot search them. And there is no formula to look up. You have to invent an arrangement. Problems like this make up a big share of Codeforces rounds between…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Guess the Shortcut, Then Check the Map
articles.subtitle: Greedy in contests: find a rule from small cases, hunt for counterexamples, prove it with an exchange argument, and only then submit

complexity.time: Usually O(n log n), dominated by the sort

glossary.definition: An algorithm that builds the answer step by step, always taking the choice that looks best right now and never undoing it.
A proof that takes any optimal solution and repeatedly swaps parts of it to match the greedy choice without making it worse, showing the greedy answer is optimal too.
A specific small input on which a proposed rule gives a worse answer than the true optimum, which is enough to reject the rule.
An exchange argument for orderings: compare two neighbouring items in both orders and show the sorted order is never worse.
The rules a comparator must obey for std::sort, including that an item is never less than itself and that 'less than' is transitive.
Running a fast solution and a slow brute force on many small random inputs and comparing their outputs to find a failing case.

quiz.q: Coins are 1, 3 and 4, and you must pay 6 with as few coins as possible. What does 'always take the largest coin that fits' give?
quiz.explain: Greedy takes 4, then 1 and 1, for 3 coins. Paying 3 + 3 uses only 2, so this rule is wrong for these coins.

quiz.q: Groups wait for orders; order i takes t minutes and has w people waiting. When should order i go before order j to minimise total waiting?
quiz.explain: Swapping two neighbours changes the cost only through w_j · t_i versus w_i · t_j. Putting i first is better when t_i · w_j < t_j · w_i, which is sorting by t/w without division.

quiz.q: What does an exchange argument show?
options: That any optimal solution can be changed step by step into the greedy one without getting worse
That greedy works on random inputs
quiz.explain: If every optimal answer can be morphed into the greedy answer without losing value, then the greedy answer is also optimal.

articles.excerpt: Eight minutes into a contest you read problem B. A rule jumps out: sort, then pair the biggest with the smallest. It passes the samples. You submit, and the verdict comes back: wrong answer on test 7. Greedy ideas are the fastest solutions to write and the easiest to get wrong. Strong contestants…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Find What Never Changes
articles.subtitle: Invariants and observations: the reasoning behind most Div. 2 problems from 1200 to 1600

complexity.time: Usually O(n) once the observation is found

glossary.definition: A quantity or property that every allowed move leaves unchanged, such as the parity of a sum.
A quantity that only ever moves in one direction, such as a count that can only decrease, which proves a process must end.
Whether a number is even or odd. Many moves change numbers but keep their parity.
Something that must be true for an answer to exist. An invariant usually gives one.
Something that, when true, guarantees an answer exists. Proving it usually needs a construction.

quiz.q: A move adds 1 to two different elements. What is invariant?
options: The parity of the sum of all elements
quiz.explain: Each move adds 2 to the total, so the sum's parity (even or odd) never changes.

quiz.q: In Coin Piles, each move removes 2 from one pile and 1 from the other. Why must a + b be divisible by 3 to empty both piles?
options: Every move removes exactly 3 coins in total
It does not need to be
quiz.explain: The total drops by 3 each move, so it can reach 0 only if it starts as a multiple of 3.

quiz.q: You found an invariant that rules out some inputs. What is still needed?
options: A proof or construction showing every remaining input really is solvable
A brute force for all n
quiz.explain: An invariant gives a necessary condition. You still need to show it is sufficient, usually by constructing an answer, or by checking it against a brute force.

articles.excerpt: A chessboard has two opposite corners cut off, leaving 62 squares. Can you cover it exactly with 31 dominoes? People try for minutes, shuffling dominoes around in their heads. Then someone notices the colours: every domino covers one black and one white square, but the two removed corners are the…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Pacing a Two-Hour Race
articles.subtitle: Contest strategy: problem order, when to skip, penalties, and keeping your nerve when the clock runs

glossary.definition: Extra cost for wrong submissions or late solves. In many formats each rejected attempt on a solved problem adds penalty time.
The live scoreboard showing how many contestants solved each problem, a useful hint about relative difficulty.
Time already spent that cannot be recovered. It should not decide whether you keep going on a problem.
On Codeforces, the tests run during the contest. Passing them does not guarantee passing the full system tests afterwards.
A fixed amount of time you allow yourself for a task before you stop and reassess.

quiz.q: You have spent 35 minutes on problem C with no progress, and many contestants have solved D. What should you usually do?
options: Keep going on C until the end
Read D, since the standings suggest it may be easier for you, and come back to C later
quiz.explain: Problem difficulty is personal, and the standings are evidence. A fresh problem often unlocks progress, and your mind keeps working on C in the background.

quiz.q: Why test before submitting even when you are confident?
options: Each wrong submission can cost penalty time or points, and a quick edge-case test is cheaper
quiz.explain: A minute spent on n = 1, maximum values and the samples usually costs less than a rejected attempt.

quiz.q: What does passing pretests on Codeforces mean?
options: It passed the tests run during the contest; full system tests later may still fail it
quiz.explain: Pretests are a subset. Hacks and system tests can still find bugs like overflow or time limits on maximum inputs.

articles.excerpt: Two contestants know exactly the same algorithms. One finishes with four problems solved; the other with two. The difference is not intelligence. The second spent seventy minutes fighting problem C, never read problem D, and submitted B three times without testing it. Contests reward knowledge, but…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Doing Maths on a Clock Face
articles.subtitle: Modular arithmetic: why answers come 'modulo 10^9 + 7', and the rules that keep huge numbers small and correct

glossary.definition: The number you divide by when taking a remainder, such as 10^9 + 7 in many contest problems.
What is left after dividing: 17 mod 5 is 2, because 17 = 3 × 5 + 2.
Two numbers are congruent modulo m when they have the same remainder after dividing by m.
When a result is too large for its type and wraps around to a wrong value.
A modulus that is a prime number, such as 10^9 + 7 or 998244353, which makes division possible through modular inverses.

quiz.q: Why is it safe to take the remainder after every addition and multiplication?
options: It is not safe; only take it at the end
Because (a + b) mod m and (a × b) mod m only depend on a mod m and b mod m
Because the judge rounds the answer
quiz.explain: Adding or multiplying the remainders gives the same final remainder as using the full numbers, so you can reduce at every step and keep numbers small.

quiz.q: In C++, what is (-7) % 3?
quiz.explain: C++ keeps the sign of the left operand, so the result is -1. To get a value in [0, m), add m and take mod again: ((x % m) + m) % m.

quiz.q: a and b are both below 10^9 + 7. Why must a × b be computed in long long?
options: The product can be about 10^18, which overflows a 32-bit int but fits in a 64-bit long long
quiz.explain: 10^9 × 10^9 is 10^18. A 32-bit int holds about 2.1 × 10^9, while a long long holds about 9.2 × 10^18.

articles.excerpt: "Print the number of ways, modulo 10⁹ + 7." This line appears under thousands of contest problems. The true answer might have a million digits; the number of ways to arrange 100,000 items is astronomically large. No integer type can hold it. So the problem asks for the remainder instead. That seems…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Raising to the Power of a Billion in Thirty Steps
articles.subtitle: Fast exponentiation: square and multiply along the bits of the exponent

glossary.definition: How many times a base is multiplied by itself: in a^b, b is the exponent.
Building a^2, a^4, a^8 and so on by squaring the previous value, so each step doubles the exponent.
Writing a number as a sum of powers of two, like 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, which is 1101 in binary.
For a prime p and a not divisible by p, a^(p−1) leaves remainder 1 modulo p. It lets you shrink exponents and compute inverses.

quiz.q: How many multiplications does binary exponentiation need for an exponent near 10^18?
options: About 120 at most (60 squarings and up to 60 extra multiplications)
quiz.explain: 10^18 has about 60 bits. Each bit costs one squaring and possibly one extra multiplication.

quiz.q: Using 13 = 8 + 4 + 1, how is a^13 built?
quiz.explain: Exponents add when powers multiply, so a^13 = a^(8+4+1) = a^8 × a^4 × a^1.

quiz.q: To compute a^(b^c) mod p for prime p, which exponent do you reduce first?
quiz.explain: By Fermat's little theorem, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 mod p when p does not divide a, so exponents only matter modulo p − 1.

articles.excerpt: Compute 3 to the power 1,000,000,000, modulo 10⁹ + 7. Multiplying by 3 a billion times takes about a billion steps: seconds in C++, too slow when there are a hundred thousand such queries. There is a way that takes about thirty steps. It is one of the oldest algorithms in mathematics, and it shows…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Washing Away Every Multiple
articles.subtitle: The Sieve of Eratosthenes, its smallest-prime-factor upgrade, and factorising a million numbers instantly

complexity.time: O(n log log n) to build; O(log x) to factorise each x

glossary.definition: A whole number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself, such as 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11.
A whole number greater than 1 that is not prime, so it has a divisor other than 1 and itself.
An algorithm that finds all primes up to n by crossing out the multiples of each prime.
For a number x, the smallest prime that divides it. Storing it for every x lets you factorise any x quickly.
Writing a number as a product of primes, such as 360 = 2^3 × 3^2 × 5.

quiz.q: When sieving with prime p, why can you start crossing out at p × p?
options: Every smaller multiple k × p with k < p has a smaller prime factor and was already crossed out
quiz.explain: A multiple k × p with k < p has a prime factor of k, which is smaller than p, so an earlier prime already crossed it out.

quiz.q: With a smallest-prime-factor table, how do you factorise 360?
quiz.explain: spf[360] = 2 gives 180, then 90, 45; spf[45] = 3 gives 15, then 5; spf[5] = 5 gives 1. Each step divides by a prime, so there are at most about log2 x steps.

quiz.q: Roughly how long does sieving up to 10^7 take in C++?
quiz.explain: The sieve does about n log log n simple operations, a few times 10^7 for n = 10^7, well under a second, though memory for the array matters.

articles.excerpt: A problem gives you 100,000 numbers up to a million and asks, for each one, how many divisors it has. Factoring each by trial division up to its square root costs about a thousand steps per number: a hundred million in total, uncomfortably slow. More than two thousand years ago, the Greek scholar…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: The Largest Tile That Fits the Floor
articles.subtitle: GCD, LCM and Euclid's algorithm, plus the extended version that finds the numbers behind the answer

practice_problems.name: Find Greatest Common Divisor of Array
Number of Subarrays With LCM Equal to K

glossary.definition: Greatest common divisor: the largest number that divides both a and b exactly.
Least common multiple: the smallest positive number that both a and b divide exactly.
A method that finds the GCD by repeatedly replacing (a, b) with (b, a mod b) until b becomes 0.
Integers x and y with a·x + b·y = gcd(a, b). They always exist and are found by the extended Euclidean algorithm.
Two numbers are coprime when their GCD is 1, meaning they share no prime factor.

quiz.q: Why does gcd(a, b) equal gcd(b, a mod b)?
options: Any number dividing both a and b also divides a − kb, which is a mod b, and vice versa, so both pairs have the same common divisors
Because a mod b is prime
quiz.explain: a mod b is a minus a multiple of b. Subtracting multiples of b does not change which numbers divide both, so the GCD is unchanged.

quiz.q: How should you compute lcm(a, b) safely?
quiz.explain: Both formulas are equal mathematically, but a × b can overflow before the division. Dividing first keeps intermediate values smaller.

quiz.q: Roughly how many steps does Euclid's algorithm take for numbers up to 10^18?
options: On the order of 90 at most
quiz.explain: The numbers shrink at least as fast as Fibonacci numbers grow backwards, so the step count is logarithmic, under about 90 for 64-bit inputs.

articles.excerpt: A room is 1,071 cm by 462 cm, and you want to tile it with identical square tiles, no cutting. What is the largest tile size that fits exactly? You could try every size from 462 downward. Or you could use an algorithm written down by Euclid more than two thousand years ago, which answers in a…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Finding the Undo Button on a Clock
articles.subtitle: Modular inverses: how to divide under a modulus with Fermat or extended Euclid, and precompute a million at once

complexity.time: O(log m) per inverse; O(n) for n factorial inverses

practice_problems.name: Count Ways to Make Array With Product

glossary.definition: For a number a modulo m, a value x with a × x ≡ 1 (mod m). Multiplying by x undoes multiplying by a.
For a prime p and a not divisible by p, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p). It implies the inverse of a is a^(p−2).
An algorithm that finds x and y with a·x + m·y = gcd(a, m). When the gcd is 1, x is the inverse of a.
Having greatest common divisor 1. An inverse of a modulo m exists exactly when a and m are coprime.
Precomputed values of k! and their inverses modulo p for every k up to n, so binomial coefficients cost O(1).

quiz.q: Modulo the prime 7, what is the inverse of 3?
Why does a^(p−2) give the inverse of a modulo a prime p?
options: Fermat says a^(p−1) ≡ 1, so a × a^(p−2) ≡ 1
quiz.explain: a^(p−1) = a × a^(p−2), and Fermat's little theorem says that equals 1 modulo p when p does not divide a.

quiz.q: Does 4 have an inverse modulo 6?
quiz.explain: 4 × x is always even, so it can never be 1 more than a multiple of 6. Inverses exist only when the gcd is 1.

articles.excerpt: You need n! / (k! (n − k)!) modulo 10⁹ + 7 for n up to a million: the number of ways to choose a team. Computing the factorials modulo p is easy. But then you need to divide, and as Doing Maths on a Clock Face warned, division does not survive taking remainders. The fix is to never divide at all.…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: How Many Ways to Pick the Team?
articles.subtitle: Binomial coefficients in contests: Pascal's triangle, factorial tables, and stars and bars

glossary.definition: C(n, k), the number of ways to choose k items from n distinct items when order does not matter.
A triangle of numbers where each entry is the sum of the two above it; row n lists C(n, 0) to C(n, n).
A counting trick for splitting n identical items into k groups: arrange n stars and k − 1 bars in a row.
An ordered arrangement. Choosing k items in order gives n! / (n − k)! possibilities.
The number of ways to arrange items with repeats, n! divided by the factorial of each repeated group's size.

quiz.q: Why is C(n, k) = C(n − 1, k − 1) + C(n − 1, k)?
options: Look at one particular item: either it is chosen, leaving k − 1 to pick from n − 1, or it is not, leaving k to pick from n − 1
It is only true for small n
quiz.explain: Every selection either includes a given item or does not; the two cases are counted separately and added.

quiz.q: How many ways can 5 identical apples be shared among 3 children (some may get none)?
quiz.explain: Stars and bars: 5 stars and 2 bars in a row of 7 places, so C(7, 2) = 21.

quiz.q: A grid path goes from the top-left to the bottom-right of a 3 by 3 grid of squares, moving only right or down. How many paths?
quiz.explain: Any path is 3 rights and 3 downs in some order: C(6, 3) = 20.

articles.excerpt: A cricket coach has 15 players and must pick 11. How many different teams are possible? Writing them out would take a lifetime: there are 1,365. Now pick 50 out of a million, modulo 10⁹ + 7, a hundred thousand times. Counting problems like this fill contest rounds from about 1400 rating upward. All…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Counting Without Double Counting
articles.subtitle: Inclusion-exclusion: add the singles, subtract the pairs, add back the triples, and enumerate it all with bitmasks

complexity.time: O(2^k · cost of one intersection) for k conditions

glossary.definition: A rule for counting the size of a union of sets by adding single sets, subtracting pairwise overlaps, adding triple overlaps, and so on.
Everything that is in at least one of the sets.
Everything that is in all of the chosen sets at once.
Counting the things you do not want and subtracting from the total, often easier than counting what you want directly.
A permutation where no element stays in its original position, such as a gift exchange where nobody gets their own gift.

quiz.q: How many numbers from 1 to 30 are divisible by 2 or 3?
quiz.explain: 15 divisible by 2, 10 by 3, minus 5 divisible by both (by 6): 15 + 10 − 5 = 20.

quiz.q: With k conditions, how many terms does the full inclusion-exclusion formula have?
quiz.explain: Each non-empty subset of the conditions contributes one term, with sign depending on the subset's size.

quiz.q: In the formula, which subsets get a minus sign?
quiz.explain: Singles are added, pairs subtracted, triples added: subsets of even size carry a minus sign.

articles.excerpt: How many numbers from 1 to 10¹⁸ are divisible by at least one of the primes 2, 3, 5 and 7? You cannot loop to 10¹⁸. Counting multiples of each prime is easy, n / p, but adding them counts 6, 10, 14 and friends twice, and 210 four times. The fix is a counting rule that corrects its own overcounting,…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Counting the Numbers That Share Nothing With n
articles.subtitle: Euler's totient function: the product formula from prime factors, a sieve for all values, and Euler's theorem for exponents

complexity.time: O(sqrt n) for one value; O(n log log n) for all values up to n

glossary.definition: φ(n), the count of integers from 1 to n that are coprime to n.
Two numbers are coprime when their greatest common divisor is 1.
A function where f(a·b) = f(a)·f(b) whenever a and b are coprime. φ is multiplicative.
If a and n are coprime, then a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n). Fermat's little theorem is the special case where n is prime.
A number of the form p^k for a prime p, such as 8 = 2^3 or 9 = 3^2.

quiz.q: What is φ(12)?
What is φ(p) for a prime p?
quiz.explain: Every number from 1 to p − 1 is coprime to a prime p; only p itself is not.

quiz.q: How does Euler's theorem help compute a^b mod n for a huge b when gcd(a, n) = 1?
options: Exponents can be reduced modulo φ(n), since a^φ(n) ≡ 1
Bases can be reduced modulo φ(n)
quiz.explain: Because a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n), a^b ≡ a^(b mod φ(n)) (mod n) when a and n are coprime.

articles.excerpt: A clock has 12 positions. You start at 0 and jump forward by the same step each time. With a step of 5 you visit every position before returning to 0; with a step of 4 you only ever visit 0, 4 and 8. The steps that visit every position are exactly those that share no factor with 12: 1, 5, 7 and 11.…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Three Clocks That Agree Only Once
articles.subtitle: The Chinese remainder theorem: combine congruences into one, constructively for coprime moduli and with extended GCD when they are not

complexity.time: O(k log M) for k congruences

glossary.definition: A statement x ≡ r (mod m), meaning x leaves remainder r when divided by m.
If the moduli are pairwise coprime, a system of congruences has exactly one solution modulo the product of the moduli.
Every pair of numbers in a set has greatest common divisor 1, such as 3, 5 and 7.
An extension of Euclid's gcd algorithm that also finds integers p and q with a·p + b·q = gcd(a, b).
Least common multiple: the smallest positive number divisible by each of the given numbers.

quiz.q: Which x in [0, 15) satisfies x ≡ 2 (mod 3) and x ≡ 3 (mod 5)?
quiz.explain: 8 = 2·3 + 2 and 8 = 1·5 + 3. Since 3 and 5 are coprime, it is the only solution in [0, 15).

quiz.q: Does x ≡ 3 (mod 4), x ≡ 4 (mod 6) have a solution?
options: No, because 4 − 3 is not divisible by gcd(4, 6) = 2
quiz.explain: The first says x is odd, the second says x is even. In general a solution exists only if the remainders agree modulo the gcd of the moduli.

quiz.q: When combining x ≡ r1 (mod m1) with x ≡ r2 (mod m2) for non-coprime moduli, what is the modulus of the result?
quiz.explain: Solutions repeat every lcm(m1, m2). Only for coprime moduli is that equal to the product.

articles.excerpt: There is a number. Divided by 3 it leaves 2, divided by 5 it leaves 3, divided by 7 it leaves 2. What is it? This puzzle comes from an ancient Chinese mathematical text, the Sunzi Suanjing, and its answer, 23, can be found by a method that still powers contest solutions and real systems today. In…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Counting Outfits Without Trying Them On
articles.subtitle: The combinatorics toolkit for contests: product and sum rules, complement counting, Catalan numbers and Burnside's lemma for symmetric objects

complexity.time: O(n) after O(n) factorial precomputation for most formulas

glossary.definition: If a choice is made in independent stages with a, b, c options, the total number of outcomes is a × b × c.
If outcomes split into separate cases that do not overlap, the total is the sum of the counts of each case.
Counting what you do not want and subtracting it from the total.
A one-to-one pairing between two sets of objects, which proves they have the same size.
The sequence 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, ... counting balanced bracket sequences and many structures equivalent to them.
The number of distinct objects up to symmetry equals the average, over all symmetries, of the number of objects each symmetry leaves unchanged.

quiz.q: How many strings of length 4 over the 26 lowercase letters contain at least one 'a'?
quiz.explain: Count the complement: strings with no 'a' number 25⁴. Subtract from all 26⁴ strings: 456,976 − 390,625 = 66,351.

quiz.q: How many balanced bracket sequences of length 8 are there?
quiz.explain: Length 8 means n = 4 pairs, and the 4th Catalan number is C(8, 4) / 5 = 70 / 5 = 14.

quiz.q: Using Burnside's lemma, how many distinct necklaces of 4 beads in 2 colours exist, counting rotations as the same?
quiz.explain: Rotations by 0, 1, 2, 3 positions fix 16, 2, 4 and 2 colourings. The average is (16 + 2 + 4 + 2) / 4 = 6.

articles.excerpt: A contest problem asks: how many valid bracket sequences of length 10⁶ are there, modulo 10⁹ + 7? Another asks for the number of distinct necklaces of 10⁶ beads in 10⁹ colours, where rotating a necklace does not make it different. Listing the objects is out of the question; even for length 40 there…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Averaging Over a Thousand Parallel Universes
articles.subtitle: Expected value and linearity of expectation: indicator variables, probability DP, and printing expected values modulo a prime

complexity.time: Often O(n) with linearity; O(n · states) for probability DP

glossary.definition: A number whose value depends on the outcome of a random experiment, such as the sum of two dice.
The probability-weighted average of a random variable's values: what you get on average over many repetitions.
The rule E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y], which holds for any random variables, independent or not.
A random variable that is 1 if an event happens and 0 otherwise. Its expected value equals the event's probability.
Two events are independent when knowing one happened does not change the probability of the other.

quiz.q: A random permutation of n items is drawn. What is the expected number of items left in their original position?
quiz.explain: Each of the n positions is a fixed point with probability 1/n. By linearity, the expected count is n × 1/n = 1, for every n.

quiz.q: Does linearity of expectation require the variables to be independent?
options: No, E[X + Y] = E[X] + E[Y] holds for any random variables
quiz.explain: Linearity holds for dependent variables too. Independence is needed for E[XY] = E[X]E[Y], not for sums.

quiz.q: An expected value is 7/2 and the problem asks for it modulo 10⁹ + 7. What do you print?
quiz.explain: A fraction P/Q is printed as P × Q⁻¹ modulo the prime. The inverse of 2 is 500000004, and 7 × 500000004 mod 10⁹ + 7 = 500000007.

articles.excerpt: You shuffle a deck of 52 cards. On average, how many cards end up in their original position? Trying to answer by listing all 52! orders is hopeless, and even computing the probability of exactly k fixed points needs inclusion-exclusion. Yet the expected number is exactly 1, and the proof takes one…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Jumping a Billion Steps Ahead in a Recurrence
articles.subtitle: Matrix exponentiation: write a linear recurrence as a matrix, raise it to the n-th power in O(k³ log n), and count paths in graphs the same way

complexity.time: O(k^3 log n) for a k × k matrix

glossary.definition: A sequence where each term is a fixed weighted sum of a fixed number of previous terms, such as F(n) = F(n−1) + F(n−2).
The last k terms of a sequence stacked into a column, enough to compute the next term.
The k × k matrix that turns the state vector at step n into the state vector at step n + 1.
The matrix with ones on the diagonal and zeros elsewhere; multiplying by it changes nothing, like multiplying by 1.
A matrix where entry (i, j) is the number of edges from vertex i to vertex j.

quiz.q: To compute F(n) for n = 10^18 with a 2 × 2 matrix, roughly how many matrix multiplications are needed?
quiz.explain: Binary exponentiation needs about log2(10^18) ≈ 60 squarings plus up to 60 extra multiplications.

quiz.q: For the recurrence f(n) = f(n−1) + f(n−2) + ... + f(n−6), what size is the transition matrix?
quiz.explain: The state needs the last 6 terms, so the matrix is 6 × 6: one row computes the new term, five rows shift the others down.

quiz.q: If A is a graph's adjacency matrix, what does entry (i, j) of A^k count?
options: Walks of exactly k edges from i to j
quiz.explain: Each multiplication extends every walk by one edge, summing over the middle vertex.
