Yet the answer comes back in microseconds with a trick built from two things you already know: the recurrence, and fast exponentiation from Raising to the Power of a…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: A Million Numbers, Each Asking How Many Divisors It Has
articles.subtitle: Counting divisors for many queries by letting every number drop a token into its multiples, and why that costs only N log N

complexity.time: O(N log N) precomputation, O(1) per query

glossary.definition: A positive integer d divides n when n / d is a whole number. For example, the divisors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 12.
d(n), the number of positive divisors of n. d(12) = 6.
The sum 1 + 1/2 + 1/3 + ... + 1/N, which grows like the natural logarithm of N.
A precomputed table storing the smallest prime dividing each number up to N, which lets you factorise any number in O(log n) steps.
Computing answers for every possible input once, before reading queries, so each query becomes a table lookup.

quiz.q: Why does the 'add 1 to every multiple of d' loop cost about N ln N in total?
options: Each d visits N/d multiples, and N/1 + N/2 + ... + N/N is N times the harmonic series, about N ln N
quiz.explain: The work for d is N/d. Summing over d gives N(1 + 1/2 + ... + 1/N) ≈ N ln N, about 1.4 × 10⁷ for N = 10⁶.

quiz.q: What is d(72), using 72 = 2³ × 3²?
quiz.explain: Each divisor picks an exponent 0..3 for 2 and 0..2 for 3: (3 + 1)(2 + 1) = 12.

quiz.q: For the maximum gcd of any pair in an array, what do you check for each candidate d from large to small?
options: Whether at least two array elements are multiples of d
Whether d divides the array sum
Whether d is in the array
quiz.explain: Two multiples of d have gcd at least d. Scanning d downwards, the first d with two multiples present is the answer.

articles.excerpt: Counting the divisors of one number is a beginner exercise: try every candidate up to its square root. Now do it for 100,000 numbers, each up to a million, inside a one-second limit. Suddenly the beginner method is borderline, and the problem is really asking whether you know a different way to…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Shuffling Letter Tiles When Some Tiles Are Twins
articles.subtitle: Counting distinct arrangements of a word with the multinomial coefficient, factorials modulo a prime and modular inverses

glossary.definition: An ordering of items. n distinct items have n! orderings.
n! / (c₁! c₂! ... c_k!), the number of distinct orderings of n items where cᵢ items are identical copies of type i.
Precomputed values of 0!, 1!, ..., n! modulo a prime, so any factorial is available in O(1).
For a prime p and x not divisible by p, the number x⁻¹ with x · x⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p). It replaces division in modular arithmetic.
A counting method for distributing identical items into distinct groups by arranging items and dividers in a row.

quiz.q: How many distinct strings can be made from the letters of 'banana'?
Why can you not compute n! mod p and then divide by c! mod p with ordinary integer division?
options: After reducing mod p the true quotient is lost; you must multiply by the modular inverse instead
quiz.explain: n! mod p is not divisible by c! mod p in general. Modular division means multiplying by an inverse, which exists because p is prime.

quiz.q: In how many ways can 2 identical apples be given to 3 children (some may get none)?
quiz.explain: Stars and bars: arrange 2 apples and 2 dividers in a row, C(4, 2) = 6.

articles.excerpt: How many different strings can you make by rearranging the letters of "mississippi"? If all 11 letters were different, the answer would be 11! = 39,916,800. But swapping two of the s's produces the same string, so most of those orderings are repeats. The real answer is much smaller, and finding it…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: A Tower of Powers on a Clock That Repeats
articles.subtitle: Computing a^(b^c) mod p with Fermat's little theorem: reduce the exponent modulo p − 1, never modulo p, and watch the zero cases

complexity.time: O(log c + log p) per query

glossary.definition: For a prime p and an integer a not divisible by p, a^(p−1) ≡ 1 (mod p).
An expression like a^(b^c), evaluated from the top down: first b^c, then a raised to that.
The smallest k > 0 with a^k ≡ 1 (mod p). It always divides p − 1.
Computing a^e mod m with about 2 log e multiplications by squaring and multiplying according to the bits of e.
The generalisation of Fermat: a^φ(n) ≡ 1 (mod n) whenever gcd(a, n) = 1.

quiz.q: To compute 3^(2^3) mod 7, what exponent should you actually use?
quiz.explain: By Fermat, 3^6 ≡ 1 (mod 7), so exponents repeat every 6. 8 mod 6 = 2 and 3² = 9 ≡ 2 (mod 7).

quiz.q: Why does reducing the exponent modulo p give wrong answers?
options: Powers repeat with period dividing p − 1, not p, so exponents are equivalent modulo p − 1
Exponents cannot be reduced at all
quiz.explain: Fermat's little theorem gives a^(p−1) ≡ 1, so the cycle length divides p − 1. Using p shifts the exponent by one step per wrap.

quiz.q: When does Fermat's reduction fail outright?
options: When a is a multiple of p, since then a^(p−1) ≡ 0, not 1
quiz.explain: Fermat requires a not divisible by p. If a ≡ 0, the answer is 0 for any positive exponent and 1 for exponent 0, which must be handled separately.

Now raise the stakes: compute a^(b^c) mod p, where b and c are each up to 10⁹. The exponent b^c can have billions of digits. You cannot even write it down, let…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: A Tournament Bracket for Your Array
articles.subtitle: Segment trees from scratch: build, point update and range query in O(log n), recursive and iterative, plus a first look at lazy propagation

complexity.time: O(n) build; O(log n) per update and query

glossary.definition: A binary tree over an array where every node stores the combined answer for one contiguous segment, and each node's segment is split in half between its two children.
The rule that combines the answers of two adjacent segments into the answer for their union, such as min, max, sum, xor or gcd.
A value that leaves any answer unchanged when merged with it: 0 for sum and xor, plus infinity for min, minus infinity for max.
Changing a single array element, after which only the nodes on the path from that leaf to the root need recomputing.
A question about a contiguous block a[l..r], answered by merging a few nodes whose segments exactly tile that block.
A technique for range updates where a node records a pending change for its whole segment and passes it to its children only when someone needs to look inside.

quiz.q: In a min segment tree, what should a query return for a node whose segment does not overlap the query range at all?
options: Plus infinity, the neutral element for min
quiz.explain: A non-overlapping node must not affect the answer. Plus infinity is neutral for min; returning 0 would wrongly win every comparison against positive values.

quiz.q: After a point update at index i, which nodes must be recomputed?
options: The leaf for i and each of its ancestors up to the root
All leaves to the right of i
quiz.explain: Only segments containing i change, and those are exactly the leaf and its ancestors: one node per level, so O(log n) work.

quiz.q: Why does a range query visit only O(log n) nodes?
options: Because the tree has only log n nodes
Because at each level at most two nodes are partially covered, and only those recurse further
quiz.explain: Inside a contiguous range, only the two boundary nodes on each level can be cut in half. Every other node is either fully inside or fully outside and stops immediately.

A loop over the block costs up to 200,000 steps per question, so the worst case is 4 × 10¹⁰ steps, far past any time limit. Prefix sums answer range…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Renaming Huge Numbers as 1, 2, 3
articles.subtitle: Coordinate compression: map values up to 10^9 onto their ranks so arrays, Fenwick trees and segment trees can index them

complexity.time: O(n log n) to build; O(log n) per lookup

practice_problems.name: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

glossary.definition: Replacing each value by its rank among all distinct values, so huge or sparse values become small consecutive indices.
A value's position in the sorted list of distinct values, for example 0 for the smallest.
A mapping where a < b exactly when map(a) < map(b), so comparisons give the same answers after compression.
Reading all input and queries first, then answering them, which lets you compress every value that will ever appear.
A structure over an array of counts that supports prefix sums and point updates in O(log n), indexed by position.

quiz.q: Values [1000000000, 5, 70, 5] compress to which ranks (starting from 0)?
quiz.explain: Distinct sorted values are 5, 70, 1000000000, with ranks 0, 1, 2. Duplicates share a rank.

quiz.q: Why must you include query values, not just the initial array, when compressing for a problem with updates and queries?
options: A value that appears only in a later update or query would otherwise have no index
quiz.explain: Compression is a fixed dictionary. Every value you will ever need to index, including those in future updates and range bounds, must be in it.

quiz.q: What property makes compression safe for problems about comparisons and ranges?
options: It keeps exact differences between values
It is order-preserving, so less-than and equality relations are unchanged
It removes duplicates from the input
quiz.explain: Ranks keep the order of values, so any question that depends only on order gives the same answer. Questions that depend on actual distances do not survive.

articles.excerpt: You want to count, for each number in an array, how many smaller numbers appear after it. A Fenwick tree over values would do it in O(n log n): walk from the right, query "how many values below x have I seen?", then add x. There is one problem. Values go up to 10⁹, and an array of a billion…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Splitting a Long Road Into Neighbourhoods
articles.subtitle: Square root decomposition: cut the array into about √n blocks, keep a summary per block, and answer range queries and updates in O(√n)

complexity.time: O(n) build; O(√n) per query and update

glossary.definition: Splitting an array into blocks of about √n elements and storing a summary per block, so any range is a few whole blocks plus two short partial pieces.
One contiguous group of B elements; block b holds indices b·B to b·B + B − 1, and the last block may be shorter.
The number of elements per block, B, chosen to balance the work on partial pieces (up to about 2B) against the work on whole blocks (up to about n / B).
A block that the query range only partly covers, so its elements are handled one at a time.
A value stored per block meaning 'add this to every element of the block', used so a range update touches whole blocks in O(1) each.

quiz.q: With n = 10,000 and blocks of size 100, at most how many whole blocks can a single query use?
quiz.explain: There are only 10,000 / 100 = 100 blocks in total, so a query never touches more than 100 whole blocks, plus fewer than 200 loose elements at the ends.

quiz.q: Why is a block size near √n a good default?
options: It balances the two costs, about 2B loose elements and about n / B whole blocks, so neither dominates
Smaller blocks always use less memory
quiz.explain: Loose elements grow with B while whole blocks shrink with B. Their sum is smallest when the two are about equal, which happens around √n.

quiz.q: During a range add, a block is covered completely. What should you update?
options: Only the block's lazy tag and its stored sum
quiz.explain: Adding v to a whole block raises its sum by v × B and is recorded once in the tag. Partial blocks are the only places where single elements change.

articles.excerpt: A problem gives you 200,000 numbers and asks two kinds of questions: add a value to a range, and sum a range. A plain loop is O(n) per operation, which means billions of steps. Prefix sums answer sums instantly but must be rebuilt after every change. A segment tree solves this in O(log n), but…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: A Sorted Shelf That Knows Every Book's Position
articles.subtitle: GCC's policy-based ordered set: k-th element and rank queries in O(log n), duplicates with pairs, Josephus and nested ranges

complexity.time: O(log n) per insert, erase, order_of_key and find_by_order

practice_problems.name: Count of Smaller Numbers After Self

glossary.definition: A sorted set that, besides insert, erase and find, can report the k-th smallest element and how many elements are smaller than a value.
The number of elements strictly smaller than a value, which is also the 0-indexed position the value has or would have in sorted order.
The k-th smallest element of a collection. The 0-th order statistic is the minimum.
The number of nodes in the subtree below and including a node. Storing it in every node is what lets a balanced tree answer rank questions.
A GCC library extension, in the __gnu_pbds namespace, that builds trees and hash tables from chosen policies, including one that keeps subtree sizes.
An extra unique field, such as the original index, paired with a value so that equal values become distinct keys in a set.

quiz.q: A pbds ordered set holds {3, 8, 15, 21, 40}. What does order_of_key(16) return?
quiz.explain: order_of_key counts elements strictly smaller than the key. 3, 8 and 15 are smaller than 16, so the answer is 3.

quiz.q: You insert the values 5, 5 and 5 into ordered_set<int>. What is its size?
quiz.explain: It is a set, so equal keys are stored once. To keep duplicates, store pairs (value, unique index).

quiz.q: Which statement about the pbds ordered set is true?
options: It is part of standard C++17
It is a GCC libstdc++ extension, fine on judges that use GNU G++ but not portable
quiz.explain: The header lives under ext/ in GCC's standard library. Codeforces and CSES compile with GNU G++, so it is safe there, but not in interview code or with MSVC.

articles.excerpt: You are reading numbers one at a time, and after each one you must say how many earlier numbers were smaller. Or children stand in a circle, and you must repeatedly remove the child k places ahead, among those still standing. Both questions ask about positions in a sorted order that keeps changing.…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Rolling the Odometer Without Passing the Limit
articles.subtitle: Digit DP: count numbers up to 10^18 with a digit property by filling digits left to right with a tight flag

practice_problems.name: Numbers At Most N Given Digit Set

glossary.definition: A dynamic programming technique that counts numbers in a range by choosing their digits one at a time, from the most significant digit, while tracking a small state.
A boolean saying whether every digit chosen so far equals the upper bound's digit. While tight, the next digit cannot exceed the bound's next digit.
Answering a range [L, R] as f(R) − f(L − 1), where f(x) counts valid numbers in [0, x].
Zeros written before a number's first real digit when it is padded to the bound's length, such as 007 for 7.
A boolean saying whether a non-zero digit has been placed yet, used to tell padding zeros apart from real zeros.
Caching the result of a function for each argument combination so that each state is solved only once.

quiz.q: You are filling digits of a number at most R = 245. The first digit chosen is 1. What is the tight flag now, and how many choices does the next digit have?
quiz.explain: 1 is smaller than R's first digit 2, so every number starting with 1 is already below 245. The bound no longer restricts later digits.

quiz.q: How do you count valid numbers in [L, R] with digit DP?
options: Run the DP once with both bounds
f(R) − f(L − 1), where f(x) counts valid numbers in [0, x]
quiz.explain: Counting from 0 to a single bound is easy. Subtracting the count up to L − 1 leaves exactly the numbers from L to R.

quiz.q: Why are tight states usually not memoised, or memoised separately?
options: Only one tight path exists, along the bound's own digits, so there is little to reuse; the free states are the ones shared by many prefixes
quiz.explain: Exactly one prefix of each length is tight. All the reuse comes from free states, which many different prefixes reach.

articles.excerpt: How many numbers between 1 and 10¹⁸ have a digit sum divisible by 7? How many have no two equal adjacent digits? How many contain at most three non-zero digits? Looping over 10¹⁸ numbers is impossible, and the property depends on the digits, which plain maths does not handle well. Problems of this…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Playing the Board Game With Every Roll at Once
articles.subtitle: DP over probabilities and expectations: push probability forward through states, pull expected values backward, and handle self-loops

glossary.definition: A DP whose table entries are probabilities of being in each state after some number of steps, filled by pushing probability mass along transitions.
A DP whose entries are expected remaining costs or steps from each state, usually filled backwards from the end states.
A state the process never leaves, such as 'the game is over'. Its expected remaining steps are 0.
A transition from a state back to itself, such as a roll that changes nothing. It makes the expectation equation refer to itself.
The expected value of a sum equals the sum of expected values, even when the parts are dependent.

quiz.q: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is at least 9?
quiz.explain: Sums 9, 10, 11, 12 occur in 4, 3, 2 and 1 ways out of 36: 10/36 = 5/18.

quiz.q: Why is expected number of steps usually computed backwards, from the end states?
options: The expected remaining steps from a state depend on the states it can move to, and at the end they are known to be 0
quiz.explain: E[s] = 1 + Σ p · E[next]. The end states anchor the recursion with E = 0, so you fill towards the start.

quiz.q: A state stays put with probability 1/2 and otherwise moves to a state with expected remaining steps 4. What is its expected remaining steps?
quiz.explain: E = 1 + (1/2)·E + (1/2)·4. Moving the self term over gives (1/2)·E = 3, so E = 6.

articles.excerpt: You roll a die 100 times. What is the probability that the total lands between 300 and 400? You could simulate a million games and estimate it, but the judge wants six correct decimal places, and simulation will not deliver that. Listing all 6¹⁰⁰ outcomes is out of the question. Yet the answer…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Packing When the Shop Has Only Three of Each
articles.subtitle: Knapsack variants for contests: bounded counts with binary splitting, value-indexed DP for huge weights, and bitsets for subset sums

complexity.time: O(W × Σ log c) bounded; O(n × V) value-based; O(n × S / 64) bitset

glossary.definition: A knapsack where each item type can be taken at most a given number of times, between 0/1 (once) and unbounded (any number).
Rewriting c copies of an item as bundles of 1, 2, 4, … copies plus a remainder, so any count from 0 to c is a subset of bundles.
A knapsack table indexed by total value, storing the minimum weight needed, used when weights are huge but values are small.
A fixed-size array of bits that the CPU processes 64 at a time, so shifting and OR-ing a whole subset-sum table is very fast.
The question of which totals can be formed by choosing some of the given numbers.

quiz.q: An item has 13 copies. Which bundles does binary splitting create?
quiz.explain: Take 1, 2 and 4 (total 7), then the remainder 13 − 7 = 6. Every count from 0 to 13 is a sum of some of these, and none can exceed 13.

quiz.q: Weights go up to 10^9 but the total value of all items is at most 10^5. Which DP fits?
options: dp[value] = min weight, then the largest value whose min weight fits
quiz.explain: A table indexed by weight would need 10^9 cells. Index by value instead, which is small, and store the lightest way to reach each value.

quiz.q: Why is the bitset version of subset sum about 64 times faster than a boolean array?
options: One machine instruction processes 64 sums at once when shifting and OR-ing
quiz.explain: reach |= reach << x updates the whole table, and each 64-bit word holds 64 entries.

articles.excerpt: You know the classic 0/1 knapsack from Packing a Backpack With a Weight Limit: each item once, a table over capacities, done. Then the contest changes one detail, and the template breaks: the shop has up to 1,000 copies of each book, and expanding them one by one is too slow; weights go up to 10⁹,…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: The Lowest Road at Every Point
articles.subtitle: The convex hull trick: when a DP transition is a minimum over lines, keep only the lower envelope and cut O(n²) to O(n)

complexity.time: O(n) with monotone slopes and queries; O(n log n) otherwise

practice_problems.name: Kalila and Dimna in the Logging Industry

glossary.definition: A DP optimisation for transitions of the form min over j of (m_j · x + c_j), which keeps only the lines that can ever be the minimum.
For a set of lines, the curve formed by the smallest line value at each x. Lines that never touch it can be discarded.
A line y = m·x + c has slope m (how steeply it rises) and intercept c (its value at x = 0).
A double-ended queue of lines kept in slope order, from which useless lines are removed at the back when adding and at the front when queries move right.
A segment tree over x values that stores one line per node and answers minimum-at-x queries in O(log C) for lines inserted in any order.

quiz.q: A DP has dp[i] = min over j < i of (dp[j] + b[j] · a[i]). What are the lines and the query point?
options: Slope dp[j], intercept b[j], query a[i]
Slope b[j], intercept dp[j], query x = a[i]
quiz.explain: For each j, the expression is a line in x with slope b[j] and intercept dp[j]. Evaluating all of them at x = a[i] and taking the minimum gives dp[i].

quiz.q: Lines are added in decreasing slope order and queries come in increasing x. Why can a line be removed from the front of the deque forever?
options: Once the next line is at least as good at the current x, it stays at least as good for all larger x, and queries only move right
quiz.explain: With decreasing slopes, the newer line decreases faster as x grows, so once it wins it keeps winning for all later queries.

quiz.q: When is a Li Chao tree the better choice than the monotone deque?
options: When slopes or query points arrive in arbitrary order
When there are fewer than 10 lines
When the DP is over a tree
quiz.explain: The deque relies on sorted slopes and sorted queries. A Li Chao tree accepts lines and queries in any order at O(log C) each.

articles.excerpt: A frog hops along stones of increasing height. Jumping from stone j to stone i costs (hᵢ − hⱼ)² plus a fixed fee C, and the frog wants the cheapest way to the last stone. The DP is obvious: dp[i] = min over j < i of dp[j] + (hᵢ − hⱼ)² + C. With 2 × 10⁵ stones that is 2 × 10¹⁰ transitions, far too…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: No Two Neighbours Alike, Up to a Quintillion
articles.subtitle: CSES Counting Numbers: a digit DP with previous digit, tight and started flags, and why leading zeros need care

glossary.definition: Two digits next to each other in a number's decimal representation, such as 2 and 3 in 1234.
Whether every digit chosen so far matches the upper bound exactly, which limits the next digit.
Whether a non-zero digit has been placed. Before that, zeros are padding, not real digits.
The last real digit placed, needed to forbid the next digit from repeating it.
f(x), the number of valid integers in [0, x], so that a range [a, b] is f(b) − f(a − 1).

quiz.q: How many integers in [100, 120] have no two equal adjacent digits?
quiz.explain: 100 fails (0, 0), 101 to 109 pass (9 numbers), 110 to 119 fail (1, 1), and 120 passes: 10 in total.

quiz.q: Why does treating padding zeros as real digits give wrong counts?
options: A number like 7, written 007, would be rejected for having two adjacent zeros even though 7 is valid
quiz.explain: When the bound has more digits than the number, the padding zeros are not part of the number and must not be compared.

quiz.q: What is the answer for a = 0, b = 0?
quiz.explain: The single number 0 has no adjacent digits at all, so it is valid. f(0) − f(−1) = 1 − 0 = 1.

articles.excerpt: How many numbers between a and b, where b can be as large as 10¹⁸, have no two equal digits next to each other? 1213 is fine, 1223 is not. A loop over the range is hopeless, and there is no neat closed formula once the bounds are arbitrary. This CSES problem is the cleanest possible exercise in…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: The Freelancer Who Never Double-Books
articles.subtitle: Weighted interval scheduling: sort by end day, binary search the last gig that fits, and take or skip each one

practice_problems.name: Maximum Number of Events That Can Be Attended II

glossary.definition: Choosing a set of non-overlapping intervals, each with a value, so that the total value is as large as possible.
Two gigs are compatible when they do not overlap, so one person can do both.
For gig i in end-sorted order, the number of gigs that end strictly before gig i starts. All of them are compatible with gig i.
A DP rule that compares two choices for item i: skip it and keep the best answer so far, or take it and add its value to the best answer among compatible items.
A proof style for greedy algorithms that shows any optimal answer can be swapped, piece by piece, into the greedy answer without getting worse.

quiz.q: Gigs are sorted by end day. Gig i starts on day s. Which gigs can safely come before it when days are inclusive?
options: Gigs that end strictly before s, which form a prefix of the sorted list
quiz.explain: A gig ending on day s would share day s with gig i. Because the list is sorted by end, every gig ending before s sits in one prefix, whose length lower_bound(ends, s) returns.

quiz.q: Why does the greedy 'earliest end first' rule fail here, when it is optimal for Movie Festival?
options: It maximises the number of gigs, but a few long, well-paid gigs can be worth more than many cheap ones
quiz.explain: The exchange argument behind the greedy only works when every gig is worth the same. With rewards, you must compare taking and skipping, which is what the DP does.

quiz.q: In the LeetCode version a job may start at the exact time another ends. What changes in the code?
options: Use upper_bound instead of lower_bound, so gigs ending exactly at the start time count as compatible
quiz.explain: upper_bound counts ends that are less than or equal to the start. That one-character change flips the boundary rule from 'strictly before' to 'touching is fine'.

articles.excerpt: Riya is a freelance designer with a calendar full of offers. A logo from day 2 to day 5 pays 80, a poster from day 7 to day 9 pays 60, and a third gig overlaps both. She cannot work two gigs on the same day, and she wants the most money by the end of the month. Grabbing the best-paid gig first…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: A Fingerprint for Every Substring
articles.subtitle: Polynomial string hashing: compare any two substrings in O(1), keep collisions rare with two moduli or a random base, and survive anti-hash tests

complexity.time: O(n) preprocessing; O(1) per substring hash

glossary.definition: A number computed from a string by treating its characters as digits in base B and reducing modulo a large prime M.
An array where entry i holds the hash of the first i characters, from which the hash of any substring follows in O(1).
A hash that can be updated in O(1) when a window slides by one character, by removing the oldest character and appending a new one.
Two different strings that happen to receive the same hash value.
Hashing every string with two independent (base, modulus) pairs and treating strings as equal only when both hashes agree.
An input deliberately built so that two different strings collide under a specific, predictable hash function.
The fact that among k random values from M possibilities, some pair is likely to match once k is around the square root of M, far sooner than intuition suggests.

quiz.q: With prefix hashes h and powers p, what is the hash of s[l..r) (half-open)?
quiz.explain: h[r] contains the prefix h[l] shifted left by r − l digits. Subtracting h[l] · B^(r−l) removes it and leaves exactly the substring's digits.

quiz.q: Why should 'a' map to 1 rather than 0?
options: With 'a' = 0, strings like 'b', 'ab' and 'aab' all get the same hash because leading zeros vanish
quiz.explain: A digit 0 at the front of a number adds nothing, so prefixes of 'a' become invisible. Mapping letters to 1..26 makes every character count.

quiz.q: You insert about one million substring hashes into a set using a single modulus near 10^9. What should you expect?
options: No collisions, since 10^6 is far below 10^9
Hundreds of colliding pairs, by the birthday paradox
The set rejects duplicates, so collisions cannot matter
quiz.explain: Expected colliding pairs are about k²/(2M) = 10^12 / (2 × 10^9), roughly 500. Two moduli, or a modulus near 2^61, bring that close to zero.

articles.excerpt: A problem asks, a hundred thousand times, "is this piece of the string equal to that piece?" Each piece can be a hundred thousand characters long. Comparing letter by letter is correct and hopeless: up to 10¹⁰ character checks. What if every substring carried a short number, so that equal…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Counting Backwards From the Last Move
articles.subtitle: Combinatorial game theory for contests: winning and losing positions, Nim and XOR, and Sprague-Grundy numbers for sums of games

glossary.definition: A two-player game with no hidden information or luck, where both players have exactly the same moves from every position.
The convention that the player who cannot move loses. Most contest games use it.
The opposite convention: the player who makes the last move loses.
A position where the player about to move loses if the opponent plays perfectly. Every move from it leads to a winning position.
A position where the player about to move can force a win, because at least one move leads to a losing position.
A number assigned to a position: the smallest non-negative integer not among the Grundy numbers of the positions it can move to. Zero means losing.
Minimum excluded value: the smallest non-negative integer missing from a set, such as mex{0, 1, 3} = 2.

quiz.q: In Nim with heaps 3, 4 and 5, who wins with perfect play, and how?
options: The first player, by reducing the heap of 3 to 1 so the XOR becomes 0
The first player, by emptying the heap of 5
quiz.explain: 3 XOR 4 XOR 5 = 2, which is non-zero, so the first player wins. Changing 3 to 3 XOR 2 = 1 leaves 1 XOR 4 XOR 5 = 0, a losing position for the opponent.

quiz.q: A position can move to positions with Grundy numbers 0, 1 and 3. What is its Grundy number?
quiz.explain: The mex of {0, 1, 3} is 2, the smallest non-negative integer not in the set.

quiz.q: Two independent games are played side by side; on each turn a player moves in exactly one of them. When is the combined position losing?
options: When the XOR of their Grundy numbers is 0
When their Grundy numbers sum to 0
quiz.explain: The Sprague-Grundy theorem says a sum of games behaves like a Nim heap whose size is the XOR of the parts' Grundy numbers.

articles.excerpt: "Alice and Bob take turns removing 1, 3 or 4 stones from a pile. Whoever cannot move loses. Who wins with 10,000 stones if both play perfectly?" Statements like this look like they need a clever trick or a lot of game tree search. In fact, a ten-line DP answers every pile size at once, and a single…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Every Small Game Is a Nim Pile in Disguise
articles.subtitle: Why the Sprague-Grundy theorem works, how to handle moves that split a game in two, and how to spot periodic Grundy values

glossary.definition: The number g(p) = mex of the Grundy values of every position reachable from p in one move. A position is losing for the player to move exactly when g(p) = 0.
Minimum excluded value: the smallest non-negative integer missing from a set, such as mex{0, 2, 3} = 1.
Several independent games played side by side, where each turn makes exactly one move in exactly one of them.
A move to a position of higher Grundy value, which the opponent can always undo by moving straight back down to the original value.
A move that turns one game into two or more independent games, such as breaking a row of pins into two shorter rows.
A sequence that, after some starting index, repeats the same block of values forever.

quiz.q: One move breaks a row into two independent rows with Grundy values 3 and 5. What value does that option contribute to the mex?
quiz.explain: The two rows form a sum of games, whose Grundy value is the XOR of the parts: 3 XOR 5 = 6. The mex is taken over these XORs, one per possible move.

quiz.q: A position has Grundy value 2. Which statement must be true?
options: It can move to positions of value 0 and 1, and it cannot move to a position of value 2
It cannot move to any position of value above 2
quiz.explain: That is exactly what mex means. Moves to higher values may exist, but they are reversible, so the position behaves like a Nim heap of size 2.

quiz.q: In Wythoff's game a move may take the same number of stones from both piles. Why does XORing two single-pile Grundy values fail here?
options: A single move changes both piles, so the piles are not independent games
Wythoff's game has no losing positions
XOR only works for three piles
quiz.explain: The theorem covers sums where every move touches one component. Taking from both piles at once breaks that, and indeed (1, 2) is losing although 1 XOR 2 = 3.

articles.excerpt: A contest problem puts three things on one table: a row of five bowling pins, a heap of eight stones, and a Nim pile of three matchsticks. On your turn you knock down pins, or split the heap into two unequal heaps, or take matchsticks. The rules of the three games have nothing in common. Who wins?…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Left Turn or Right Turn at the Junction
articles.subtitle: Contest geometry with integers: points as vectors, the cross product for orientation, segment intersection and polygon area

complexity.time: O(1) per orientation or intersection test, O(n) for polygon area

glossary.definition: A direction and length, written as (x, y). The vector from point A to point B is B − A.
For 2D vectors u and v, the number u.x·v.y − u.y·v.x. Its sign says whether v turns left or right from u, and its size is twice the triangle area.
Whether three points A, B, C make a left turn (counter-clockwise), a right turn (clockwise) or lie on one line.
Lying on the same straight line. Three points are collinear when their cross product is zero.
A formula for a polygon's area: half the absolute value of the sum of cross products of consecutive vertices.

quiz.q: A = (0, 0), B = (4, 0), C = (2, 3). What does cross(B − A, C − A) = 12 tell you?
options: C is to the right of AB
C is to the left of AB, a counter-clockwise turn
quiz.explain: A positive cross product means a left (counter-clockwise) turn. Its value, 12, is also twice the area of triangle ABC.

quiz.q: Two segments AB and CD are not collinear. When do they cross?
options: When C and D are on opposite sides of AB and A and B are on opposite sides of CD
When any cross product is zero
quiz.explain: Opposite signs of the two cross products in both directions mean each segment straddles the other's line.

quiz.q: Why are integer coordinates preferred in contest geometry?
options: Cross products of integers are exact, so tests like 'is it exactly zero?' never suffer from rounding errors
quiz.explain: With up to 10⁹ coordinates, cross products fit in 64-bit integers and are exact. Floating point can misjudge collinear or touching cases.

articles.excerpt: Geometry problems scare many contestants: angles, trigonometry, floating-point errors, special cases everywhere. But the vast majority of contest geometry needs exactly one tool, used over and over. It decides whether a point is left or right of a line, whether two segments cross, whether a polygon…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Snapping a Rubber Band Around Nails
articles.subtitle: Andrew's monotone chain: sort the points, keep only left turns, and decide exactly what happens to points lying on an edge

glossary.definition: The smallest convex polygon that contains every point of a set. Its corners are always points of the set.
A polygon with no dents: walking around it counter-clockwise, every turn at a corner is a left turn.
Andrew's hull algorithm: sort points by x then y, build the lower hull left to right and the upper hull right to left, popping any point that makes a non-left turn.
The part of the hull seen from below, running from the leftmost point to the rightmost point along the bottom.
The part of the hull seen from above, running from the rightmost point back to the leftmost point along the top.
A point lying exactly on the straight line through two others, so the cross product of the three is zero.

quiz.q: While building the lower hull, the last two kept points are A and B and the new point is C. cross(A, B, C) = −5. What happens?
options: Pop B, because A to B to C turns right, so B is inside the band
quiz.explain: A negative cross product is a clockwise (right) turn. On a counter-clockwise hull every turn must be left, so B cannot be a corner and is removed.

quiz.q: You pop on cross ≤ 0. What happens to a point lying exactly in the middle of a hull edge?
options: It is kept as a corner
It is removed, because a zero cross product counts as not turning left
quiz.explain: With ≤ 0, straight-ahead points are popped, so only true corners remain. Pop only on < 0 when the problem wants every boundary point.

quiz.q: How does the convex hull trick from DP optimisation relate to this algorithm?
options: Both keep a convex chain with a stack-like pop rule, but CHT works on lines to answer minimum queries, while the hull wraps a set of points
They are unrelated in every way
quiz.explain: CHT keeps the lower envelope of lines. Its name comes from duality: the lines on the envelope correspond to points on a hull. The tasks and the code differ.

Which ones are on the fence, and in what order? With ten posts you could eyeball it. With 200,000 posts, given only as coordinates,…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Twenty Questions With the Judge
articles.subtitle: How interactive problems work, why flushing matters, how to read a query limit, and how to test without a judge

glossary.definition: A problem where your program talks to a judge program: it prints questions, reads the judge's answers, and finally prints its answer.
The judge-side program that holds the hidden data, reads your queries, and replies to each one.
Forcing buffered output to actually be sent now, instead of waiting until the buffer fills or the program ends.
The maximum number of questions you may ask. Exceeding it gives Wrong Answer, and its size is a strong hint about the intended algorithm.
An interactor that does not fix the hidden answer in advance and may pick any answer consistent with its previous replies, so only worst-case strategies are safe.
A Codeforces verdict meaning your program sat waiting for input that never came, usually because a query was never flushed.

quiz.q: Your program prints '? 50' and then reads the reply with cin, but the judge reports Idleness limit exceeded. What is the most likely bug?
options: The query was not flushed, so it sat in your buffer while both programs waited for each other
quiz.explain: With cin.tie(nullptr) in your template, cin no longer flushes cout before reading. The query never left your program, the judge never replied, and both sides waited.

quiz.q: A hidden number is between 1 and 1,000,000 and each query answers yes or no. What is the smallest query limit that always suffices?
quiz.explain: k yes/no answers can tell apart at most 2^k cases. 2^19 is 524,288, too few, and 2^20 is 1,048,576, enough. So 20 queries.

quiz.q: The judge replies -1 to one of your queries. What should your program do?
quiz.explain: Statements that use -1 mean you made an invalid query or ran out of queries. Exiting at once gets a clean Wrong Answer instead of an unpredictable verdict from reading a closed stream.

articles.excerpt: You open problem D and there is no input file. Instead the statement says: "The judge has hidden a number between 1 and 10⁹. You may ask at most 30 questions of the form '? x', and the judge will tell you whether its number is at least x." Your first submission prints a perfect binary search and…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Counting Billions of Subarrays Without Listing One
articles.subtitle: Two pointers in contests: the monotonicity argument, counting subarrays and pairs, at most K distinct values, and fixing one element to scan the rest

complexity.time: O(n) per scan, plus O(n log n) to sort
complexity.space: O(1) to O(n) for the window's state

glossary.definition: A subarray [l, r] that satisfies the problem's condition, such as having sum at most S or at most K distinct values.
A property of a condition: whenever a segment is good, every shorter segment inside it is good too.
For a right end r, the smallest l such that [l, r] is good. Written L(r) here.
A pointer that only ever moves in one direction during the whole scan, which caps its total movement at n.
Counting the objects you want as all objects minus the ones you do not want, when the second count is easier.

quiz.q: For each right end r, every start from L(r) to r gives a good segment. How many good segments end at r?
quiz.explain: The starts L(r), L(r) + 1, ..., r are all valid because the condition is closed under shrinking, and there are r − L(r) + 1 of them.

quiz.q: Why does 'subarray sum at most S' break two pointers when the array has negative numbers?
options: The condition is no longer closed under shrinking: removing a negative element can push the sum above S
quiz.explain: With [5, −4] and S = 3, the whole segment has sum 1, but its part [5] has sum 5. A good segment can contain a bad one, so L(r) can jump backwards.

quiz.q: In a sorted array, you count pairs i < j with a[i] + a[j] ≤ X. As i increases, what happens to the largest valid j?
options: It never increases, so one pointer sweeping down from the end suffices
quiz.explain: A larger a[i] needs a partner that is no larger, so the boundary only moves left. Both pointers move monotonically and the scan is O(n).

articles.excerpt: "Count the subarrays whose sum is at most S." The array has 200,000 positive numbers, so there are about 2 × 10¹⁰ subarrays. You cannot even list the answer's members in time, let alone check each one. Yet the intended solution is a single pass that finishes in well under a second. In The…

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Why XOR Decides Who Takes the Last Matchstick
articles.subtitle: The proof behind the Nim rule, the misère twist and its exception, staircase Nim, and bounded-removal variants

glossary.definition: A game with several piles of objects. On each turn a player removes any positive number of objects from one pile. Under normal play, whoever cannot move loses.
The XOR of all pile sizes. The player to move loses normal-play Nim exactly when it is 0.
A position whose Nim-sum is 0: in binary, every power of two appears an even number of times across the piles.
The convention where the player who takes the last object loses, instead of winning.
A game with coins on numbered stairs, where a move slides any positive number of coins from one stair to the stair directly below. Coins on the bottom stair can no longer move.
Nim where each move removes between 1 and k objects from one pile. Each pile then behaves like a Nim pile of size n mod (k + 1).

quiz.q: Piles are 6, 9, 13 and 7 under normal play. Which move wins?
options: Take all 9 from the second pile
quiz.explain: 6 ⊕ 9 ⊕ 13 ⊕ 7 = 5. Pile 13 has the 4s bit set, and 13 ⊕ 5 = 8 < 13, so reducing it to 8 leaves 6 ⊕ 9 ⊕ 8 ⊕ 7 = 0. Reducing 6 to 3 or 7 to 2 also works.

quiz.q: Misère Nim with piles 1, 1 and 4. What should the first player do?
options: Empty the pile of 4, as in normal Nim
Reduce the 4 to 1, leaving three piles of size 1
Nothing works, it is a loss
quiz.explain: Emptying the 4 leaves 1, 1: the opponent takes one and you are forced to take the last. Leaving 1, 1, 1 means the opponent takes the first and the last of the three, so they lose.

quiz.q: In staircase Nim, why can moves from an even stair be ignored?
options: Whatever coins land on an odd stair, the winner can push those same coins one stair further down, restoring the odd stairs exactly
They do not change the game
quiz.explain: Such moves are reversible. The odd-stair piles return to exactly what they were, so only moves from odd stairs, which act like Nim moves, matter.

articles.subject: cp
articles.title: Twelve Weeks From Unrated to Confident
articles.subtitle: A week-by-week contest practice plan that fits beside placement preparation, linked to the articles in this subject

glossary.definition: A group of 5 to 10 problems on one technique, solved in a row to make the technique automatic.
A past contest replayed with its original timer and scoreboard, used for realistic practice at any time.
A running list of the real causes of your wrong answers, reviewed before contests.
Practising just beyond your current ability, with feedback, on specific weaknesses, rather than repeating what you already do well.
A point in the plan where you measure progress and adjust what comes next.

quiz.q: What should most of your practice problems be?
options: Easy ones you can solve quickly
Problems slightly above your current level, with upsolving afterwards
Only problems from one topic forever
quiz.explain: Deliberate practice in the stretch zone, followed by upsolving, builds skill fastest.

quiz.q: Why mix topic sets with contests?
options: Topic sets build a technique; contests train recognising which technique a fresh problem needs, under time pressure
quiz.explain: In a contest, the topic is not labelled. You need both the tool and the skill of choosing it.

quiz.q: At a checkpoint you notice most failures are Wrong Answers from edge cases. What should change?
options: Add stress testing and an edge-case checklist to every submission
quiz.explain: The weakness is verification, not knowledge, so the fix is a testing habit.

Without a plan, practice drifts: some days of easy problems, a contest that goes badly, a week off, then guilt. Twelve weeks later, very little has changed. With a plan, the same hours compound.…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: The Data Structure That Is Allowed to Lie
articles.subtitle: Bloom filters answer 'definitely not' or 'probably yes' using a tiny fraction of the memory

glossary.definition: A bit array plus several hash functions that can say an item is definitely not in a set, or probably in it.
When the filter says 'probably yes' for an item that was never added.
When a structure says 'no' for an item that was actually added. A Bloom filter never does this.
A function that turns an item into a number that looks random but is always the same for the same item.
A long row of bits, each either 0 or 1, stored compactly so millions fit in a few megabytes.

quiz.q: A Bloom filter says an item is NOT present. How sure can you be?
options: It depends on the item's length
quiz.explain: If the item had been added, all of its bits would be 1. Finding any 0 bit proves it was never added, so there are no false negatives.

quiz.q: Why can you not simply delete an item from a plain Bloom filter by clearing its bits?
options: Bits cannot be changed after creation
Other items may share those bits, so clearing them would create false negatives
It would change the hash functions
quiz.explain: Bits are shared. Clearing one item's bits could erase part of another item's fingerprint, and then the filter would wrongly say that other item is absent.

quiz.q: How does a database like RocksDB use Bloom filters?
options: To skip reading files on disk that cannot contain the key
quiz.explain: Each on-disk file has a small filter. If it says 'definitely not here', the database skips that file and saves a slow disk read.

articles.excerpt: Your database holds a billion keys spread across hundreds of files on disk. A request arrives for a key that does not exist. Without help, the database might open file after file, paying for a slow disk read each time, only to answer "not found". Now imagine a little helper sitting in memory that…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Counting a Billion Things on a Postcard
articles.subtitle: Count-Min Sketch: approximate counts for huge streams, in a fixed few kilobytes

glossary.definition: A small summary of a huge data stream that answers certain questions approximately, using far less memory than storing the data.
Data that arrives one item at a time, too fast or too large to store in full, like clicks, searches or network packets.
An item that appears very often in a stream, such as a trending hashtag or an IP address sending a flood of traffic.
A reported count that is higher than the true count. A Count-Min Sketch can overestimate but never underestimate.
When two different items hash to the same counter and their counts get mixed together.

quiz.q: Why does Count-Min Sketch take the minimum across rows?
options: Every counter is the true count plus noise from collisions, so the smallest one has the least noise
Because the maximum is always zero
quiz.explain: Collisions only ever add to a counter. Each row's counter is at least the true count, so the minimum is the closest to the truth.

quiz.q: Can a Count-Min Sketch report a count lower than the true count (with only additions)?
quiz.explain: Every time an item is added, all of its counters go up. Other items can only add more, so no counter is ever below the true count.

quiz.q: Which question is a Count-Min Sketch NOT good at answering on its own?
options: Roughly how many times was this hashtag used?
Is this IP address sending a lot of traffic?
List every distinct item that appeared
Roughly how popular is this search query?
quiz.explain: The sketch stores counters, not items, so it cannot list what it has seen. Systems keep a small heap of candidate heavy hitters alongside it.

articles.excerpt: Every second, a busy network router sees hundreds of thousands of packets from countless IP addresses. Somewhere in that flood, one address is sending far more than its share: maybe a misconfigured server, maybe an attack. The router has a few megabytes of fast memory and no time to keep a full…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Counting a Billion Visitors With Twelve Kilobytes
articles.subtitle: HyperLogLog estimates how many distinct things you have seen by looking for unusually lucky hashes

glossary.definition: The number of distinct items in a collection. A list of a million page views might have a cardinality of only 50,000 distinct visitors.
One small counter inside a HyperLogLog. Each register remembers the longest run of leading zeros it has seen.
The zeros at the start of a binary number before the first 1. A random hash starts with k zeros with probability about 1 in 2 to the power k.
A way of averaging that is much less affected by a few huge values than the ordinary average.
Two summaries can be combined into the summary of the union, without the original data.

quiz.q: Why does a long run of leading zeros in a hash suggest many distinct items?
options: Each extra leading zero halves the chance, so seeing a long run usually means you hashed many different items
Long runs mean the hash function is broken
quiz.explain: A random hash starts with k zeros about once in 2^k tries. If the longest run you have seen is 20, you have probably seen around a million distinct items.

quiz.q: Why does adding the same item twice not change a HyperLogLog?
options: The same item always gives the same hash, so it updates the same register to the same value
It keeps a list of items
quiz.explain: Hashing is deterministic. A repeat produces exactly the same register and the same zero count, so nothing changes. That is why it counts distinct items.

quiz.q: How do you combine the HyperLogLogs of two servers to count distinct users across both?
options: Take the maximum of each register pair
quiz.explain: Each register stores a maximum. The maximum over both streams is simply the larger of the two registers, so merging is a register-by-register max.

articles.excerpt: A news site wants to show "1.2 million people read this today." Counting page views is easy: add one per view. Counting distinct readers is not. The obvious way is to keep a set of every reader ID seen today, and for a popular site that set has millions of entries, for every article, every day.…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Spotting Near-Duplicates Without Comparing Them
articles.subtitle: MinHash turns 'how similar are these two documents?' into a quick vote among tiny signatures

glossary.definition: The size of the overlap of two sets divided by the size of their union. 1 means identical, 0 means nothing in common.
A short overlapping piece of a document, such as every run of 5 consecutive words, used to turn text into a set.
For one hash function, the smallest hash value among a set's elements. Two sets share their MinHash with probability equal to their Jaccard similarity.
A short list of MinHash values, one per hash function, that stands in for a whole set when estimating similarity.
A document that is almost the same as another, such as a copied article with a different header or a few edited words.

quiz.q: A = {a, b, c, d} and B = {b, c, d, e}. What is their Jaccard similarity?
quiz.explain: The overlap {b, c, d} has 3 elements; the union {a, b, c, d, e} has 5. So the similarity is 3/5 = 0.6.

quiz.q: Why does the probability that two sets have the same MinHash equal their Jaccard similarity?
options: The element with the smallest hash in the union is equally likely to be any union element, and the MinHashes match exactly when it lies in the overlap
It only holds for equal-sized sets
quiz.explain: A random hash makes every element of the union equally likely to be the minimum. The two MinHashes agree only when that minimum element is in both sets.

quiz.q: How does using more hash functions in the signature help?
options: Each hash is one vote, and more votes make the estimated similarity more precise
It removes the need for shingles
quiz.explain: The fraction of matching positions is an average of independent yes-or-no votes, so its error shrinks as the number of votes grows.

Showing ten copies of one article in the results is useless. But comparing every…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Adding a Server Without Moving Everything
articles.subtitle: Consistent hashing: the ring that lets caches and databases grow without a mass migration

glossary.definition: A way of assigning keys to servers so that adding or removing a server moves only a small share of the keys.
The range of hash values bent into a circle, on which both servers and keys are placed.
One of many positions a single physical server takes on the ring, used to spread load evenly.
Splitting data across several machines so each one holds only part of it.
Moving data between machines after servers are added or removed.

quiz.q: With plain 'hash(key) mod n' and n going from 4 to 5 servers, roughly how many keys move?
options: Most of them, around four fifths
quiz.explain: A key stays put only if its hash gives the same remainder mod 4 and mod 5, which happens for about one in five keys. The rest move.

quiz.q: On a consistent hashing ring, which server owns a key?
options: The server with the smallest id
The first server clockwise from the key's position
The server that was added most recently
quiz.explain: Walk clockwise from the key's point on the ring; the first server you meet owns it.

quiz.q: Why do real systems give each server many virtual nodes?
options: To spread keys evenly and share the load when a server leaves
quiz.explain: With one point per server, arcs can be very uneven. Many points per server average out the arc sizes, and a departing server's keys scatter across many others.

Within seconds, almost every cache lookup starts missing, the database behind the cache is flooded with requests, and the site slows to a crawl. Adding capacity made things worse.…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Ordering Events Without Trusting Any Clock
articles.subtitle: Lamport clocks: a single counter per machine that captures what could have caused what

glossary.definition: Event a happened before event b if they are on the same machine in that order, or a is sending a message that b receives, or a chain of these links them.
A counter that orders events by cause and effect instead of by physical time.
Two events where neither could have influenced the other, because no chain of messages connects them.
The difference between the physical clocks of two machines, which can be milliseconds or more even with synchronisation.
An ordering in which every pair of events is ranked, with ties broken by a fixed rule such as machine id.

quiz.q: A machine with Lamport clock 5 receives a message stamped 9. What is its clock after receiving?
quiz.explain: On receive, the clock becomes max(local, received) + 1, which is max(5, 9) + 1 = 10.

quiz.q: If event a happened before event b, what must be true of their Lamport timestamps?
quiz.explain: This is the clock condition. Every step along a happened-before chain increases the counter, so the earlier event has a smaller timestamp.

quiz.q: L(a) = 3 and L(b) = 7. What can you conclude?
options: b did not happen before a, but a and b may be concurrent
They are on the same machine
quiz.explain: Smaller timestamps do not prove causality. You only know b could not have caused a. Detecting concurrency needs vector clocks.

articles.excerpt: Two servers record events with their own clocks. Server A logs "user deleted the file" at 10:00:00.120. Server B logs "user edited the file" at 10:00:00.100. So the edit came first? Not necessarily: B's clock might run 50 milliseconds fast. Physical clocks on different machines never agree exactly,…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Catching Two Edits That Never Saw Each Other
articles.subtitle: Vector clocks: one counter per machine, so a system can tell 'came before' from 'happened at the same time'

glossary.definition: A list of counters, one per machine, attached to each event or version, recording how much of every machine's history it has seen.
Vector A dominates vector B when every entry of A is at least the matching entry of B, and at least one is bigger. Then B happened before A.
Two versions where neither vector dominates the other. Neither writer knew about the other's change.
One of several concurrent versions of the same key that a store keeps until someone resolves the conflict.
Deciding what the final value should be when concurrent versions exist, for example by merging a shopping cart.

quiz.q: Version A has clock [2, 1, 0] and version B has [2, 2, 0]. What is their relationship?
quiz.explain: Every entry of B is at least A's, and the second entry is bigger, so B dominates A. A happened before B, and B can replace it.

quiz.q: Version A is [3, 0] and version B is [2, 1]. What should a store do?
options: Keep A, it has the bigger first entry
Keep both as siblings, because they are concurrent
quiz.explain: A is bigger in the first entry and B in the second, so neither dominates. The writes were concurrent and the conflict must be resolved.

quiz.q: When machine i receives a message with vector V, how does it update its own vector?
options: Take the entry-wise maximum with V, then add 1 to its own entry
quiz.explain: The maximum merges everything both sides have seen; the increment records the receive event itself.

Both requests reach different replicas of the cart service during a brief network hiccup. When the replicas sync, which cart is right? If the system simply keeps the "latest" write, one of your…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: How Rumours Keep a Thousand Servers in Sync
articles.subtitle: Gossip protocols: random chatter between pairs spreads news to a whole cluster in a handful of rounds

glossary.definition: A way of spreading information in which each node periodically shares what it knows with a few randomly chosen peers.
One period of gossip, such as one second, in which every node contacts its chosen peers once.
How many peers each node contacts per round.
A background process where pairs of nodes compare their data and repair any differences.
Each node's view of which nodes are in the cluster and whether they seem alive.
A guarantee that if updates stop, all nodes will eventually hold the same data, without promising when.

quiz.q: Roughly how many gossip rounds does it take for news to reach all n nodes?
quiz.explain: The number of informed nodes roughly doubles or more each round, so the time grows like log n. A thousand nodes need only around ten to twenty rounds.

quiz.q: Why is gossip robust to failures?
options: There is no single path; news travels along many random routes, so a few dead nodes barely slow it
It retries forever on one path
It requires all nodes to be online
quiz.explain: Because every node picks random peers, information flows through many redundant paths and the loss of some nodes does not stop it.

quiz.q: What does gossip NOT give you?
options: Strong consistency, where everyone sees an update at the same moment
quiz.explain: Gossip is eventually consistent. Different nodes learn news at different times, so it suits membership and metadata, not bank balances.

articles.excerpt: In an office of five hundred people, nobody sends an email to announce that the manager is leaving. Yet by lunch, everyone knows. Each person mentions it to a couple of colleagues at the coffee machine, those colleagues tell a couple more, and the news races through the building with no one in…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Is That Server Dead, or Just Slow?
articles.subtitle: SWIM: detecting failed machines with random probes, second opinions and a polite period of suspicion

glossary.definition: A component that decides which machines in a cluster are alive and which have failed, usually by sending probes.
A regular 'I am alive' message. Missing several in a row suggests a machine has failed.
Asking a few other members to ping a silent machine on your behalf, to rule out a problem on your own network path.
A temporary state in which a member is thought to have failed but is given time to prove it is alive before being removed.
Attaching membership updates to messages that are being sent anyway, such as probes, so they spread at no extra cost.

quiz.q: Why does SWIM ask other members to ping a silent node before declaring it dead?
options: The silence might come from a problem on the path between the two nodes, not from the node itself
Because only the leader can declare failures
quiz.explain: If others can reach the node, it is alive and only one link is bad. Indirect probes avoid removing healthy members because of a local network glitch.

quiz.q: How does the message load per member change as the cluster grows in SWIM?
options: It grows linearly with cluster size
It stays roughly constant, because each member probes one random member per period
quiz.explain: Unlike all-to-all heartbeats, each member sends a fixed number of probes per period, so per-member load does not grow with the cluster.

quiz.q: What does the suspicion state prevent?
options: Removing members that are just briefly slow, such as during a garbage collection pause
quiz.explain: A suspected member can refute the suspicion if it is alive, so short pauses do not cause false removals.

articles.excerpt: In a cluster of a thousand machines, some machine is always having a bad moment: a long garbage collection pause, a saturated network card, a reboot. The cluster must notice real failures quickly, so it can stop routing traffic to dead machines. But if it panics at every hiccup, it will keep…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: One Fingerprint for a Billion Files
articles.subtitle: Merkle trees: hash the pieces, hash the hashes, and prove or find any change with a handful of comparisons

glossary.definition: A function that turns any data into a short fingerprint, where changing even one bit of the data changes the fingerprint completely.
A tree where each leaf holds the hash of a data block and each parent holds the hash of its children's hashes.
The single hash at the top of a Merkle tree, which summarises every block below it.
The short list of sibling hashes needed to show that one block is part of a tree with a known root hash.
A background process where replicas compare their data and repair differences.

quiz.q: One block in a Merkle tree of 1,024 blocks changes. Which hashes change?
options: The leaf and every ancestor up to the root, about 11 hashes
quiz.explain: A change propagates upward: the leaf, its parent, grandparent and so on. With 1,024 leaves that is about log2 of 1,024 plus one, around 11 hashes.

quiz.q: Two replicas each hold a Merkle tree of their data. How do they find which blocks differ?
options: Send all blocks to each other
Compare root hashes; if different, compare children, and descend only into subtrees whose hashes differ
quiz.explain: Matching subtrees are skipped entirely. Only the paths to changed blocks are explored.

quiz.q: How many hashes does an inclusion proof need for one block among about a million?
quiz.explain: You need one sibling hash per level, and a tree over about 2^20 blocks has about 20 levels.

Comparing every record would mean shipping terabytes across the ocean. What if each side could summarise all billion…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: How Five Servers Agree on One Truth
articles.subtitle: Raft: leader election, log replication and the majority rule behind etcd, Consul and modern Kafka

glossary.definition: Getting a group of machines to agree on the same value or the same sequence of commands, even if some of them fail.
The one server in Raft that accepts client commands and tells the others what to append to their logs.
A numbered period of time in Raft that starts with an election. Terms only increase and act like a logical clock.
An ordered list of commands that every server keeps. If all servers apply the same log in the same order, they end in the same state.
More than half of the servers, such as 3 of 5. Any two majorities share at least one server.
An entry is committed once the leader has stored it on a majority. Committed entries are never lost and can be applied safely.

quiz.q: A five-server Raft cluster can keep working with how many failed servers?
quiz.explain: It needs a majority, 3 of 5, to elect a leader and commit entries. So up to 2 servers can fail.

quiz.q: Why are election timeouts randomised?
options: So that usually one follower times out first and wins, instead of many splitting the vote forever
quiz.explain: If everyone timed out together, they would all become candidates and split the votes. Random timeouts make simultaneous candidacies rare.

quiz.q: When does a Raft leader consider a log entry committed?
options: As soon as it writes it locally
When a majority of servers have stored it
When every server has stored it
quiz.explain: A majority is enough: any future leader must win votes from a majority, and that majority overlaps with the one holding the entry, so the entry cannot be lost.

If etcd's servers ever disagreed about what is stored, your cluster would start doing contradictory things. Yet those servers crash, reboot and lose network links all the time. They stay in…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: How the Internet Avoids Gridlock
articles.subtitle: TCP congestion control: slow start, additive increase, multiplicative decrease, and why every connection backs off together

glossary.definition: The number of bytes (or packets) a TCP sender allows to be in flight, unacknowledged, at once. Its size sets the sending rate.
The time for a packet to reach the receiver and its acknowledgement to come back, often written RTT.
The start-up phase where the congestion window roughly doubles every round trip to find available bandwidth quickly.
Additive increase, multiplicative decrease: grow the window a little each round trip, and cut it sharply, often by half, when congestion is detected.
When a packet never arrives, usually because a router's queue was full and it dropped the packet.
A separate TCP mechanism that stops a sender from overwhelming the receiver's buffer, using the receive window.

quiz.q: What does TCP traditionally treat as the main signal of congestion?
options: Packet loss, detected through timeouts or duplicate acknowledgements
The size of the web page
quiz.explain: When router queues overflow, packets are dropped. Classic TCP variants interpret loss as a sign the network is congested and slow down.

quiz.q: Why multiplicative decrease rather than subtracting a small fixed amount?
options: Halving reacts quickly to congestion, and together with additive increase it pushes competing flows toward a fair share
quiz.explain: Large cuts relieve congested queues fast, and the combination of gentle increase with proportional decrease makes flows converge to fairness.

quiz.q: How is congestion control different from flow control?
options: Flow control protects the receiver's buffer; congestion control protects the network between sender and receiver
Congestion control only applies to Wi-Fi
quiz.explain: The receiver advertises how much it can accept (flow control); the sender separately estimates how much the network can carry (congestion control) and sends the smaller amount.

articles.excerpt: In October 1986, the link between Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory and UC Berkeley, a few hundred metres apart, saw its throughput fall from 32 kilobits per second to about 40 bits per second. The network was not broken. It was so full of retransmitted packets that almost nothing useful got through: a…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: The Punch Card That Says Slow Down
articles.subtitle: Token bucket rate limiting: allow short bursts, cap the long-run rate, and do it with two numbers per user

glossary.definition: Capping how many requests a client may make in a period, to protect a service from overload and abuse.
A rate limiter where tokens refill at a steady rate up to a maximum, and each request spends a token.
How many tokens are added to the bucket per second. It sets the long-run average rate allowed.
The maximum number of tokens the bucket can hold. It sets the largest burst allowed at once.
A related algorithm where requests queue up and leave at a fixed rate, smoothing traffic instead of allowing bursts.
Computing how many tokens to add only when a request arrives, from the time elapsed, instead of running a timer.

quiz.q: A bucket has capacity 10 and refills 2 tokens per second. It is full. How many requests can pass instantly?
quiz.explain: A full bucket holds 10 tokens, so a burst of 10 passes immediately. After that, requests pass at about 2 per second.

quiz.q: What two numbers does a token bucket store per client?
options: Current tokens and the time of the last refill
quiz.explain: Capacity and rate are shared settings. Per client you only need the current token count and when you last updated it.

quiz.q: How does a token bucket differ from a leaky bucket?
options: Token bucket allows bursts up to its capacity; leaky bucket releases traffic at a steady rate
quiz.explain: A token bucket lets saved-up tokens be spent quickly, so short bursts pass. A leaky bucket drains at a fixed rate, smoothing everything.

articles.excerpt: A popular API serves millions of developers. One of them writes a loop with a bug and starts sending ten thousand requests a second. Without a limit, that one script can slow the service for everyone else. But most real clients are bursty, not abusive: an app opening a screen fires twenty requests…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Why Your App Waits a Random Moment Before Retrying
articles.subtitle: Exponential backoff with jitter: retrying failures without turning a small outage into a stampede

glossary.definition: Sending a failed request again, hoping the failure was temporary.
Waiting longer before each retry, typically doubling the wait each time, so a struggling service gets room to recover.
Randomness added to retry delays so that many clients do not all retry at exactly the same moment.
A surge where many clients act at the same instant, such as all retrying together, overwhelming a service.
A cap on how much extra load retries may add, for example retries may be at most 10% of normal requests.

quiz.q: Why add randomness to backoff delays?
options: So clients that failed together do not all retry at the same instant
quiz.explain: Without jitter, clients that failed at the same moment retry at the same moments too, hitting the service in synchronized waves.

quiz.q: With a base delay of 100 ms doubling each time and a cap of 2 seconds, what is the maximum wait before the 6th retry?
quiz.explain: Uncapped it would be 100 × 2^5 = 3,200 ms, but the cap limits it to 2 seconds.

quiz.q: Which requests should NOT be retried automatically?
options: A non-idempotent payment without an idempotency key
quiz.explain: If the first attempt might have succeeded, retrying a non-idempotent action can repeat it, such as charging twice.

articles.excerpt: A database hiccups for two seconds. Ten thousand app servers see errors and immediately retry. Then retry again. And again. The database comes back to find not its normal load but several times it, all arriving in the same instant, and falls over again. A two-second blip becomes a twenty-minute…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Pick Two Lines at Random, Join the Shorter
articles.subtitle: The power of two choices: a tiny change to random load balancing that makes the worst server dramatically less overloaded

glossary.definition: A component that spreads incoming requests across many servers.
The load on the busiest server. It decides tail latency, because requests on that server wait longest.
Sending each request to a server chosen uniformly at random.
Sampling two servers at random and sending the request to the less loaded of the two.
A strategy that sends each request to the server with the fewest active connections, which needs up-to-date load information for every server.

quiz.q: How does the power of two choices pick a server?
options: Always the least loaded server overall
Two random servers, then the less loaded of those two
The server with the lowest id
quiz.explain: It samples just two servers and compares only them, so it needs very little load information.

quiz.q: With n balls thrown into n bins, how does the fullest bin grow with n for one random choice versus two choices?
options: Roughly log n / log log n for one choice, versus roughly log log n for two choices
quiz.explain: Classic results show one random choice gives a maximum load of about log n / log log n, while two choices reduce it to about log log n, an exponential improvement.

quiz.q: Why not always pick the globally least loaded server?
options: It needs fresh load information for every server, and many balancers acting on the same stale view all pile onto the same 'least loaded' server
It is slower to compute than random
quiz.explain: Global least-loaded decisions are expensive and herd-prone with stale data. Two random samples avoid both problems.

Checking all twenty lines works well but takes ages, and everyone rushes to the same "shortest" line. Now try something lazy:…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Why Modern Databases Write So Fast
articles.subtitle: LSM trees: buffer writes in memory, flush sorted files, merge them in the background, and use Bloom filters to keep reads quick

glossary.definition: Log-structured merge tree: a storage design that buffers writes in memory and writes them to disk as sorted, immutable files that are merged over time.
The in-memory sorted structure where new writes land first.
Sorted string table: an immutable file on disk containing key-value pairs sorted by key.
A background process that merges SSTables, keeping the newest value for each key and dropping deleted or overwritten data.
A special marker written to record that a key was deleted, since immutable files cannot be edited in place.
How many bytes the storage engine writes to disk for each byte the user writes, because data is rewritten during compaction.

quiz.q: Why are LSM trees fast for writes?
options: Writes go to memory and are later written to disk in large sequential batches, avoiding random in-place updates
They only allow one write per second
quiz.explain: Appending sorted batches is sequential I/O, which disks and SSDs handle far better than many small random updates.

quiz.q: How does an LSM tree delete a key?
options: It erases it from every file immediately
It writes a tombstone; compaction later removes the key and the tombstone
quiz.explain: Files are immutable, so a delete is a new record saying 'this key is gone'. Reads that see the tombstone treat the key as missing.

quiz.q: What keeps reads from checking every SSTable for a missing key?
options: A Bloom filter per SSTable that says 'definitely not here' for most files
quiz.explain: Each file's small Bloom filter rules it out without a disk read, so a lookup only opens files that might contain the key.

articles.excerpt: A messaging app stores billions of messages, and every second hundreds of thousands more arrive. A storage engine that updates records in place, seeking to the right spot on disk for every write, would spend most of its time jumping around. Many modern databases take a different approach: never…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Write It in the Ledger Before You Hand Over the Cash
articles.subtitle: Write-ahead logging: the append-only diary that lets databases survive crashes without losing a committed write

glossary.definition: An append-only file where a database records each change before applying it to its main data structures.
The guarantee that once a write is confirmed, it survives crashes and power loss.
An operating system call that forces buffered data to be physically written to storage before returning.
A point where the database has written all changes up to some log position into its main files, so older log entries are no longer needed.
Reading the log after a crash and re-applying every change after the last checkpoint to rebuild the correct state.
Batching the log writes of many transactions into one fsync to share its cost.

quiz.q: Why write to the log before updating the main data files?
options: If the machine crashes mid-update, the log still records the intended change, so it can be replayed
quiz.explain: The log is the source of truth for recent changes. Whatever state the main files were left in, replaying the log brings them up to date.

quiz.q: What does a checkpoint allow?
