options: Deleting or recycling log entries older than the checkpoint, and shorter recovery
quiz.explain: Once all changes up to a log position are safely in the main files, older log entries are no longer needed for recovery.

quiz.q: Why does group commit improve throughput?
options: One fsync is shared by many transactions, so the slow flush cost is paid less often per transaction
quiz.explain: fsync is slow. Waiting a moment and flushing several transactions' log records together amortises that cost.

articles.excerpt: A bank's database is halfway through moving money: it has subtracted ₹5,000 from your account, but not yet added it to your friend's. Then the power fails. When the machine restarts, did the money vanish? In a well-built database, no. Before touching the real data, it wrote one line in an…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Readers Never Wait for Writers
articles.subtitle: Multi-version concurrency control: keep old versions, give every transaction a consistent snapshot, and clean up later

glossary.definition: Multi-version concurrency control: storing several versions of each row so readers can see a consistent past version while writers create new ones.
The consistent view of the database a transaction sees, as of a particular moment, ignoring changes committed later.
A number given to each transaction, used to decide which row versions it is allowed to see.
An isolation level where each transaction reads from its own snapshot and a write fails if another transaction already changed the same row.
An anomaly under snapshot isolation where two transactions read overlapping data, each writes different rows, and together they break a rule neither would break alone.
Removing old row versions that no running transaction can still see, called vacuum in PostgreSQL.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of MVCC compared with locking every row a reader touches?
options: Readers see a consistent snapshot without blocking writers, and writers do not block readers
quiz.explain: Because old versions stay around, a reader can keep seeing the version that existed when it started while a writer creates a new one.

quiz.q: A transaction started at time 100. Row R has versions committed at 90 and 120. Which version does it see?
quiz.explain: Its snapshot includes only changes committed before it started, so it sees the version from 90.

quiz.q: Why does MVCC need garbage collection?
options: Old versions pile up; once no running transaction can see them, they must be removed to reclaim space
quiz.explain: Every update leaves an old version behind. A long-running transaction can keep old versions alive, causing bloat.

articles.excerpt: An analyst starts a report that reads every order from the last year, which takes ten minutes. Meanwhile, the shop keeps selling: thousands of new orders and refunds per minute. If the report locked every row it read, the shop would freeze for ten minutes. If it read rows without any protection, it…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Turning a Map Into a String
articles.subtitle: Geohash: repeatedly halve the world, interleave the bits, and nearby places share a prefix

glossary.definition: A short string encoding a latitude and longitude, built by repeatedly halving the map and interleaving the choices as bits.
Coordinates for a point on Earth: latitude runs from −90 (south) to 90 (north), longitude from −180 (west) to 180 (east).
Alternating bits from two numbers, here longitude then latitude, so a single sequence describes both.
The first few characters of a string. Points whose geohashes share a longer prefix lie in the same smaller cell.
The rectangle of the map that a geohash of a given length represents. Longer geohashes mean smaller cells.
Writing 5 bits at a time as one character from a 32-character alphabet, which keeps geohashes short and readable.

quiz.q: Two restaurants have geohashes tdr1v9 and tdr1vf. What does the shared prefix tdr1v tell you?
options: Both lie inside the same 5-character cell, a few kilometres across
They are exactly the same place
quiz.explain: Sharing a 5-character prefix means both points fell into the same cell after 25 halvings, which is roughly a 5 km square.

quiz.q: Why is searching only a point's own cell not enough for 'nearby' queries?
options: A nearby point can sit just across a cell boundary with a completely different prefix, so the neighbouring cells must be searched too
quiz.explain: Boundaries split close neighbours. The standard fix is to search the point's cell and its 8 neighbours.

quiz.q: What does each extra bit of a geohash do?
options: Halves the cell along either longitude or latitude
quiz.explain: Bits alternate between longitude and latitude, and each one picks one half of the current range.

articles.excerpt: A food delivery app has 300,000 restaurants and a hungry user at a particular latitude and longitude. "Show restaurants within 3 km" sounds easy, but computing the distance to all 300,000 for every search, thousands of times a second, is wasteful. And a normal database index sorts by one number at…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Writing Ditto Marks Instead of Repeating Yourself
articles.subtitle: LZ77: replace repeated text with short back-references into a sliding window, the idea inside ZIP, gzip and PNG

glossary.definition: Shrinking data so that decompressing gives back exactly the original bytes, with nothing lost.
An instruction that says: copy some bytes that already appeared earlier in the output, instead of storing them again.
The most recent stretch of already-processed text, which the encoder searches for matches and the decoder keeps in memory.
A back-reference written as (how far back to start copying, how many bytes to copy).
A byte written out as itself because no useful earlier match exists.
A measure of how unpredictable data is. Data with high entropy, such as random bytes, cannot be compressed losslessly.

quiz.q: What does the token (distance 3, length 6) tell the decoder to do?
options: Go back 3 bytes in the output and copy 6 bytes forward, one at a time
quiz.explain: A back-reference copies from earlier output. Because it copies byte by byte, the length may exceed the distance, so the copy can overlap the bytes it is producing.

quiz.q: Why can't LZ77 shrink a file of truly random bytes?
options: Random data has no repeated phrases to point back to, so every byte becomes a literal plus overhead
quiz.explain: Compression removes redundancy. Random data has none, so no lossless method can shrink it on average.

quiz.q: Why does the decoder not need a copy of the dictionary sent separately?
options: The dictionary is the text already decoded, which the decoder rebuilds as it goes
It is stored in the file header
quiz.explain: Both sides use the recent text as the dictionary. The decoder has produced exactly that text itself, so nothing extra is transmitted.

articles.excerpt: Open a web page and the HTML, CSS and JavaScript usually arrive compressed, often to a fraction of their size. Download a ZIP file, save a PNG, or look at a server log archived as .gz, and the same trick is at work. Text, code and logs repeat themselves constantly: the same tags, the same variable…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Shorthand, Then Shorter Shorthand
articles.subtitle: DEFLATE: LZ77 removes repeated phrases, Huffman coding gives frequent symbols short codes, and together they power gzip, ZIP and PNG

glossary.definition: Giving each symbol a code whose length depends on how often it appears, so common symbols cost few bits and rare ones cost more.
A method that builds an optimal prefix code from symbol frequencies by repeatedly merging the two least frequent symbols.
A set of codes where no code is the beginning of another, so a bit stream can be decoded without separators.
A standard way of assigning Huffman codes so that the code lengths alone are enough to rebuild every code.
A chunk of compressed data in DEFLATE with its own header saying whether it is stored, uses fixed codes, or carries its own dynamic codes.
DEFLATE's main symbol set: 256 byte values, an end-of-block marker, and codes for match lengths.

quiz.q: What does each of DEFLATE's two stages remove?
options: LZ77 removes repeated phrases; Huffman coding removes the waste of giving every symbol the same number of bits
LZ77 sorts the data; Huffman encrypts it
Huffman finds matches; LZ77 assigns codes
quiz.explain: LZ77 replaces repeats with back-references. Huffman coding then gives common symbols, literals and lengths alike, shorter bit codes.

quiz.q: In 'abracadabra', a appears 5 times, b and r twice, c and d once. With optimal Huffman codes, how many bits does the whole string take?
quiz.explain: One optimal set of lengths is a: 1 bit, b, r, c, d: 3 bits each. That is 5×1 + 6×3 = 23 bits, compared with 33 bits at a fixed 3 bits per letter.

quiz.q: Why does DEFLATE transmit only code lengths, not the codes themselves?
options: Canonical Huffman codes can be rebuilt exactly from the lengths, which take far less space
Codes are not needed for decoding
quiz.explain: With a canonical assignment, encoder and decoder derive identical codes from the list of lengths, so the header stays small.

articles.excerpt: Every time a web page loads, there is a good chance its HTML, CSS and JavaScript travelled across the network squeezed by gzip. Every ZIP file you have opened, and every PNG image on your screen, used the same compressor inside. It was designed in the early 1990s by Phil Katz for his PKZIP program…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Sorting Rotations So Letters Huddle Together
articles.subtitle: The Burrows-Wheeler transform: a reversible shuffle that groups similar letters, making text easier to compress and to search

glossary.definition: Sort all rotations of a string and output the last column. The result is a permutation of the input that tends to group equal letters.
A string formed by moving some prefix of the text to its end, such as 'nanaba' from 'banana'.
A unique symbol, written $, appended to the text and treated as smaller than every letter, so the original can be identified after sorting.
The rule that the k-th occurrence of a letter in the last column is the same text character as the k-th occurrence of that letter in the first column. It drives inversion.
Replacing each symbol by its position in a list of recently used symbols, then moving it to the front, so runs of the same symbol become runs of zeros.

quiz.q: What is the BWT of 'banana$' (with $ smallest)?
quiz.explain: Sorted rotations end in a, n, n, b, $, a, a, so the last column reads annb$aa.

quiz.q: Does the BWT make the data smaller by itself?
options: No, it is a permutation of the same characters; it makes later stages such as move-to-front and entropy coding more effective
Yes, it removes the end marker
quiz.explain: The output has exactly the same letters as the input, just reordered so that equal letters cluster.

quiz.q: Why can the transform be reversed with only the last column?
options: Sorting the last column gives the first column, and the LF mapping links each last-column letter to the character before it in the text
The end marker contains the text
quiz.explain: First and last columns are related by the LF mapping, which lets you walk the text backwards one character at a time.

articles.excerpt: Some ideas look like magic tricks. Take a text, write down every way of rotating it, sort those rotations alphabetically, and keep only the last letter of each. You get a scrambled string with the same letters as before, except that equal letters now tend to sit together. Stranger still, from that…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Writing Only the Change in the Score
articles.subtitle: Varints, zigzag and delta encoding: store small numbers in few bytes, and turn big sorted numbers into small ones

glossary.definition: A variable-length integer encoding that uses one byte for small numbers and more bytes only as the number grows.
The top bit of each varint byte: 1 means another byte follows, 0 means this is the last byte.
Little Endian Base 128: the varint layout that stores 7-bit groups starting with the least significant group, used by Protocol Buffers and WebAssembly.
A mapping that interleaves negative and positive integers (0, −1, 1, −2, 2 become 0, 1, 2, 3, 4) so small negatives stay small.
Storing the difference between each value and the previous one instead of the value itself.

quiz.q: How is 300 encoded as a Protocol Buffers varint?
quiz.explain: 300 = 0b10_0101100. The low 7 bits 0101100 go first with the continuation bit set (0xAC), then the remaining 0000010 (0x02).

quiz.q: Why does zigzag encoding exist?
options: Because a negative number in plain two's complement looks huge and would take the maximum number of varint bytes
To save the sign bit only
quiz.explain: −1 in 64-bit two's complement has every bit set, so a plain varint needs 10 bytes. Zigzag maps −1 to 1, which takes one byte.

quiz.q: Sorted ids [1000, 1003, 1010, 1100, 1105] become [1000, 3, 7, 90, 5] after delta encoding. Why does that help?
options: Small gaps fit in one varint byte each, so the list shrinks from 10 bytes to 6
quiz.explain: Each original id needs two varint bytes, but the gaps after the first are all below 128, so they need one byte each.

articles.excerpt: A typical int64 field takes 8 bytes. But most numbers that real systems send are small: a count of 3, a status of 1, an age of 27, a field number of 5. Spending 8 bytes on the number 3 means seven of them are zeros, sent over the network, written to disk and read back millions of times a second.…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: The Remainder That Notices Smudges
articles.subtitle: Cyclic redundancy checks: divide the data by a fixed polynomial over bits, send the remainder, and catch accidental corruption

glossary.definition: An error-detecting code: the remainder of dividing the data, viewed as a polynomial over bits, by a fixed generator polynomial.
The fixed divisor agreed by sender and receiver, such as x³ + x² + 1, written in bits as 1101.
Long division where subtraction is replaced by XOR, so there are no borrows or carries.
Corruption of several bits close together, such as a scratch, a noise spike or a dropped byte.
A short value computed from data and sent with it, so the receiver can recompute it and detect changes.

quiz.q: Data 101101 with generator 1101 (degree 3). What does the sender transmit?
quiz.explain: Append three zeros, divide by 1101 with XOR, and the remainder is 010. The sender transmits the data followed by the remainder: 101101010.

quiz.q: How does the receiver check a frame?
options: It divides the whole received frame by the same generator; a zero remainder means no error was detected
quiz.explain: Appending the remainder makes the frame an exact multiple of the generator, so any non-zero remainder signals corruption.

quiz.q: Why should a CRC never be used to protect data against attackers?
options: It is linear and unkeyed, so anyone can change data and fix up the CRC to match
quiz.explain: CRCs catch accidents, not adversaries. Integrity against tampering needs a cryptographic MAC or signature.

articles.excerpt: Every Ethernet frame your computer sends ends with 4 extra bytes. They contain no data at all. They exist so that the receiving network card can tell, almost for free, whether any of the preceding bits were flipped by electrical noise on the way. If the check fails, the frame is silently dropped…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: The Grid That Points at the Wrong Bit
articles.subtitle: Hamming codes: overlapping parity checks whose failures spell out the position of a flipped bit, so it can be fixed

glossary.definition: An extra bit chosen so that a group of bits has an even number of 1s. If one bit in the group flips, the count becomes odd.
A code that protects 4 data bits with 3 parity bits, making 7-bit codewords that can correct any single flipped bit.
The pattern of failed parity checks. In a Hamming code, read as a binary number, it equals the position of the flipped bit.
The number of positions in which two bit strings differ.
Single error correction, double error detection: a Hamming code plus one overall parity bit, used in ECC memory.

quiz.q: Which positions does the parity bit at position 2 check in Hamming(7,4)?
quiz.explain: Parity bit p checks every position whose binary number has bit p set. Positions 2, 3, 6 and 7 have the '2' bit set.

quiz.q: A received codeword fails the checks for parity bits 1 and 4 but passes 2. Which bit flipped?
quiz.explain: The syndrome is 1 + 4 = 5, so position 5 flipped.

quiz.q: What happens if two bits flip in a plain Hamming(7,4) codeword?
options: The syndrome points to a third, innocent position, and 'correcting' it makes things worse
It is always detected and flagged
quiz.explain: Minimum distance 3 allows correcting one error or detecting two, not both at once. SECDED adds an overall parity bit to tell one error from two.

articles.excerpt: As Richard Hamming later told the story, in the late 1940s he was using relay computers at Bell Labs that could detect certain errors but not fix them. When the machine detected an error it simply stopped, and over a weekend his job would sit unfinished until someone restarted it. His frustration…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Why a Stained QR Code Still Scans
articles.subtitle: Reed-Solomon codes: treat data as a polynomial, store extra points on it, and rebuild lost or damaged pieces from any large enough subset

glossary.definition: An error-correcting code that encodes k data symbols as a polynomial of degree below k and stores its values at n points, so any k values rebuild everything.
The unit Reed-Solomon works on, usually a byte, rather than a single bit.
A set of numbers with addition, subtraction, multiplication and division that stays inside the set, such as integers mod a prime, or the 256-element field used for bytes.
A missing symbol whose position is known, such as a failed disk or an unreadable block.
Rebuilding the unique polynomial of degree below k that passes through k given points.
Storing data as k data pieces plus m parity pieces so that any k of the k + m pieces can rebuild the data.

quiz.q: A Reed-Solomon code has k = 4 data symbols and n = 10 total symbols. How many erasures (known missing symbols) can it recover?
quiz.explain: Any k = 4 of the 10 values determine the polynomial, so up to n − k = 6 symbols can be missing.

quiz.q: With the same code, how many errors at unknown positions can it correct?
quiz.explain: Unknown errors cost twice as much as erasures: up to (n − k) / 2 = 3 errors can be corrected.

quiz.q: A storage system uses 6 data + 3 parity pieces instead of 3 full replicas. What is the trade-off?
options: It uses 1.5x space instead of 3x and survives 3 lost pieces, but rebuilding a piece means reading several others
quiz.explain: Erasure coding saves space and tolerates more failures, but repair and degraded reads need data from k pieces instead of one copy.

articles.excerpt: Spill coffee on a QR code, tear off a corner, or print a logo in the middle of it, and your phone still scans it. Scratch a CD and the music still plays. Lose three disks at once in a large storage cluster, and nobody loses a file. All three survive damage for the same reason: their data is…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: A Fingerprint You Cannot Fake
articles.subtitle: Cryptographic hash functions: why changing one letter changes everything, and how Git, downloads and passwords rely on them

glossary.definition: A function that maps any input to a fixed-size output, called a digest, in a way that is practically impossible to reverse or to collide on purpose.
The fixed-size output of a hash function, such as 256 bits for SHA-256, usually shown as hexadecimal.
Given a digest, it is infeasible to find any input that produces it.
It is infeasible to find two different inputs with the same digest.
A tiny change in the input, even one bit, changes about half of the output bits, unpredictably.

quiz.q: How does a cryptographic hash differ from the hash used in a hash table?
options: It must also resist attacks: finding inputs for a given output or two inputs with the same output must be infeasible
quiz.explain: Hash table hashes only need to spread keys evenly. Cryptographic hashes must hold up against an adversary trying to forge or reverse them.

quiz.q: A downloaded file's SHA-256 matches the one published on the official site. What does that tell you?
options: The file is, with overwhelming probability, exactly the one the publisher hashed
quiz.explain: A match means no corruption or tampering since the publisher computed the digest, assuming the published digest itself came from a trusted source.

quiz.q: Why are MD5 and SHA-1 no longer recommended for security?
options: Practical collision attacks have been demonstrated against them
quiz.explain: Researchers have produced real collisions for both, so they cannot be trusted where collision resistance matters.

articles.excerpt: Type "PaperStack" into a SHA-256 calculator and you get 64 hexadecimal characters. Change one letter to "paperStack" and the output looks completely unrelated. Not a little different: about half of its bits flip, with no visible pattern. That strange property, plus the fact that nobody can work…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: A Lock That Takes a Second to Turn
articles.subtitle: Storing passwords safely: salts, deliberately slow hashes like bcrypt and Argon2, and why SHA-256 alone is not enough

glossary.definition: A random value generated per user and stored next to the password hash, so identical passwords produce different hashes.
A tunable setting that controls how slow a password hash is, such as bcrypt's cost or Argon2's time and memory parameters.
Making a hash deliberately expensive, for example by repeating it many times, so each guess costs an attacker much more.
A precomputed table mapping common passwords to their unsalted hashes, used to look passwords up instantly.
A hash that needs a lot of memory to compute, which makes cheap parallel hardware like GPUs far less effective at guessing.
A secret value, kept outside the database, mixed into every password hash as an extra layer of protection.

quiz.q: Why is a fast hash like SHA-256 a poor choice for storing passwords?
options: It is not secure for files
Attackers who steal the hashes can try enormous numbers of guesses per second, so weak passwords fall quickly
It cannot be computed on servers
quiz.explain: Speed helps the attacker. Password hashes are designed to be slow so each guess is expensive.

quiz.q: What does a per-user salt prevent?
options: Using one precomputed table for everyone, and seeing which users share a password
quiz.explain: With a unique salt, the same password hashes differently for each user, so precomputed tables and duplicate spotting stop working.

quiz.q: Why do memory-hard functions like Argon2 help against GPU attackers?
options: Each guess needs lots of memory, and GPUs have far less memory per core than compute, which limits parallel guessing
quiz.explain: GPUs win by running thousands of cheap computations in parallel. Requiring megabytes of memory per guess removes most of that advantage.

articles.excerpt: Every few months, some company announces that its user database was stolen. The question that decides how bad it is: how were the passwords stored? If they were plain text, every account is open immediately. If they were hashed with a fast hash, most weak and common passwords are cracked within…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Agreeing on a Secret While Everyone Listens
articles.subtitle: Diffie-Hellman key exchange: two strangers build a shared key over a public channel using modular exponentiation

glossary.definition: A protocol by which two parties end up with the same secret key, which they then use to encrypt their conversation.
A communication path where an eavesdropper can read every message, such as the open internet.
A number g whose powers modulo a prime p produce many different values, ideally all of 1 to p − 1.
Given g, p and g^a mod p, find a. Believed to be infeasible for well-chosen large primes, and the basis of Diffie-Hellman's security.
An attacker sits between two parties, pretending to each to be the other, and runs a separate key exchange with each.
A property where stealing a long-term key later does not reveal past conversations, achieved by using fresh Diffie-Hellman keys per session.

quiz.q: With p = 23, g = 5, Alice's secret a = 4 and Bob's secret b = 3, what is the shared secret?
quiz.explain: A = 5^4 mod 23 = 4, B = 5^3 mod 23 = 10. Alice computes 10^4 mod 23 = 18, Bob computes 4^3 mod 23 = 18.

quiz.q: What does an eavesdropper need to solve to recover the shared secret from g, p, A and B?
options: Essentially a discrete logarithm: find a from g^a mod p
quiz.explain: Computing g^a mod p is fast, but undoing it to find a is believed infeasible for large well-chosen parameters.

quiz.q: Why is plain Diffie-Hellman vulnerable to a man-in-the-middle attack?
options: Nothing proves who sent A and B, so an attacker can substitute their own values
quiz.explain: Diffie-Hellman gives secrecy against listeners, not authentication. TLS adds certificates and signatures so each side knows whose public value it received.

articles.excerpt: You open a website you have never visited. Within a fraction of a second, your browser and a server on another continent agree on a secret key that encrypts everything you send. They have never met, they share no password, and every message they exchanged to agree on that key crossed networks where…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: A Padlock Anyone Can Close but Only You Can Open
articles.subtitle: RSA: public-key encryption and signatures from two secret primes, modular exponentiation and the difficulty of factoring

glossary.definition: The pair (n, e) that anyone may know and use to encrypt messages to you or verify your signatures.
The exponent d (with the primes behind it), kept secret and used to decrypt or sign.
The number n = p × q, the product of two large secret primes, which all RSA arithmetic is done modulo.
φ(n), the count of numbers from 1 to n coprime to n. For n = p × q with distinct primes it is (p − 1)(q − 1).
A function that is easy to compute, hard to invert, but easy to invert for someone holding a secret, here the primes p and q.
Structured randomness added to a message before RSA is applied, such as OAEP for encryption or PSS for signatures, without which RSA is insecure.

quiz.q: With p = 11, q = 17 and e = 7, what is the private exponent d?
quiz.explain: φ(n) = 10 × 16 = 160. d is the inverse of 7 modulo 160: 7 × 23 = 161 ≡ 1 (mod 160).

quiz.q: Why is it safe to publish n and e?
options: Computing d needs φ(n), which needs the factors p and q, and factoring a large n is believed infeasible
quiz.explain: Knowing p and q makes φ(n) and hence d easy. Without them, no efficient classical method is known for 2048-bit moduli.

quiz.q: Why is 'textbook' RSA, applying m^e mod n directly, insecure?
options: It is deterministic, so equal messages give equal ciphertexts and guesses can be checked, and it has exploitable algebraic structure
quiz.explain: Real systems add randomised padding (OAEP, PSS) so the same message encrypts differently each time and the structure cannot be abused.

articles.excerpt: Diffie-Hellman showed in 1976 that two strangers can agree on a secret in public. But it left an obvious question open: could you publish one thing, once, so that anyone in the world could send you a secret message, or check that a message really came from you, without ever talking to you first? A…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: A Chain of Notaries Behind Every Padlock Icon
articles.subtitle: Digital signatures and certificates: sign with a private key, verify with a public one, and chain trust from a few root authorities to every website

glossary.definition: A value computed from a message with a private key, which anyone holding the matching public key can check, proving who signed and that the message is unchanged.
A signed document (usually in X.509 format) binding a public key to a name such as a domain, signed by a certificate authority.
An organisation trusted to check identities and sign certificates.
A self-signed CA certificate shipped inside operating systems and browsers, the starting point of trust.
A sequence of certificates, each signed by the next, ending at a root the verifier already trusts.
The signer cannot plausibly deny having signed, since only their private key could have produced the signature.

quiz.q: Which key does a website use to sign its part of the TLS handshake?
options: The website's private key, which the browser checks with the public key in its certificate
quiz.explain: Signing always uses the signer's private key. The certificate tells the browser which public key belongs to the site.

quiz.q: Why does a browser trust a certificate signed by an intermediate CA it has never seen?
options: The intermediate's own certificate is signed by a root CA in the browser's trust store, so the chain ends at a trusted root
quiz.explain: The browser verifies each signature up the chain until it reaches a root certificate it already holds.

quiz.q: Does signing a message keep it secret?
options: No, a signature proves origin and integrity; the message itself stays readable unless it is separately encrypted
quiz.explain: Signatures and encryption solve different problems. Anyone can read a signed message; they just cannot forge or alter it undetected.

articles.excerpt: You type your bank's address and a padlock appears. Your browser has never met this server, and the network in between could be a café's Wi-Fi run by anyone. Yet within a fraction of a second it decided: this really is the bank, not someone pretending. That decision rests on two ideas. A digital…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: The Index at the Back of Every Search Engine
articles.subtitle: Inverted indexes: map each word to the documents that contain it, intersect sorted lists to answer queries, and compress them to fit

glossary.definition: A map from each term to the list of documents that contain it, the reverse of storing each document's list of words.
The sorted list of document ids (and optionally positions or counts) stored for one term.
Splitting text into terms, usually by lowercasing and breaking on spaces and punctuation.
Reducing words to a common root, such as 'running' and 'runs' to 'run', so they match each other.
Very common words such as 'the' or 'and' that appear in almost every document and carry little meaning on their own.
Storing differences between consecutive sorted ids instead of the ids themselves, so the numbers are small and compress well.
A relevance score that grows with how often a term appears in a document and shrinks with how many documents contain it.

quiz.q: Postings: cat → [1, 3], dog → [2, 3]. Which documents match 'cat AND dog'?
quiz.explain: AND is the intersection of the two posting lists: only document 3 appears in both.

quiz.q: Why are posting lists kept sorted by document id?
options: So intersections and unions can be done with a linear merge, and gaps between ids are small for compression
quiz.explain: Sorted lists allow two-pointer merging in O(m + n) and make gap encoding effective.

quiz.q: What is the cost of removing stop words from the index?
options: Queries that depend on them, such as exact phrases like 'to be or not to be', can no longer be answered precisely
quiz.explain: Stop words carry little meaning alone but matter in phrases, so modern engines usually keep them and handle them at query time.

articles.excerpt: Type three words into a search box and results from billions of pages appear in a fraction of a second. Reading every page for those words would take far longer than that, even for a huge data centre. The search engine is not reading pages when you search. It did the reading long before, and built…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: A Word That Appears Everywhere Tells You Nothing
articles.subtitle: TF-IDF and BM25: score documents by how often they use rare query words, with saturation and length normalisation

glossary.definition: How many times a query term appears in a document.
How many documents in the collection contain the term at least once.
A weight that is high for rare terms and low for common ones, typically a logarithm of (total documents / documents containing the term).
In BM25, the way extra occurrences of a term add less and less to the score, approaching a ceiling.
Adjusting scores so long documents do not win just because they contain more words.
A number estimating how well a document matches a query, used to sort search results.

quiz.q: A term appears in every document in the collection. What is its TF-IDF weight with IDF = log(N / df)?
quiz.explain: A term in every document cannot tell documents apart, so plain IDF gives it no weight at all.

quiz.q: What does the k1 parameter in BM25 control?
options: How quickly extra occurrences of a term stop adding to the score
quiz.explain: With k1 = 1.2 the frequency factor is 1.0 for one occurrence, about 1.375 for two and about 1.96 for ten, approaching k1 + 1 = 2.2: diminishing returns.

quiz.q: What does b = 0 mean in BM25?
options: No length normalisation: long and short documents are treated alike
quiz.explain: b scales how much document length matters. b = 1 normalises fully, b = 0 not at all; 0.75 is a common default.

articles.excerpt: You search a recipe site for "tomato pasta". A lookup in an inverted index, as in The Index at the Back of Every Search Engine, instantly finds every document containing either word: a pasta recipe, a soup page that says "tomato" three times, an essay on the history of tomatoes, a quick pasta…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Copying Only the Paragraphs That Changed
articles.subtitle: The rsync algorithm: a cheap rolling checksum finds matching blocks at any offset, a strong hash confirms them, and only the differences cross the network

glossary.definition: Sending only the differences between an old and a new version of a file, plus instructions to rebuild the new version from the old one.
A fixed-size piece of the old file, for example a few kilobytes, that the receiver fingerprints.
A weak checksum over a window of bytes that can be updated in constant time when the window slides by one byte.
A cryptographic-quality hash used to confirm that a block whose weak checksum matched really is identical.
A weak checksum match between two blocks that are actually different, which the strong hash catches.

quiz.q: Why can't rsync simply compare block 1 of the old file with block 1 of the new file?
options: Inserting a single byte near the start shifts every later block, so fixed-offset comparison finds no matches
Files must be the same length
quiz.explain: Content that did not change has moved by one byte. Checking every byte offset with a rolling checksum finds it again.

quiz.q: Why does rsync use two checksums instead of one?
options: The weak rolling checksum is cheap enough to compute at every offset; the strong hash is expensive but rules out accidental matches
quiz.explain: Computing a strong hash at every byte would be too slow. The weak checksum filters candidates, the strong hash confirms them.

quiz.q: A window [3, 1, 4, 1] has a = 9 and b = 24. The window slides to [1, 4, 1, 5]. What is the new a?
quiz.explain: a' = a − outgoing + incoming = 9 − 3 + 5 = 11. Then b' = b − 4 × 3 + a' = 24 − 12 + 11 = 23.

articles.excerpt: You have a 2 GB database backup on a remote server, and today's version on your laptop differs from yesterday's in a few scattered places. Uploading 2 GB again over a slow link takes an hour. If both machines could somehow agree on which parts are the same, you would send a few megabytes instead.…

articles.subject: famous-algos
articles.title: Dead Reckoning Meets a Foggy Lighthouse
articles.subtitle: The Kalman filter: predict where you are, measure noisily, and blend the two in proportion to how much you trust each

glossary.definition: The quantities being tracked, such as position and velocity.
A number measuring uncertainty: the larger the variance, the less sure we are. Its square root is the standard deviation.
Using a motion model to move the estimate forward in time, which adds uncertainty.
Blending the prediction with a new measurement, which reduces uncertainty.
The weight, between 0 and 1 in one dimension, that decides how far to move the estimate toward a new measurement.
Uncertainty added by the motion itself, such as currents pushing a ship off course, written Q.
Uncertainty in the sensor reading, written R.

quiz.q: In one dimension, predicted variance P = 3 and measurement variance R = 1. What is the Kalman gain?
quiz.explain: K = P / (P + R) = 3 / 4 = 0.75. The measurement is more trustworthy than the prediction, so the estimate moves three quarters of the way toward it.

quiz.q: What happens to the uncertainty during the prediction step?
options: It grows, because process noise is added
quiz.explain: Moving forward in time without looking adds uncertainty: P becomes P + Q.

quiz.q: When does the Kalman filter give the best possible estimate?
options: When the system is linear and the noise is Gaussian, it is optimal; otherwise it is an approximation
quiz.explain: Under linear dynamics and Gaussian noise it is the optimal estimator. For non-linear systems, variants such as the extended Kalman filter approximate it.

articles.excerpt: The blue dot on your phone's map moves smoothly as you walk, even though the GPS reading behind it jumps around by several metres, and even when it drops out under a flyover. Your phone is not trusting any single source. It combines a prediction from the phone's motion sensors with each noisy GPS…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Forty-Five Minutes to Design Instagram
articles.subtitle: A step-by-step framework that turns any open-ended design question into a structured conversation

glossary.definition: Something the system must do for users, such as post a photo or follow a friend.
A quality the system must have, such as low latency, high availability, durability or a target scale.
A quick, rough calculation of load, storage or bandwidth, used to decide which design choices matter.
The big boxes of a system and how requests and data flow between them, before any detail.
A focused, detailed discussion of one hard part of the design, such as how the feed is built or how data is sharded.
A choice where gaining one property, like speed, costs you another, like consistency or money.

quiz.q: What should you do first when asked to 'design a chat app'?
options: Ask which features and what scale matter
quiz.explain: The question is deliberately vague. Agreeing on features and scale first decides everything else and shows the interviewer you design for real needs.

quiz.q: Why do back-of-envelope estimates matter in a design interview?
options: They show which parts of the system are under real pressure, which tells you where to spend design effort
They replace the need for a diagram
They are only needed for databases
quiz.explain: Knowing that reads outnumber writes 100 to 1, or that storage grows by terabytes a day, tells you where caching, sharding or queues are actually needed.

quiz.q: Which statement best describes a good answer to a design question?
options: One perfect architecture with no weaknesses
A design that matches the requirements, with trade-offs explained and weaknesses acknowledged
The architecture of a famous company copied exactly
quiz.explain: There is no perfect design. Interviewers look for designs that fit the stated needs and for honest reasoning about what each choice costs.

articles.excerpt: "Design Instagram." Three words, then silence. There is no input format, no constraints, no expected output. Just a whiteboard and forty-five minutes. Candidates who freeze usually know plenty: caches, queues, databases. What they lack is a route through the conversation. The good news is that one…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: How Much Rice Does a Wedding Need?
articles.subtitle: Back-of-envelope estimates: five minutes of rough maths that decide your whole design

glossary.definition: Queries per second: how many requests a system handles each second.
Daily active users: how many distinct people use the product on a given day.
The highest traffic the system sees, often several times the daily average, for example during evenings or sales.
How many copies of each piece of data are stored, usually for durability; three is common.
How much data per second flows in or out of a system, for example megabytes per second.

quiz.q: About how many seconds are in a day, for quick estimates?
quiz.explain: A day has 86,400 seconds. Rounding to 100,000 makes the arithmetic easy and is accurate enough for design decisions.

quiz.q: 10 million uploads a day, 2 MB each, stored with replication factor 3. Roughly how much storage per day?
quiz.explain: 10 million times 2 MB is 20 TB of raw data. Three copies make about 60 TB per day.

quiz.q: Why estimate peak load and not just the daily average?
options: Systems must survive their busiest moments, which can be several times the average
Peak load only matters for databases
quiz.explain: Traffic is uneven. A design sized for the average fails at 8 pm or during a sale, so capacity is planned for the peak.

articles.excerpt: A caterer planning a wedding for 500 guests does not weigh every grain of rice. They think: about 150 grams per guest, so roughly 75 kilograms, round up to 80 for safety. Two seconds of arithmetic, and they know whether to rent one pot or ten. System design works the same way. Before you draw a…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: If a CPU Cycle Took One Second
articles.subtitle: The latency numbers every engineer should feel, and why they decide where data lives

glossary.definition: How long one operation takes from start to finish, such as one memory read or one network round trip.
How many operations a system completes per second. A system can have high throughput and still high latency.
The time for a message to travel to another machine and for the reply to come back.
Keeping data close to where it is used, in the same cache, the same machine, the same data centre or the same region.
The latency of the slowest requests, such as the 99th percentile, which users notice even when the average is fast.

quiz.q: Roughly how does a main memory read compare with a round trip within the same data centre?
options: Memory is roughly a thousand times faster
The network round trip is faster
Memory is about ten times faster
quiz.explain: A memory read is on the order of 100 nanoseconds; a round trip inside a data centre is on the order of half a millisecond, thousands of times longer.

quiz.q: A page needs 20 sequential calls to a service in another continent. Why is that a problem?
options: Each cross-continent round trip is on the order of 100 milliseconds, so 20 in a row add up to seconds
Services cannot be called more than once
quiz.explain: Latencies add up when calls are sequential. Twenty round trips of about 100 ms each is about 2 seconds of waiting.

quiz.q: Why do latency tables say 'approximate' and use orders of magnitude?
options: Exact values change with hardware and setup, but the ratios between levels stay roughly stable
They are measured in different units each year
quiz.explain: Specific numbers vary across machines and years. What stays useful is the gap between levels: caches, memory, SSDs, networks and continents differ by factors of tens to thousands.

articles.excerpt: Nanoseconds, microseconds, milliseconds: the words blur together, and so do the numbers. That blur hides the most important fact in system design. A trip to another continent is not "a bit slower" than reading memory. It is roughly a million times slower. Scale the numbers to human time and the…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Everything That Happens Before a Page Appears
articles.subtitle: Follow one request from your browser to a server and back: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP and what each costs

glossary.definition: The Domain Name System, which turns a name like example.com into the IP address of a server.
A protocol that gives two machines a reliable, ordered stream of bytes over an unreliable network.
The encryption layer behind HTTPS. It proves the server's identity and agrees on keys so traffic cannot be read or altered.
The request and response protocol of the web: a client sends a method, a path and headers, and the server replies with a status, headers and a body.
Reusing one open connection for many HTTP requests, so the setup cost is paid only once.
How long a message takes to reach the other side and for the reply to come back. Often shortened to RTT.

quiz.q: Before the first byte of HTTP is sent over HTTPS with TCP, which steps must happen?
options: DNS lookup (unless cached), TCP handshake, then TLS handshake
quiz.explain: The browser needs the IP address, then a TCP connection, then encryption keys. Only then can it send the HTTP request.

quiz.q: Why does keep-alive make pages faster?
options: Later requests reuse an already open connection, skipping new TCP and TLS handshakes
It sends requests in random order
quiz.explain: Handshakes cost round trips. Reusing a warm connection lets later requests go straight to sending HTTP.

quiz.q: What does HTTP/3 change compared with HTTP/2?
options: It runs over QUIC on UDP, so one lost packet does not stall every stream on the connection
It uses a new HTML format
quiz.explain: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over one TCP connection, where a lost packet blocks everything behind it. QUIC handles streams independently and also combines transport and encryption setup.

articles.excerpt: You type a web address and press Enter. Half a second later, a page appears. It feels like one action. It is actually a relay race: at least four separate conversations with machines you never see, each one costing a trip across the network before the next can start. Knowing those legs is not…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: The Phone Book That Holds the Internet Together
articles.subtitle: How DNS turns names into addresses, why caching makes it fast, and how it doubles as a load balancer

glossary.definition: The DNS server your device asks first, often run by your ISP or a public service. It does the legwork of finding the answer.
The DNS server that holds the official records for a domain and gives the final answer.
Time to live: how many seconds a DNS answer may be cached before it must be looked up again.
One entry in DNS, such as an A record (name to IPv4 address) or a CNAME (name to another name).
Answering the same name with different addresses depending on where the user is, to send them to a nearby server.

quiz.q: A record has a TTL of 300 seconds. You change the IP address. When will every user see the new address?
options: Within roughly 300 seconds for well-behaved caches, sometimes longer for caches that ignore TTLs
quiz.explain: Caches may keep the old answer until its TTL expires. Most respect it, but some clients and resolvers hold answers longer.

quiz.q: Who walks the chain from root to TLD to authoritative server?
quiz.explain: Your device asks the resolver one question. The resolver does the iterative lookups and caches what it learns.

quiz.q: Why is DNS-based load balancing coarse?
options: DNS cannot return more than one address
Answers are cached for the TTL, so traffic shifts slowly and the DNS server cannot see actual server load
DNS only works for one region
quiz.explain: Once a client caches an address, it keeps using it until the TTL ends. That makes DNS good for rough geographic steering, not fine-grained balancing.

articles.excerpt: Every website you visit begins with a question your browser asks before anything else: "where is this name?" If that question cannot be answered, a perfectly healthy service simply vanishes. Several of the internet's most visible outages have come not from servers crashing but from DNS answers…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: The Menu Is a Promise to the Kitchen
articles.subtitle: API design for interviews and real systems: REST, gRPC, GraphQL, pagination, versioning and errors

glossary.definition: Application programming interface: the contract that says which requests a service accepts and what it returns.
In REST, a thing the API exposes, such as a user or an order, identified by a URL like /users/42.
Safe to repeat. Sending the same idempotent request twice has the same effect as sending it once.
Paging through results by passing an opaque marker for where the last page ended, instead of a page number.
A formal description of the data an API sends and receives, such as a Protocol Buffers file or a GraphQL schema.
A change that makes existing clients fail, such as removing a field or changing its meaning.

quiz.q: Why is cursor pagination usually better than offset pagination for a fast-changing feed?
options: New items inserted at the top do not shift pages, and the database can seek directly instead of skipping rows
It does not need an index
quiz.explain: With offsets, inserts move items between pages and the database must skip all earlier rows. A cursor says 'continue after this item', which is stable and uses an index.

quiz.q: Which HTTP methods are idempotent by definition?
quiz.explain: Repeating GET, PUT or DELETE leaves the same state. POST usually creates something new each time, which is why payment APIs add idempotency keys.

quiz.q: When is gRPC a better fit than a public REST API?
options: For browsers calling a public endpoint with no tooling
For high-volume internal service-to-service calls where a typed schema and efficient binary encoding help
quiz.explain: gRPC shines between services you control: strict schemas, generated clients, HTTP/2 streaming and compact messages.

articles.excerpt: A mobile app ships with a call to GET /feed?page=2. A year later the backend team changes how pages work. The app in millions of pockets cannot be updated overnight, and suddenly half your users see duplicated posts or blank screens. APIs are the part of a system that is hardest to take back. Once…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Checking the Mailbox vs Hearing the Doorbell
articles.subtitle: Polling, long polling, server-sent events and WebSockets: how servers push updates and what each costs

glossary.definition: The client asks the server for updates on a fixed schedule, such as every five seconds, whether or not anything changed.
The client asks for updates and the server holds the request open until something happens or a timeout passes, then the client asks again.
A browser standard where the server keeps an HTTP response open and streams text events to the client, one direction only.
A protocol that upgrades an HTTP connection into a long-lived, two-way channel for messages in both directions.
A fleet of servers whose job is to hold many open client connections and route messages to them.
Delivering one event to many recipients, such as a message to every member of a group chat.

quiz.q: What is the main cost of short polling every 2 seconds?
options: Most requests return nothing new, wasting bandwidth and server work, and updates still arrive up to 2 seconds late
quiz.explain: Polling pays for a request every interval even when nothing changed, and latency is bounded by the interval.

quiz.q: When are server-sent events a good fit?
options: Two-way chat with frequent client messages
One-way streams from server to browser, like live scores or notifications
quiz.explain: SSE is simple and works over plain HTTP, with automatic reconnection in browsers, but data flows only from server to client.

quiz.q: Why do chat systems usually have a separate gateway tier for WebSockets?
options: WebSockets are illegal on app servers
Holding millions of mostly idle connections is a different job from business logic, so it is scaled and deployed separately
It removes the need for a database
quiz.explain: Connection holding is memory-heavy and long-lived; business logic is CPU-heavy and stateless. Separating them lets each scale and deploy independently.

articles.excerpt: HTTP was designed for asking: the client requests, the server replies, the conversation ends. But a chat message, a driver's location or a cricket score is something the server learns first. How does the server tell you, when you did not ask? There are four answers, from crude to elegant, and every…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: When the Phone Line Between Branches Goes Dead
articles.subtitle: CAP and PACELC without the myths: what you really give up during partitions, and every other day

glossary.definition: A failure where some machines can no longer reach others, splitting the system into groups that cannot communicate.
The strongest everyday consistency: the system behaves as if there were one copy of the data and every operation happened at a single instant.
In CAP, every request to a working node gets a non-error response, even during a partition.
A system that, during a partition, refuses some requests rather than return possibly inconsistent data.
A system that, during a partition, keeps answering on both sides, accepting that answers may be inconsistent.
An extension of CAP: if there is a Partition, choose Availability or Consistency; Else, choose Latency or Consistency.

quiz.q: What does CAP actually force you to choose?
options: Any two of three properties at design time
During a network partition, between staying available and staying consistent
quiz.explain: Partitions are not optional in real networks. When one happens, a system must either refuse some requests or risk inconsistent answers.

quiz.q: Why does PACELC add the 'Else' part?
options: Even without partitions, stronger consistency usually costs latency, which is a choice systems make every day
quiz.explain: Partitions are rare, but waiting for replicas or a distant leader on every request is a constant cost. PACELC names that everyday trade-off.

quiz.q: A bank ledger and a social media like counter: which pair of choices is most sensible during a partition?
quiz.explain: Money must not diverge, so the ledger refuses risky writes. A like counter can keep accepting likes and reconcile later.

articles.excerpt: "CAP theorem: consistency, availability, partition tolerance. Pick two." It is the most quoted line in system design interviews, and in its popular form it is misleading. You do not get to pick "CA" for a distributed system, and you are not making the choice once at design time. The real statement…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Why Your Like Count Can Be Wrong for a Second
articles.subtitle: Strong vs eventual consistency in plain words, and the guarantees users actually notice

glossary.definition: A copy of the same data kept on another machine, for durability, availability or faster reads.
Every read sees the latest completed write, as if there were a single copy of the data.
If writes stop, all replicas eventually agree, but a read in the meantime may return an older value.
The delay between a write landing on one replica and reaching the others.
A guarantee that after you write something, your own later reads always see it, even if other users might not yet.
A guarantee that once you have seen a value, you never later see an older one.

quiz.q: A user posts a comment, refreshes, and the comment is missing for two seconds. Which guarantee is being violated?
quiz.explain: The user's own read went to a replica that had not yet received their write. Read-your-writes guarantees the author sees their own changes.

quiz.q: Which data most clearly needs strong consistency?
options: The view count on a video
A bank account balance used to approve withdrawals
quiz.explain: Approving a withdrawal on a stale balance can overdraw an account. A view count being slightly behind harms nobody.

quiz.q: Why do systems accept eventual consistency at all?
options: It allows reads from nearby replicas and keeps working during network problems, giving lower latency and higher availability
quiz.explain: Waiting for every replica, or for a distant leader, costs latency and fails during partitions. Relaxing freshness buys speed and availability.

articles.excerpt: You like a friend's photo. The heart turns red. You refresh, and the like count drops by one. You refresh again, and it is back. Nothing is broken. You just watched two copies of the same data disagree for a moment. Every large system keeps several copies of its data, and copies take time to agree.…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: What Three Nines Actually Buys You
articles.subtitle: Availability, SLIs, SLOs and error budgets: turning 'always up' into numbers you can design for

glossary.definition: The fraction of time, or of requests, for which a service works correctly, often written as a percentage like 99.9%.
Service level indicator: a measured number describing service health, such as the fraction of requests that succeed within 300 ms.
Service level objective: the target for an SLI over a period, such as 99.9% of requests succeeding each month.
Service level agreement: a contract with customers that promises a level of service, with penalties if it is missed.
The amount of failure an SLO allows, such as 0.1% of requests in a month, which a team can spend on releases and risk.
Running spare copies of a component so that one failing does not take the service down.

quiz.q: Roughly how much downtime per 30-day month does 99.9% availability allow?
quiz.explain: 0.1% of 30 days is 0.001 × 43,200 minutes, about 43 minutes.

quiz.q: A request passes through two services in sequence, each 99.9% available. What is the end-to-end availability, roughly?
quiz.explain: Both must work, so multiply: 0.999 × 0.999 ≈ 0.998, or about 99.8%. Chains of dependencies lose nines.

quiz.q: Two independent replicas each have 99% availability, and either one can serve. What is the combined availability?
quiz.explain: The service fails only if both fail: 0.01 × 0.01 = 0.0001. So availability is 1 − 0.0001 = 99.99%, assuming failures are independent.

articles.excerpt: Ask a product manager how often the app may be down and the answer is "never". Ask an engineer what "never" costs and the answer is "infinitely much". Neither answer helps anyone design anything. The industry's way out is to turn reliability into numbers: how many nines, measured how, over what…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Pressing the Pay Button Twice Should Charge Once
articles.subtitle: Stateless servers and idempotent APIs: the two habits that make retries, scaling and failover safe

glossary.definition: A server that keeps no client-specific memory between requests, so any server can handle any request.
Information about a user's ongoing interaction, such as who is logged in or what is in their cart.
An operation that has the same effect whether it runs once or many times.
A unique id the client sends with a request so the server can recognise and ignore duplicates of it.
A guarantee that a message or request will arrive, possibly more than once, which is what retries naturally give you.
Adding more servers behind a load balancer to handle more traffic.

quiz.q: Why do stateless servers make scaling easy?
options: Any server can handle any request, so you can add or remove servers freely behind a load balancer
They do not need a database
quiz.explain: With no per-user memory on the server, requests can go anywhere, and losing a server loses nothing important.

quiz.q: A payment request times out. The client does not know whether it succeeded. What makes a retry safe?
options: Sending the same idempotency key, so the server returns the original result if it already processed the request
Retrying with a new request id
quiz.explain: The key lets the server recognise the duplicate and return the stored outcome instead of charging again.

quiz.q: Which operation is naturally idempotent?
options: Set the delivery address to X
quiz.explain: Setting a value to X twice leaves it at X. Adding, appending and sending repeat their effect each time.

articles.excerpt: You tap "Pay" on a train with patchy signal. The spinner turns, then an error: "Request timed out." Did the payment go through? You have no idea. So you tap again. If the system is built well, you are charged once, and the second tap simply shows the same receipt. If not, you are charged twice, and…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: The Front Desk and the Key Card
articles.subtitle: Sessions, JWTs, OAuth 2.0, OpenID Connect and RBAC: how systems know who you are and what you may do

glossary.definition: Proving who someone is, for example with a password, a passkey or a one-time code.
Deciding what an already identified user or program is allowed to do.
Server-side state that remembers a logged-in user, found through a random session id stored in a cookie.
JSON Web Token: a compact, signed set of claims (header, payload, signature) that a server can verify without a database lookup.
A long-lived credential used only to obtain new short-lived access tokens, and which the server can revoke.
A framework that lets a user grant an application limited access to their data on another service without sharing their password.
Proof Key for Code Exchange: a one-time secret that binds an OAuth authorisation code to the app that requested it, so a stolen code is useless.
Role-based access control: permissions are attached to roles, and users get permissions by being assigned roles.

quiz.q: A JWT payload contains a user's phone number. Who can read it?
options: Only the server that holds the signing key
Anyone who has the token, because the payload is only base64url-encoded, not encrypted
Nobody, because the signature hides it
quiz.explain: A signed JWT is readable by anyone who holds it. The signature proves it was not modified; it does not hide the contents.

quiz.q: Why does a mobile app using the OAuth authorisation code flow add PKCE?
options: So a code intercepted on the way back to the app cannot be exchanged for tokens without the secret verifier only the app knows
quiz.explain: The app sends a hash of a random verifier at the start and the verifier itself at the token step. An attacker holding only the code cannot produce the verifier.

quiz.q: Access tokens are self-contained JWTs valid for 15 minutes. An admin bans a user. What is the simplest way to cut them off within seconds?
options: Wait for the tokens to expire
Revoke the refresh token and check a small denylist or per-user revocation time on each request
Rotate the signing key every second
Ask the client to delete the token
quiz.explain: Without some server-side check, a valid JWT works until it expires. A denylist or a 'tokens issued before T are invalid' stamp closes that window at the cost of a fast lookup.

articles.excerpt: A support engineer gets a ticket: a user changed their password after their laptop was stolen, yet the thief is still reading their messages twenty minutes later. The login system works. The password change worked. So how is the thief still inside? The answer hides in a design choice made months…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: The Host Who Seats Every Guest
articles.subtitle: Load balancers: L4 vs L7, the algorithms inside, health checks, sticky sessions and avoiding a single point of failure

glossary.definition: A component that receives incoming requests and spreads them across a pool of servers.
Balancing at the transport level, using IP addresses and ports, without reading the HTTP request.
Balancing at the application level, using HTTP details such as the path, headers or cookies to decide where a request goes.
A regular probe, such as a request to /health, that tells the load balancer whether a server can take traffic.
Sending all of one user's requests to the same server, usually via a cookie, often because that server holds their session state.
Letting a server finish its in-flight requests before removing it from the pool, so deploys do not cut users off.

quiz.q: What can a Layer 7 load balancer do that a Layer 4 one cannot?
options: Route by URL path or header, for example /api to one pool and /images to another
quiz.explain: Layer 7 reads the HTTP request, so it can make routing decisions on application-level details.

quiz.q: Why are health checks essential?
options: They let the load balancer stop sending traffic to servers that are down or unhealthy
quiz.explain: Without health checks, a crashed server would keep receiving its share of requests, and those users would see errors.

quiz.q: How do you stop the load balancer itself from being a single point of failure?
options: Run several load balancers, for example an active-passive pair with a floating IP, or many behind DNS or anycast
quiz.explain: Redundant load balancers with automatic failover, or many instances behind DNS or anycast, remove the single point of failure.

articles.excerpt: One server can handle so many requests per second. Your app needs ten times that. So you run ten servers. But users type one address, not ten. Something has to stand at the front door, take every request, and decide which server gets it, quickly, fairly, and without sending anyone to a server that…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Keep the Spices on the Counter
articles.subtitle: Caching strategies, eviction and hit ratios: the single most effective trick for making systems fast

glossary.definition: A small, fast store that keeps copies of frequently used data so it can be served without going to the slower source.
The fraction of requests answered by the cache. A 95% hit ratio means only 5% of reads reach the database.
A pattern where the application checks the cache first, and on a miss reads the database and stores the result in the cache.
A pattern where every write goes to the cache and the database together, keeping the cache fresh.
A pattern where writes go to the cache first and reach the database later, which is fast but can lose data if the cache fails.
Time to live: how long a cached entry may be used before it expires and must be fetched again.
The rule for choosing what to remove when the cache is full, such as least recently used.

quiz.q: A database read takes about 10 ms and a cache read about 1 ms. With a 90% hit ratio, what is the average read time?
quiz.explain: 0.9 × 1 ms + 0.1 × 10 ms = 0.9 + 1.0 = 1.9 ms, about five times faster than going to the database every time. (Counting the wasted cache check on a miss adds only 0.1 ms.)

quiz.q: In cache-aside, what happens on a cache miss?
options: The application reads the database, returns the value and stores it in the cache
The cache reads the database by itself
quiz.explain: The application owns the logic: check the cache, fall back to the database, then fill the cache for next time.

quiz.q: Which strategy risks losing recent writes if the cache crashes?
quiz.explain: Write-back acknowledges writes once they are in the cache and flushes them to the database later. A crash before the flush loses them.

articles.excerpt: A product page is viewed a million times a day. Its price, title and photos change maybe once a week. Yet without a cache, every single view asks the database the same question and waits for the same answer. Caching is the idea of remembering answers you will need again. It is the most effective…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Local Warehouses for the Whole Internet
articles.subtitle: Content delivery networks: serving files from nearby edges, cache keys, invalidation and when a CDN helps

glossary.definition: Content delivery network: a large set of servers spread around the world that cache and serve content close to users.
A CDN server in a location near users, sometimes called a point of presence, that answers requests from its cache.
Your own servers or storage, where the original copy of the content lives.
The parts of a request, such as the URL and some headers, that decide whether two requests can share one cached response.
Telling the CDN to drop or refresh cached copies before their TTL runs out, for example after a file changes.
The fraction of requests served from the edge without contacting the origin.

quiz.q: What is the main reason a CDN makes a page load faster for a distant user?
options: Content is served from an edge server nearby, cutting long round trips to the origin
It upgrades the user's internet connection
It removes the need for DNS
quiz.explain: Most of the delay for a distant user is round trips. A nearby edge answers in a short hop instead of crossing oceans.

quiz.q: Why do many sites put a version or hash in static file names, like app.3f9a2c.js?
options: So a new version gets a new URL, making invalidation unnecessary and allowing very long cache TTLs
quiz.explain: A changed file gets a new name, so old cached copies are simply never requested again. The files themselves can be cached for a long time.

quiz.q: What can go wrong if a personalised page is cached without the right cache key?
options: One user may be served another user's private page
The CDN refuses to cache it
quiz.explain: If the cache key ignores who is logged in, the first user's response may be stored and handed to everyone after them.

articles.excerpt: A student in Chennai opens a video site whose servers are in Virginia. Every image, script and video segment would have to cross the Pacific or the Atlantic and back, each request paying a few hundred milliseconds of travel. Multiply by a hundred files per page and a million viewers, and the origin…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Filing Cabinet, Labelled Boxes or Giant Spreadsheet?
articles.subtitle: Choosing a database honestly: relational, key-value, document, wide-column and graph stores, and the questions that decide

glossary.definition: A database that stores data in tables with rows and columns, linked by keys, and queried with SQL.
The declared structure of data: which tables and columns exist and what types they hold.
A query that combines rows from two or more tables using a shared key, such as orders with their customers.
A group of operations that either all succeed or all fail, with isolation from other transactions and durable results.
A database that stores values under keys and is optimised for fast get and put by key.
A database that stores self-contained documents, often JSON, which can nest related data together.
A database that groups data by a partition key and sorts it within each partition, designed to spread huge write volumes across many machines.

quiz.q: Which question most often decides the database choice?
options: What the main access patterns and consistency needs are
Which one has the best logo
How many servers you have today
quiz.explain: Databases are optimised for particular ways of reading and writing data. Matching those to your access patterns and consistency needs matters most.

quiz.q: Your data has many relationships queried in flexible ways, and transfers between accounts must be atomic. What fits best?
quiz.explain: Relational databases excel at joins across related data and at ACID transactions, which money movement needs.

quiz.q: Why do wide-column stores like Cassandra ask you to design tables around queries?
options: They spread data by partition key and avoid joins, so each query should read from one partition in a predictable order
quiz.explain: Without joins, the data for a query must already be grouped together. You often store the same data in several tables, one per query pattern.

articles.excerpt: "Which database would you use?" is asked in almost every design interview, and the weakest answers are slogans: "SQL doesn't scale", "NoSQL is faster", "just use MongoDB". Real systems at large companies run on relational databases, key-value stores, document stores and wide-column stores, often…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Why Some Queries Are Instant and Others Take Minutes
articles.subtitle: Database indexes: B+ trees, composite column order, covering indexes, and what every index costs on writes

glossary.definition: An extra data structure that lets a database find rows by a column's value without scanning the whole table.
Reading every row of a table to find the matching ones. Fine for small tables, very slow for large ones.
A balanced tree with many keys per node, used by most relational databases for indexes. Leaves are linked, which makes range scans fast.
An index on several columns in a specific order, such as (user_id, created_at).
An index that contains every column a query needs, so the database never has to visit the table rows.
How well a condition narrows down rows. A condition matching 0.1% of rows is highly selective; one matching 50% is not.

quiz.q: A composite index is on (user_id, created_at). Which query can use it fully?
quiz.explain: The index is sorted by user_id first, then created_at within each user. Filtering on user_id and ordering by created_at follows that order exactly.

quiz.q: Why does every extra index slow down writes?
options: Each insert, update or delete must also update every index on the affected columns
Indexes are stored in memory only
quiz.explain: An index is a separate sorted structure. Changing a row means changing its entry in each relevant index too.

quiz.q: About how many levels does a B+ tree need to index a billion rows if each node holds a few hundred keys?
quiz.explain: With a fan-out of a few hundred, each level multiplies capacity by hundreds: three to four levels reach a billion.

articles.excerpt: A query that took 3 milliseconds yesterday takes 40 seconds today. The code did not change. The table grew from ten thousand rows to fifty million, and the query was quietly reading every one of them. One line, CREATE INDEX, brings it back to milliseconds. Indexes are the most powerful performance…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: The Ticket Rail Between Waiters and Cooks
articles.subtitle: Message queues and pub-sub: decoupling services with Kafka-style logs and RabbitMQ-style queues, and the guarantees each gives

glossary.definition: A buffer where producers put messages and consumers take them out later, so the two sides do not have to work at the same speed or time.
The producer sends messages; the consumer receives and processes them.
A pattern where each message published to a topic is delivered to every interested subscriber group.
One ordered slice of a topic. Messages within a partition keep their order; different partitions are processed in parallel.
A set of consumers that share the work of a topic, each partition being read by one member of the group.
A separate queue for messages that keep failing, so they can be inspected without blocking everything else.

quiz.q: What is the main benefit of putting a queue between two services?
options: The producer can keep working even if the consumer is slow or down, and spikes are absorbed by the buffer
It removes the need for a database
quiz.explain: Decoupling in time and speed is the core benefit: work piles up safely in the queue and is processed when the consumer can.

quiz.q: In Kafka-style systems, how do you keep all events for one user in order?
options: Use one consumer for the whole system
Use the user id as the message key, so all of that user's events go to the same partition
quiz.explain: Order is guaranteed only within a partition. Keying by user id routes each user's events to one partition.

quiz.q: With at-least-once delivery, what must consumers do?
options: Handle duplicates, for example by making processing idempotent or tracking processed message ids
quiz.explain: A message can be redelivered after a crash or timeout, so processing it twice must not cause harm.

articles.excerpt: When you upload a video, the site answers "Upload complete" in a second. But converting that video into ten resolutions takes minutes. If the upload request waited for all of it, uploads would time out, and a burst of uploads after a viral moment would crash the converters. Instead, the upload…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: The Cloakroom That Never Loses a Coat
articles.subtitle: Blob storage: how S3-style systems keep billions of files safe with buckets, metadata, replication, erasure coding, pre-signed URLs and multipart uploads

glossary.definition: Binary large object: any file treated as an opaque sequence of bytes, such as an image, a video or a backup.
A storage system that keeps whole objects addressed by a key inside a bucket, instead of files in a folder hierarchy or rows in tables.
A named container for objects, with its own access rules and settings.
Splitting data into k pieces and computing m extra parity pieces, so the original can be rebuilt from any k of the k + m pieces.
A time-limited URL, signed by the server, that lets a client upload or download one specific object directly from storage.
Uploading a large object as separate parts that can be sent in parallel and retried individually, then combined into one object.
The probability that stored data is not lost over a period of time. Different from availability, which is whether you can reach it right now.

quiz.q: A (6, 3) erasure code stores 6 data pieces and 3 parity pieces. What is its storage overhead, and how many pieces can be lost?
quiz.explain: 9 pieces for 6 pieces of data is 1.5x, and any 6 of the 9 rebuild the object, so any 3 can be lost. Three full replicas cost 3x and survive only 2 losses.

quiz.q: Why do apps hand clients pre-signed URLs instead of streaming uploads through their own servers?
options: The bytes go straight to storage, so app servers are not tied up moving large files, while access stays limited to one object for a short time
quiz.explain: The app server only signs permission; the heavy transfer goes directly between client and storage.

quiz.q: Where should the metadata about a user's uploaded photo (owner, caption, storage key) live?
options: In the application database, pointing to the object key in blob storage
quiz.explain: Databases are good at small, queryable records; blob stores are good at large immutable bytes. Each stores what it is good at, linked by the key.

articles.excerpt: Every photo you post, every video you upload, every PDF attached to an email, every nightly database backup has to live somewhere. It is not in the database: a 4 GB video in a table row would make every backup, replica and query painfully slow. It sits in a different kind of system, one built for a…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: A Shared Whiteboard the Whole Fleet Can Read
articles.subtitle: Redis and distributed caches: data structures, sharding, replication, persistence, and the jobs they do in real systems

glossary.definition: A cache that runs as its own cluster of servers shared by many application servers, instead of living inside each one.
A popular in-memory data store that offers strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets and more, often used as a cache, counter or lightweight queue.
