A simple, very fast in-memory key-value cache, without Redis's richer data types or persistence.
A Redis type that keeps members ordered by a score, so ranking and range queries are fast.
A copy of a cache node that can serve reads and take over if the primary fails.
Saving in-memory data to disk, through snapshots or an append-only log, so it can be restored after a restart.

quiz.q: Why use a shared cache cluster instead of an in-memory cache inside each app server?
options: All servers see the same cached data, the cache survives app deploys, and memory is not duplicated across servers
quiz.explain: A local cache is fastest but each server has its own copy, goes cold on restart and can disagree with others. A shared cache gives one consistent cache for the fleet.

quiz.q: Which Redis data type fits a real-time leaderboard?
quiz.explain: A sorted set keeps members ordered by score, so updating a score and fetching the top N or a player's rank are fast.

quiz.q: Why is Redis often called a cache 'with care' rather than a primary database?
options: Data lives in memory, and depending on persistence settings, recent writes can be lost on a crash
quiz.explain: Persistence is configurable, and asynchronous replication can lose the latest writes on failover. Many teams treat it as rebuildable state.

articles.excerpt: Your app runs on fifty servers. Each one keeps a little in-memory cache of user profiles. A user changes their photo; one server updates its copy, and the other forty-nine keep showing the old one until their entries expire. After every deploy, all fifty caches start empty and hammer the database…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: From One Food Stall to a Restaurant Chain
articles.subtitle: How a web app grows from one server to millions of users: a separate database, a stateless web tier, caches, replicas, a CDN, queues and, last of all, sharding

glossary.definition: The one resource, such as database CPU, disk or network, that runs out first and caps the throughput of the whole system.
Application servers that keep no user data between requests, so any server can handle any request and servers can be added or removed freely.
Making one machine bigger, with more CPU, memory or faster disks, instead of adding more machines.
Adding more machines that share the work, which needs a way to spread requests and data across them.
A copy of the database that receives the primary's changes and serves read queries, taking read load off the primary.
The delay between a write landing on the primary and appearing on a replica, during which the replica returns old data.
Splitting one dataset across several independent databases by a key, so each holds and serves only part of the data.

quiz.q: You add a load balancer and three web servers, but users keep getting logged out. What is the most likely cause?
options: Sessions are stored in each web server's memory, so a request routed to another server has no session
The CDN is caching login pages
quiz.explain: Horizontal scaling needs a stateless web tier. Move sessions into a shared store or a signed token so any server can serve any request.

quiz.q: The database is at high CPU and nine out of ten queries are reads of the same popular rows. What should you try first?
options: Add a cache and read replicas
Rewrite the app in another language
quiz.explain: Repeated reads are exactly what caches and replicas absorb. Sharding is far more complex and mainly needed when writes or data size outgrow one primary.

quiz.q: A user updates their profile, refreshes, and sees the old version. Which stage most likely introduced this?
options: Reading from a replica that has not yet received the write
Moving the database to its own server
Adding a message queue for emails
quiz.explain: Replication lag means a replica can briefly serve old data. Read your own recent writes from the primary to hide it.

articles.excerpt: Your side project goes viral on a Tuesday night. At 9 pm the single server that runs your web app and its database is at 20% CPU. At 10 pm it is at 100%, pages take eight seconds, and the database starts refusing connections. You could buy a bigger server, and for a while that works. Then it stops…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: When the Bakery Reopens
articles.subtitle: Cache stampedes, hot keys, penetration and stale data: the failures caches cause and the standard fixes for each

glossary.definition: Many requests miss the cache for the same key at once and all hit the database together. Also called a thundering herd or dog-piling.
Letting only one request rebuild a missing cache entry while others wait for its result, also called single-flight.
A single cache key receiving a huge share of traffic, overloading the one cache node that owns it.
Repeated requests for keys that do not exist anywhere, so every request misses the cache and hits the database.
Caching the fact that something does not exist, for a short time, so repeated lookups do not reach the database.
Adding a small random amount to each expiry time so many keys do not expire at the same moment.
A token the cache gives one client on a miss, granting it the right to fill that key, used to coalesce rebuilds and reject stale writes.

quiz.q: A popular key expires and 5,000 requests miss at once. Which fix stops all of them reaching the database?
options: Request coalescing: one request rebuilds the value while the others wait for it
quiz.explain: A longer TTL only postpones the stampede. Coalescing ensures one database query per missing key regardless of how many requests arrive.

quiz.q: Attackers request random user ids that do not exist. What protects the database?
options: Negative caching or a Bloom filter in front of the cache
quiz.explain: Non-existent keys always miss. Caching 'not found' briefly, or checking a Bloom filter of valid ids, stops them reaching the database.

quiz.q: Why add random jitter to TTLs when warming a cache with a million keys?
options: So the keys do not all expire at the same moment and cause a mass miss
To improve hit ratio for hot keys only
quiz.explain: Keys loaded together with the same TTL expire together. Jitter spreads their expiry over time.

articles.excerpt: Your product page is served from a cache with a 99% hit ratio, and the database is relaxed at 2% CPU. Then, at exactly 12:00:00, the cached entry for the homepage's top product expires. In the next 50 milliseconds, 4,000 requests miss, and all 4,000 run the same expensive query. The database goes…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: The Dry Cleaner's Ticket
articles.subtitle: Accept work fast and finish it later: job ids, worker pools, retries with backoff, dead letter queues, and telling the client when the job is done

glossary.definition: A unit of work recorded now and executed later by a worker, outside the request that created it.
A unique identifier returned to the client when a job is accepted, used to check its status or match a later callback.
A group of processes that pull jobs from a queue and run them, sized to the arrival rate and job duration.
How long a message stays hidden from other workers after one worker takes it; if it is not acknowledged in time, it becomes available again.
Waiting longer after each failed attempt, typically doubling the delay, often with random jitter so retries do not arrive in waves.
A separate queue that receives jobs which failed too many times, so they stop blocking work and can be inspected or replayed.
An HTTP request your server sends to a URL the client registered, to tell it that something, such as a job finishing, has happened.

quiz.q: A user uploads a video that takes three minutes to process. What should the upload API return?
options: Wait three minutes and return the result
202 Accepted with a job id, then let the client poll or receive a callback
quiz.explain: Accept fast, process later. The job id is the ticket the client uses to find out when the work is done.

quiz.q: A worker crashes halfway through a job. How does a work queue make sure the job is not lost?
options: It cannot; the job is gone
The job was never acknowledged, so after the visibility timeout it becomes available to another worker
quiz.explain: Workers acknowledge only after finishing. An unacknowledged message reappears, which is why jobs must also be safe to run twice.

quiz.q: A job fails every time because of a bug in its input. What should happen after a few retries?
options: Move it to a dead letter queue and alert someone
quiz.explain: Retrying a poison job forever wastes capacity and can block others. A dead letter queue sets it aside for inspection and later replay.

articles.excerpt: You click "Export my data" and the page spins. Ten seconds. Thirty. At sixty seconds the load balancer gives up and shows an error, even though the server is still happily building your file. You click again, and now two exports are running. Multiply that by every user on a busy morning and the web…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Design a URL Shortener
articles.subtitle: The classic warm-up case study done properly: key generation, a read-heavy redirect path, caching, analytics and failure handling

glossary.definition: The few characters after the domain in a short link, such as aB3xY9k in sho.rt/aB3xY9k, that identify the long URL.
Writing numbers with 62 symbols (0-9, a-z, A-Z), so a 7-character code can represent about 3.5 trillion values.
A component that hands out unique short codes, often by assigning blocks of numeric ids to each application server.
HTTP status codes for redirects: 301 means moved permanently and browsers may cache it; 302 means temporary, so every click reaches the server.
Two different long URLs being assigned the same short code.
A workload where reads vastly outnumber writes, which makes caching extremely effective.

quiz.q: Why is a counter encoded in Base62 a popular way to generate codes?
options: Every id is unique by construction, so there are no collisions to check, and 7 characters cover trillions of ids
It hides the number of links
quiz.explain: A unique counter guarantees unique codes. Base62 keeps them short. Predictability is the downside, which can be addressed by shuffling or using ranges.

quiz.q: Why might a shortener with click analytics choose 302 over 301?
options: With 301, browsers may cache the redirect and skip the server on later clicks, so those clicks are never counted
quiz.explain: A permanent redirect can be cached by the browser. A temporary one sends every click through the service, where it can be counted.

quiz.q: What is the main reason caching works so well here?
options: The workload is read-heavy and popular links are requested over and over
quiz.explain: With about 100 reads per write and skewed popularity, a cache of hot links absorbs most redirects.

articles.excerpt: A marketing team pastes a 300-character link into a campaign and gets back sho.rt/aB3xY9k. It looks like a trivial service: store a mapping, redirect on click. Then the link goes viral, receives millions of clicks an hour, and must keep working for years. The URL shortener is the most common…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Design a Rate Limiter
articles.subtitle: Protecting an API from floods: choosing an algorithm, where to enforce it, keeping counts consistent across servers, and failing safely

glossary.definition: A component that caps how many requests a client may make in a time period and rejects or delays the rest.
What a limit is counted against, such as a user id, an API key, an IP address, or a combination with an endpoint.
Counting requests per calendar window, such as per minute, and resetting the count when the window changes.
Counting requests over the last N seconds at every moment, which avoids bursts at window boundaries.
When the limiter itself is broken, allowing requests through rather than blocking everyone.
An operation that completes as one indivisible step, so concurrent requests cannot interleave and corrupt the count.

quiz.q: What is the problem with a fixed window limit of 100 per minute?
options: A client can send 100 requests at 12:00:59 and 100 more at 12:01:00, getting 200 in two seconds
quiz.explain: Resetting at window boundaries allows double bursts across the edge. Sliding windows and token buckets avoid this.

quiz.q: Why must the check-and-increment be atomic in a shared store like Redis?
options: Two servers could both read 99, both allow the request, and both write 100, letting the client exceed the limit
quiz.explain: Without atomicity, concurrent requests race. INCR, Lua scripts or transactions make the check and update a single step.

quiz.q: Should a payment API's rate limiter fail open or closed if Redis is down?
options: It depends: many APIs fail open to stay available, but abuse-sensitive endpoints such as login may fail closed or fall back to local limits
quiz.explain: Failing open keeps service available but drops protection; failing closed protects but blocks everyone. Choose per endpoint, often with a local fallback.

articles.excerpt: A public API serves 50,000 developers. One of them deploys a script with a bug and starts sending 20,000 requests per second. Within minutes, database connections are exhausted, latencies spike for everyone, and the on-call engineer's phone starts ringing. A rate limiter would have rejected that…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Design a Unique ID Generator
articles.subtitle: From auto-increment to UUIDs to Snowflake: generating billions of unique, roughly time-ordered ids without a bottleneck

glossary.definition: A database feature that assigns the next integer to each new row. Simple, but tied to one database.
A 128-bit universally unique identifier. Version 4 UUIDs are mostly random; version 7 UUIDs start with a timestamp so they sort by time.
A 64-bit id made of a timestamp, a machine id and a per-millisecond sequence number, popularised by Twitter.
The starting moment from which a timestamp counts, such as a custom date chosen when the system was built.
A counter that distinguishes ids created by the same machine in the same millisecond.
Differences between machines' clocks, or a clock jumping backwards, which can break time-based id schemes.

quiz.q: In a Snowflake layout with 12 sequence bits, how many ids can one machine create per millisecond?
quiz.explain: 12 bits give 2^12 = 4,096 distinct sequence numbers per millisecond before the machine must wait for the next millisecond.

quiz.q: Why are random UUID v4 primary keys sometimes slow in databases?
options: Random keys insert into random places in a B-tree index, causing page splits and poor cache locality
quiz.explain: Time-ordered ids append near the end of the index; random ids scatter writes across the whole index.

quiz.q: What must a Snowflake generator do if its clock moves backwards?
options: Wait until the clock passes the last timestamp used, or refuse to generate, to avoid duplicates
Reset the sequence to zero and continue
quiz.explain: Reusing an old timestamp with a reset sequence could reproduce ids already issued, so the generator must not go backwards.

articles.excerpt: Every tweet, order, message and payment needs an id. In a small app, the database's auto-increment column hands out 1, 2, 3 and nobody thinks about it. At thousands of writes per second across many database shards and data centres, that single counter becomes a bottleneck, a single point of…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Design a Chat System
articles.subtitle: One-to-one and group messaging with WebSocket gateways, ordered message storage, delivery receipts, presence and offline delivery

glossary.definition: A server that holds long-lived WebSocket connections to clients and relays messages between them and backend services.
A fast store mapping each online user (and device) to the gateway server holding their connection.
Delivering one message to many recipients, such as every member of a group.
An acknowledgement that a message reached the recipient's device (delivered) or was opened (read).
Whether a user is currently online, and when they were last seen.
The id of the last message a device has received in a conversation, used to fetch anything it missed.
A client-generated id attached to a message so that retries do not create duplicates.

quiz.q: Bob is online, connected to gateway G7. How does the chat service find where to push Alice's message?
options: Look up Bob in the session registry, which maps users to gateways
quiz.explain: The registry, usually an in-memory store, says which gateway holds Bob's connection, so the message is routed straight there.

quiz.q: Why does each message carry a client-generated id?
options: So a resend after a timeout is recognised as a duplicate instead of stored twice
quiz.explain: Networks drop acknowledgements. The id acts as an idempotency key, making retries safe.

quiz.q: How should messages be ordered within one conversation?
options: By a per-conversation sequence number or time-ordered id assigned by the server
quiz.explain: Device clocks disagree. A server-assigned, per-conversation increasing id gives every device the same order.

Behind those ticks, your message travelled over a connection your phone kept open, through a server that knew which machine your friend's phone was connected to, into durable storage, onto their screen, and back as a receipt. articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Design a News Feed
articles.subtitle: Fan-out on write vs fan-out on read, the celebrity problem and the hybrid fix, ranking, and stable pagination with cursors

glossary.definition: Delivering a new post into every follower's stored feed when it is published, so reading a feed is a single lookup. Also called push.
Building a feed when the user opens it by fetching and merging recent posts from everyone they follow. Also called pull.
The cost explosion when an account with a huge number of followers posts and fan-out on write must update millions of feeds.
Pushing posts from ordinary accounts to followers' feeds while pulling posts from very large accounts at read time and merging them.
Turning a list of post ids into full posts by fetching their text, author, media links and counts, usually in one batched lookup.
Fetching the next page as the items after a position marker, such as the last post id seen, instead of skipping a numeric offset.
The stored set of follow relationships: who follows whom, kept in both directions for fast lookups.

quiz.q: An account with 50 million followers posts. Why is pure fan-out on write a problem?
options: One post becomes 50 million feed writes, delaying delivery and swamping the fan-out workers
quiz.explain: Write fan-out cost grows with follower count. For huge accounts, pulling their posts at read time is far cheaper.

quiz.q: Why does offset pagination show duplicate posts in a feed?
options: New posts arrive at the top between page requests, shifting every item down, so the next offset repeats items already seen
quiz.explain: A cursor anchors the next page to the last item seen, so new arrivals at the top do not shift it.

quiz.q: In a hybrid design, how does a user's feed include a celebrity's post?
options: The celebrity's post is pushed to every follower
At read time, recent posts from the few celebrities the user follows are fetched and merged with the precomputed feed
quiz.explain: Ordinary posts are pushed in advance; celebrity posts are pulled on demand and merged, which costs a handful of lookups per read.

articles.excerpt: You open the app on the train and, in under a second, a scroll of posts from hundreds of friends, pages and creators appears, already ordered. Somewhere a server had to decide which of thousands of recent posts you see first. Then a cricketer with tens of millions of followers posts a photo, and…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Design a Notification System
articles.subtitle: Push, SMS and email at scale: templates, user preferences, per-channel queues, retries, deduplication and rate limits

glossary.definition: A route for reaching a user: mobile push, SMS, email or in-app.
The external service that actually delivers on a channel, such as Apple Push Notification service, Firebase Cloud Messaging, an SMS gateway or an email service.
An identifier issued by a push provider for one app install on one device, needed to send it a push notification.
A stored message pattern with placeholders, such as 'Your order {order_id} has shipped', rendered per user and language.
An id identifying one logical notification, used to drop repeats caused by retries or duplicate events.
A queue where messages go after failing too many times, so they can be inspected without blocking the main flow.

quiz.q: Why does each channel (push, SMS, email) get its own queue and workers?
options: So a slow or failing provider on one channel cannot block delivery on the others, and each can scale and rate-limit separately
quiz.explain: If the SMS gateway slows down, push and email keep flowing. Isolation is the main reason.

quiz.q: An order service retries a 'shipped' event after a timeout. How do you stop the user getting two pushes?
options: Attach a deduplication key such as order id plus event type, and skip sends whose key was already processed
Delay all notifications by an hour
quiz.explain: At-least-once delivery means duplicates will happen. A dedup key checked before sending makes the send idempotent.

quiz.q: Where should user notification preferences (opted out of marketing SMS, quiet hours) be checked?
options: In the notification service before enqueuing, so every sender obeys them
quiz.explain: Centralising the check means no team can accidentally bypass a user's opt-out or quiet hours.

articles.excerpt: Your food is out for delivery. Your bank flags a payment. Your flight gate changed. A friend commented on your photo. Each of these reaches you as a buzz on your phone, an SMS or an email, sent by a system most users never think about until it misfires: the same alert three times, a promotional SMS…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Design Search Autocomplete
articles.subtitle: Typeahead suggestions in milliseconds: a trie with precomputed top-k lists, built offline from search logs and served from memory

glossary.definition: Suggestions shown while the user is still typing, ranked so the most likely completions appear first.
A tree where each edge is a character, so every path from the root spells a prefix and all words sharing a prefix share a subtree.
The k best completions for a prefix, stored precomputed at that prefix's trie node so a lookup needs no search.
A batch job that periodically counts queries from logs and rebuilds the suggestion data, separate from the request path.
Waiting a short pause after the last keystroke before sending a request, so fast typists do not trigger one request per letter.
Weighting recent searches more than old ones, so trending queries rise and stale ones fade.

quiz.q: Why store a precomputed top-k list at each trie node?
options: So answering a prefix is one lookup instead of walking the whole subtree and sorting at query time
quiz.explain: A short prefix like 'a' has millions of completions below it. Precomputing the best k moves that work to the offline build.

quiz.q: Where should query counting and trie building happen?
options: In the request path on every keystroke
In an offline or streaming aggregation job that publishes a new snapshot periodically
quiz.explain: Updating ranks on every keystroke would make reads contend with writes. Building snapshots separately keeps reads fast and simple.

quiz.q: What does debouncing on the client achieve?
options: Fewer requests, because a request is sent only after the user pauses briefly
quiz.explain: Users type several characters per second. Waiting a short pause skips intermediate prefixes the user has already typed past.

articles.excerpt: You type "how to m" and, before your finger reaches the next key, a list appears: "how to make pancakes", "how to meditate", "how to make money online". The suggestions changed with each letter, they reflect what millions of other people are searching for, and they arrived faster than you can type.…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Design a Video Streaming Platform
articles.subtitle: A YouTube-style system: resumable uploads, a parallel transcoding pipeline, adaptive bitrate playback, CDN delivery and view counting

glossary.definition: Converting a video from its uploaded format into other formats, resolutions and bitrates suitable for playback on different devices and networks.
One encoded version of a video at a particular resolution and bitrate, such as 720p at 3 Mbps.
A short chunk of a rendition, a few seconds long, stored as its own file so players can download video piece by piece.
A small playlist file listing the available renditions and the URLs of their segments, used by the player to choose what to fetch.
Playback where the player switches between renditions segment by segment, based on measured bandwidth and buffer level.
A set of tasks with dependencies and no cycles, used to describe which processing steps must finish before others start.

quiz.q: Why is each rendition split into short segments?
options: So the player can switch quality between segments, start playing quickly, and let CDNs cache small files
To hide the video from users
quiz.explain: Segments are the unit of adaptation and caching: the player picks a rendition per segment, and every segment is an ordinary cacheable file.

quiz.q: Average concurrent viewers are 1.7 million at 3 Mbps each. Roughly what egress bandwidth is that, and who should serve it?
options: About 5 Tbps, mostly from CDN edge caches
quiz.explain: 1.7 × 10^6 × 3 × 10^6 bits per second ≈ 5 × 10^12 bits per second. Only a CDN close to viewers can serve that economically.

quiz.q: Why is the view count updated asynchronously instead of with one database write per view?
options: Thousands of views per second on popular videos would create hot rows; aggregating events in a stream and writing periodic totals is far cheaper
quiz.explain: Batching counts trades a few seconds of delay for orders of magnitude fewer writes.

Halfway through, your train enters a tunnel and the picture turns a little blurry instead of freezing, then sharpens again when the signal returns. Meanwhile, somewhere, a creator just uploaded a 4K video from a phone, and within minutes it…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Design a Ride-Sharing App
articles.subtitle: An Uber-style system: streaming driver locations, a geospatial index, matching riders to drivers, a trip state machine and surge pricing

glossary.definition: A data structure that answers 'which items are near this point?' quickly, such as geohash cells, quadtrees, S2 or H3.
The component that ingests frequent driver location updates and keeps the latest position of each driver in memory.
Choosing which available driver to offer a ride request to, based on distance, estimated arrival time and other factors.
The fixed set of states a trip moves through, such as requested, matched, driver arriving, in progress, completed or cancelled, with allowed transitions between them.
Estimated time of arrival, computed from the road network and traffic, not from straight-line distance.
Temporarily raising prices in an area where ride requests greatly exceed available drivers.
A geographic cell with far more drivers or requests than average, such as an airport or stadium, which overloads whoever owns it.

quiz.q: 1 million active drivers each send a location every 4 seconds. How many location writes per second is that?
quiz.explain: 1,000,000 / 4 = 250,000 updates per second, which is why latest locations live in memory rather than in a disk-based database row per update.

quiz.q: Why must a driver be 'locked' when a ride is offered to them?
options: So two concurrent ride requests cannot both be assigned the same driver
quiz.explain: Matching runs concurrently. An atomic reservation, with a timeout if the driver does not accept, prevents double booking.

quiz.q: Why is straight-line distance a poor way to rank nearby drivers?
options: It is too slow to compute
Roads, one-way streets, rivers and traffic make a driver 500 m away possibly 10 minutes away
quiz.explain: The geospatial index finds candidates by distance; ranking uses road-network ETA.

articles.excerpt: You tap "Request ride". Within seconds, the app shows a car icon heading toward you, a driver's name, and "4 min away". To get there, the system knew where hundreds of thousands of drivers were, to within a few metres, a few seconds ago. It found the handful near you, estimated which could arrive…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Design a Payment System
articles.subtitle: Taking money safely: idempotency keys, a payment state machine, a double-entry ledger, provider webhooks and daily reconciliation

glossary.definition: An external company that connects to card networks and banks and actually moves money, such as a card processor or UPI gateway.
A unique key sent with a payment request so that retries of the same request return the original result instead of charging again.
An append-only record where every transaction is written as debits and credits across accounts that sum to zero, so money is never created or lost.
An HTTP callback from the provider to your system announcing an event, such as a payment succeeding or failing.
Comparing your ledger against the provider's and the bank's settlement reports to find and fix any mismatch.
The allowed statuses of a payment, such as CREATED, PENDING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, REFUNDED, and the transitions between them.

quiz.q: A client times out waiting for 'pay ₹500' and retries. What prevents a double charge?
options: The same idempotency key on both requests, so the server returns the first attempt's result
quiz.explain: The server stores the key with the outcome. A retry with the same key does not create a new charge, and the same key is passed on to the provider.

quiz.q: In a double-entry ledger, what must be true of every transaction's entries?
options: Debits and credits must sum to the same amount, so the total change is zero
quiz.explain: Money moves between accounts but is never created or destroyed. Corrections are new entries, never edits.

quiz.q: Why is daily reconciliation still needed if every step is idempotent?
options: Webhooks can be lost, providers can have bugs, and settlements can differ, so independent records must be compared to catch drift
quiz.explain: Idempotency prevents duplicates you cause. Reconciliation catches discrepancies from everyone else, including the provider and the bank.

articles.excerpt: A customer taps "Pay ₹1,000". Their phone's connection drops for two seconds. The app retries. Did the first attempt go through? If you guess wrong in one direction, the customer is charged twice and posts an angry screenshot. Guess wrong in the other, and the merchant ships goods for free. Now…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: The Promises a Messenger Can Make
articles.subtitle: Consistency models from linearizable to eventual: what each one guarantees about reads and writes on replicated data, with timelines

glossary.definition: A contract describing which values a read may return when data is replicated and accessed concurrently.
Every operation appears to take effect at a single instant between its start and its end, so once a write completes, every later read sees it. Also called strong or atomic consistency.
All clients see operations in one single order that respects each client's own program order, but that order need not match real time.
Operations that are causally related, such as a reply and the message it answers, are seen by everyone in cause-before-effect order; unrelated operations may be seen in different orders.
A session guarantee that a client always sees its own earlier writes.
A session guarantee that once a client has seen a value, it never later sees an older one.
If writes stop, all replicas eventually converge to the same value; until then reads may return stale values.

quiz.q: A's write x = 1 finishes at 10:00:02. B starts a read at 10:00:03 and gets x = 0. Which model does this break?
quiz.explain: Linearizability requires reads that start after a write completes to see it. A sequentially consistent system may still return 0, because B's read can be ordered before A's write.

quiz.q: Carol sees Bob's reply 'Great news!' before Alice's post 'Found my phone' that Bob was replying to. Which model is violated?
quiz.explain: The reply depends on the post, so causal consistency requires everyone to see the post first.

quiz.q: What is the difference between consistency models and transaction isolation levels?
options: Consistency models describe what reads see on replicated data relative to time and other clients; isolation levels describe how concurrent multi-operation transactions interfere
quiz.explain: They answer different questions and are often confused. A system can be serializable but not linearizable, and the other way round.

articles.excerpt: You change your profile picture, refresh, and the old one is back. A friend replies to your comment, but someone else sees the reply before your comment exists. A bank shows a balance that ignores a transfer you made a second ago. None of these is a crash. Each is the system keeping, or not…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Several Cashiers, One Ledger
articles.subtitle: Transaction isolation levels and the anomalies they allow: dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates and write skew

glossary.definition: A group of reads and writes that the database treats as one unit: all of it commits or none of it does.
The degree to which concurrent transactions are shielded from each other's intermediate and committed changes.
A result that could not happen if transactions ran one at a time, caused by their interleaving.
Each transaction reads from a consistent snapshot of the database taken when it started, and a write conflicts if another transaction committed a change to the same row first.
The strongest standard level: the outcome equals some order of running the transactions one after another.
Two transactions read overlapping data, each makes a decision based on it, and they write different rows, together breaking a rule that each alone respected.
A row that appears in, or disappears from, the result of the same search query when it is repeated inside one transaction, because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows.

quiz.q: Under read committed, T1 reads a balance of 100, T2 commits a change to 80, and T1 reads again. What does T1 see?
quiz.explain: Read committed only forbids seeing uncommitted data. Each statement sees the latest committed value, so the second read returns 80: a non-repeatable read.

quiz.q: Two on-call doctors each check 'at least one other doctor is on call', then each takes themselves off call, in concurrent transactions. Which level prevents both from succeeding?
quiz.explain: This is write skew: they update different rows, so snapshot isolation sees no write conflict. Only serializable detects that the combined outcome matches no serial order.

quiz.q: What is the default isolation level in PostgreSQL?
quiz.explain: PostgreSQL defaults to read committed. Assuming serializable by default is a common and costly mistake.

A hospital rota allows every doctor to go off call because each one checked that "someone else is still on". A report adds up account balances while transfers run and shows money that never existed. Every…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Everyone Says I Do, or Nobody Is Married
articles.subtitle: Two-phase commit: how a coordinator makes several databases commit together, why it blocks when the coordinator dies, and when to use it

glossary.definition: A transaction that changes data on more than one database or service and must still be all-or-nothing.
The process that runs two-phase commit: it asks every participant to prepare, then tells them all to commit or abort.
A database or resource manager taking part in the distributed transaction; it votes and then obeys the coordinator's decision.
The first phase: each participant makes its changes durable but not visible, keeps its locks, and promises it can commit if told to.
A prepared participant that has not yet heard the decision. It may neither commit nor abort on its own, so it holds its locks and waits.
The guarantee that all participants commit or all abort, never a mix.

quiz.q: Participant A votes yes and participant B votes no. What does the coordinator decide?
options: Wait for B to change its vote
quiz.explain: A single no vote means the transaction cannot commit everywhere, so the only atomic outcome is to abort everywhere.

quiz.q: Why can a participant that voted yes not simply abort after a long timeout?
options: The coordinator may already have decided commit and told others, so aborting could leave some committed and some not
quiz.explain: After voting yes, the participant gave up its right to decide alone. Only the coordinator's decision, or another participant that knows it, can resolve the transaction.

quiz.q: What must the coordinator do before sending any commit messages?
options: Write the commit decision durably to its own log
quiz.explain: If it crashes after sending some commits, it must remember the decision on restart to finish the job consistently.

articles.excerpt: A bank moves ₹5,000 from an account stored in database A to an account stored in database B. Database A subtracts the money and commits. A moment later, database B's disk fills up and its update fails. The money has left one account and arrived nowhere. Within one database, a transaction would have…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Book the Trip, Cancel the Hotel
articles.subtitle: Sagas: long business transactions as a chain of local commits with compensating actions, coordinated by events or an orchestrator

glossary.definition: A sequence of local transactions, each in one service, where every step has a compensating action that semantically undoes it if a later step fails.
A new transaction that reverses the business effect of an earlier committed step, such as a refund for a charge.
A saga style where each service reacts to events from the previous step and publishes its own, with no central controller.
A saga style where a central orchestrator tells each service what to do next and tracks the saga's state.
The step after which the saga is committed to finishing; steps after it must be retried until they succeed rather than compensated.
An application-level marker, such as an order status of PENDING, that tells other requests a record is in the middle of a saga.

quiz.q: In a trip-booking saga, the flight booking fails after the hotel was booked. What happens?
options: The database rolls back the hotel automatically
The saga runs the hotel's compensating action, cancelling the reservation
quiz.explain: Each step committed locally, so there is nothing to roll back. The saga issues a new transaction, the cancellation, to undo the business effect.

quiz.q: Why must saga steps and compensations be idempotent?
options: Messages may be delivered more than once, and retrying a step or compensation must not charge or refund twice
So they can run in parallel
quiz.explain: Sagas rely on at-least-once messaging and retries. Idempotency makes duplicates harmless.

quiz.q: What isolation do sagas give by default?
options: None between steps: other requests can see intermediate states, so designs use semantic locks or ordering to limit anomalies
quiz.explain: Each step commits on its own, so the world can observe a half-finished saga. Countermeasures are part of the design.

Each owns its own database. If Inventory finds the last unit was sold a second ago, the customer has already been charged. You cannot roll…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: Write the Letter and the Envelope Together
articles.subtitle: The dual-write problem, the transactional outbox, and change data capture: publishing events that never disagree with your database

glossary.definition: Writing the same change to two systems, such as a database and a message broker, in separate operations that can succeed or fail independently.
A table in the service's own database where events are inserted in the same transaction as the business change, to be published later.
A process that reads unpublished rows from the outbox and publishes them to the broker, marking them done afterwards.
Reading a database's own change log, such as its write-ahead log or binlog, and turning each committed change into an event.
A guarantee that every message is delivered one or more times, never zero, so consumers must tolerate duplicates.
A consumer that records processed message ids, or makes its effect naturally repeatable, so duplicates have no extra effect.

quiz.q: A service commits an order to its database and then crashes before publishing OrderCreated. What is the result without an outbox?
options: The order exists but downstream services never hear about it
quiz.explain: This is the dual-write problem. The database and the broker disagree, and nothing will repair it.

quiz.q: Why does the outbox pattern give at-least-once, not exactly-once, publishing?
options: The relay may publish a row and crash before marking it published, so it publishes it again after restart
quiz.explain: Publishing and marking are two steps. The safe failure is a duplicate, which idempotent consumers absorb.

quiz.q: What does change data capture read?
options: The database's own replication or write-ahead log of committed changes
quiz.explain: CDC tails the log the database already writes for durability and replication, so it sees exactly the committed changes in commit order.

articles.excerpt: An order service saves a new order and then publishes "OrderCreated" to a message broker so that payments, email and analytics can react. It works in every test. Then, in production, the broker is briefly unreachable during a deploy: orders are saved, but their events never go out. Customers are…

articles.subject: system-design
articles.title: A Cheque the Bank Cashes Only Once
articles.subtitle: At-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once: why networks cannot deliver exactly once, and how deduplication, idempotency and transactions give the same effect

glossary.definition: Each message is processed zero or one times: send without retrying, so losses are possible but duplicates are not.
Each message is processed one or more times: retry until acknowledged, so nothing is lost but duplicates are possible.
The observable effect of each message happens once, even though the message itself may be delivered more than once.
Recording the ids of messages already processed and skipping repeats.
An operation whose effect is the same whether it runs once or many times, such as 'set balance to 500' or 'insert if this id is absent'.
A consumer's position in a log-based queue: the index of the next message it will read in a partition.

quiz.q: A consumer processes a message, then crashes before acknowledging it. Under at-least-once delivery, what happens?
options: The message is redelivered and processed again
quiz.explain: No acknowledgement means the broker assumes failure and redelivers. Without deduplication, the effect happens twice.

quiz.q: Which change makes 'add ₹100 to the balance' safe to repeat?
options: Record the message id in the same transaction and skip ids already recorded
quiz.explain: Storing the id atomically with the effect turns a non-idempotent update into an idempotent one.

quiz.q: What do Kafka transactions make atomic in a read-process-write pipeline?
options: The output records and the consumer's offset commit, so either both happen or neither does
quiz.explain: Writing outputs and advancing the input offset in one transaction means a crash cannot produce outputs without moving the offset, or the reverse. Effects outside Kafka are not covered.

The payment service waits, hears nothing, and does the only sensible thing: it sends again. Now the customer has ₹200. Or it does not resend, and if the…
